MOON-STRUCK. The young Moon ,lee in the old Moon's arms— You can see it as plain as may be; Venus has gone, with all her charms, But Jupiter stares at the baby. The old Moon rocks in the clear blue skies— She is rocking an hour-old baby; The stars a-winking with all their eyes, And wonder whatever it may ba, In a month that baby a babe will hold, And croon to the young its A B; For a moon's whole life is but four weeks old. And then 'ti3 again a baby. F. J. O.

CHRISTIANTIR the NATUALL 11a-tacit-wt.—The eternal life which Christianity reveals, a life of perfect union and communion with God, in which the finite spirit rises above the power of change and decay and death, because it is capable of participating in the life of God—this is a doe. trine with respect to man's dectiny which explains him to himself, gives meaning and end to the infinite capabilities of man's being, and so is nat len but Immeasurably more true to reason, more consistent with the constitution of his nature, than that notion of the "immortality of the soul," which the light of nature is supposed to yield, and to which natural religion lays claim. In one word, the doctrines of Christianity have a power surpa.sing all other disclosures of truth, all ideas gathered from nature, or life, or books, or gifted teachers, to enlighten, and convince the spirit of man, to wake the loftiest aspirations and kind'e the most impas- sioned affection, and to dominate our whole inward being and life; and just because it has this surpassing power over man's nature, Christianity proves itself to be for him, in the deepest significance of the words, a system of nalural Caird, in" Good Words."

SHAESPEEE IN THE STUDY AND ON THE STateE.—What arts has the reader of Shakspere to set against this perpetual stimulus of the actor's mental powers by the practice of his calling? Granted that it in impossible to realise a Shakspere character—the actor may yet suggest beauties not evolved in the study, or clear away doubts which strike the reader as insurmountable. With his mind ata white heat—when new sparks of frenzy—new ideas and illustrations are struck from it by the intellectual collisions with his fellow-players—has the actor no special advantage over a student of the finest Perception? An eloquent look, a speaking gesture, or a suggestive pause, may be worth an infinity of foot-notes. One of the greatest charms to the spectator is to watch the by-play of the actor, to see the poison of lago's devilry stealing into Othello's soul, to observe the gradations of i passion, the transition of undoubted love into the slow agony of misgiving, and the frenzy of despair. How is the reader to realise in his mind's eye what is actually depicted on the actor's face? Can he "in a fiction, in a dream of passion, force his soul so to his own conceit, that from her working" he can evolve all the features of a fine stage picture? see the great Caesar, perturbed by presentiments of doono,or watch the eoming of the tragedy in the looks of Brutus, Cassius, and Casca ? Coleridge said that seeing Edmund Kean act was "like reading Shakspere by flashes of lightning." Vol- taire was amazed at the pathos of one of his own scenes, re- vealed to him by the voiee of Le Kahn; "and it is no ex- aggeration," as Sir Theodore Martin says," to suppose that Shakspere might have felt in the same way had he heard the ' Prithee undo this button !' of Garrik in 'Lear,' or the Fool! fool! fool!' of Edmund Kean's Othello.'" It was this same Edmund Kean whose frenzied aony as "Othello threw Byron into a swoon. What the Zombies, Mrs. Sid- dons, and Mies O'Neil, what Kean, Macreadv, and other players scarcely less eminent, did to illuminate Shakspere, we have learned from the records of the most competent critice.—Henry Irving, in "Good Words." In 1882 5 bushels of barley will do the business. In 1816 it re- quired one bushel of wheat to purchase one yard of calico. In 1882 one bushel of wheat will purchase 35 yards of a better article. A WRONG SYSTEM OF PRUNING.—A great mistake that 'is frequently made in pruning, and not by amateurs alone lacteal, RIM3V amateurs are expert pruners—but by jobbing gardeners who have not always had the best training in work of this nature. The error is this. When a tree is growing strongly, evenduxuriantly, it is thought necessary to cut it well beck, or, in gardening parlance, to "give it the knife freely," while a tree that has made little growth is not thought to need pruning. The tree process to follow is to erane the weakly tree closely, and to allow the strong tree all the extension growth possible, and also to shortee its 1 roots. If the branches of a luxuriant tree are cat closely back annually, and the roots are not disturbed, nothing but still stronger growths can follow, and if the practice is con- tinued for twenty years the tree will never bear fruit freely. , The roots should either be shortened or the branches let ' alone, save by the removal entirely of a number of them, to prevent overcrowding. In all the Prince owns 105 cows and heifers and 29 bells, and these are kept in two herds, which are located upon two dis- tinct farms, at Babingley and at Wolferton, two miles apart. The Babingley portion, which consists of 38 cows and heifers and 13 bulls, has been formed by selection from the herds belonging to the Duke of Manchester, the Earle of Dunmore, Ferersham, and Bective, Lord Fitzhardinge, Colonel Kings- cote, and Messrs. In this herd the bulls used have been Lord Feversharn's Baron Rydale (27813), the winner of the second prize at the Liverpool show of the Royal Agricul- tural Seciety in 1877, and purchased by his Royal Highness himself at Dunconabe Park in the same year, and three others—Musical Oxford (42037), Babingley Duke (42630), and Duke of Norfolk (44669). The article on potato disease is carefully illustrated, and the nature of the disease is minutely explained. The concluding paragraph is as follows ;—" The last point to which we shell briefly advert is as to the possibility of avoiding disease. Oar ad- vice is to plant the best and soundest seed that can he got, and of such varieties as are known and guaranteed to be less liable to disease than others. To purchase the seed from relieble firm. To give the plants plenty of room, for if they are planted too close together, they are eterteln to be weak and sickly in the haulm. It Is the tame with plants as with individuals; some are netetibusly liable to take certain ailments, whilst others can almost invariably throw them off. Clan, strong, he ‘lthy, and well-fed animals and plants_ e less liable to disease than dirty, weak, sickly, and etatved ones." LOSSES BY THE INJUDICIOUS FEEDING OF COTTON CABE, &c.—Laet week a Lancashire clergyman, who ie also a farmer, called upon me with the information that he had, along with some of his neighbours, lost several calves by feeding cotton ale after they had been taken indoors. Knowing that I was a contributor to the agricultural press, he wished me to issue a note of warning. He appeared sur- prised when I told him that such warnings had been iterated and reiterated during recent years in the agricultural press, and he was constrained to admit that the losses of himself and friends, from the injudicious use of cotton cake this winter, would have much more than paid the Agricultural Gazette subscriptions for more than their lifetime. On this complaint platase allow me to found a few "new year's re- -0 actions." for this clergyman had been bred and reared on a yeoman's estate, and his friends, who had lost calves from a like cause, were practical farmers. First, it would be well If manufacturers or their agents, dealing in cotton cake or other estringent feeders, would warn their customers as to the use and abuse of them. Their neglect to do so will as- suredly ultimately lead to farmers altogether avoiding the use of such, and thus their market will be a bad one; whereas, if purchasers were to be made aware in what quan- tities, and under what conditions, such feeders might be used in safety, a better tratie would result. Cotton cake may be safely given to young stock, in moderate quantities, when at grass or on roots, for then the laxative properties of the grass or roots neutralises the astringent properties of the cotton cake. If the latter, however, be fed to stock in con- junction with other dry food, then its binding nature will assuredly be fatal. Cotton cakes and other so-called artificial feeders, have been brought into use in the endeavour to save feeding milk to calves, and yet they have led us to forget that resource of our forefathers—hay tea—much superior, ranch safer than the new products, and near:y equal to the genuine article.

Doas.—TRAINING FOR THE Gux.—When young dogs are first taken into the field they hunt eagerly, have no idea of taking advantage of the wind, are apt to run with their noses too close to the ground, ond puzzle a long time in places where birds have lately left. If you neglect to give your dog the wind you cannot blame him, even an old one, should he spring the game; and when a young dog runs down the wind (his nose, of course, close to the ground), the sportanaan should call to him by name, accompanying it with hold up. A little practice of this sort will induce him to throw up his head, and he will quickly perceive the ad- vantage of carrying his head high, as well as getting the wind in his favour; but if he should not very soon carry a good head, delay not to put the puzzle peg en him—an in- strument so well known, I should suppose, as scarcely to Reed description ; it is merely a stick,: projecting about eight or nine inches before the dog's nose, with a broad end hollowed and made to fit his under-jaw; a strap runs through the•extremity of the broad end and buckles just behind the dog's ears, while a small leather thong runs through the animal's mouth, just behind his canine teeth holders. It is laughable enough to see this instrument first upon a young dog, as he will spare no exertion to rid him- , self of so unpleasanti a companion, nor will he think of run- ning with t till fully convinced of the inefficacy of all his ps attempts. Some persons use puzzle pegs with two slicks but jeeting from the nose. They may perha be superior, either way will answer the purpose, and will not fail to make a young dog carry his head well, the length of time for using it depending upon the disposition of the dog. pI von perceive on trial that he carries a good head with- out it lay it aside. Independent of making the dog throw up his head, the puzzle peg is an instrument that should be put upon any or all dogs, when taken out In the spriig, either for exercise or training, where hares are numerous ; for If a doe hare is met with in an advanced ste.ge of gestation, she may be caught and worried, a circum.

stance which the use of the puzzle peg effectually prevents. In the shooting season, too, they are very convenient on dogs that break feather, i.e., tear the birds. More on this subject we shall say next week. Preaeoss.—GonGneo.--This disease is one that affects pouters almost entirely, and even in that breed only such as have well developed crops ; but as these are very suscep- tible to it, they have to be very carefully watched. The old method of care was to pass the bird through the leg of a stocking and hang it up until the food passed off, but, the same result may be attained by placing the bird in a narrow box, padded at one end to support the crop, so as to allow the food to pass into the stomach. Large cropped pouters when allowed to feed their young are very apt to gorge, some doing so invariably; but when this happens from their taking too much water, this may be pressed out of them by gently squeezing the crop until they disgorge it, when they will be right again in a short time. When, how- ever, the crop is so gorged as to contain nearly as much as the weight of the whole bird, it is a very bad sign, and it will then be found that neither the stocking nor box remedy will be of any use, for the stomach has lost It power of ac• tion. The crop may then be cut open, cleaned out, and sewn up again, the inner and outer skins being sewn sepia-. .ately, and for this purpose silk or horse hair should be used, and each stitch tied. In cutting use a sharp knife, and make the incision a perpendicular one. The operation is often successfully performed, but in many cases it is of no use, as the powers of the stomach have become impaired, and as soon as the bird is at liberty it will be speedily gorged again, nothing that is eaten passing into the stomach. From this cease some of the best pouters ever seen have died, and with those best developed in crop it will always be one of their compleinte most to be feared. Besides cut- ting the crop open in bad CARS of gorging, Moore, in his " Culuimberian, or the Pigeon•hoase," published in 1735, seers :—" ()there will tie that part of the crop in which the undigested meat Hee tight round with a string, and let it rot off. This method never fails, though it spoils the shape of the crop." With a pouter considered valuable for stock and past his show days, a curtailment of crop is not any drawback, bat rather ;the reverse. Charcoal capsules are useful for preventing the corruption of the food in the crop of gorged pouters, andicopaibe capsules are used to make them disgorge, and are very effective sometimes. A pouter should be attended to on showing the least signs of becom• lug gorged, as delay is dangerous. There is another form of gorging to which all pigeons are at times subject, which is caused by an obstruction at the lower part of the croo. It is known by the swelling of the same, and when taken hold of the food can be felt in it. Tnis is not difficult of cure, and the operation is one that need not give any pigeon- keeper trouble or anxiety. The crop must be cut as already described, and the food emptied, taking care to see that the dcwn passage is cleared. Then the incision must be stitched up, and the bird fad on smell quantities of soft food, but no water for a few days, when it can gradually be allowed to resume its ordinary diet. CAGE BIRDS —THE SONG CANARY.—The song canary ia its perfection is undoubtedly a creation of the Germens,and it has been developed by generations of careful breeding and training, the best specimens coming from the Hartz Mona- Wm. Of late years the quality of the German songsters worted !rt nk,and has fallen off very consider- -. Jay, and it is netwo more diflicali ii6W tirafe rt ouee WAS to obtain a really drat-class bird. At one time the demand for the birds was chiefly in England. RUSSIA, and Holland, but recently an enormous demand has sprung up in America, much greater than all the other countries combined. Tne result of the keea competition for the best birds naturally following upon this demand, has been that the great care In breeding and training has been relaxed, and thus we do not the see- - " T fsT qustity or songsters. au s,nanany tt,o htgner prices can be got for the very beet birds than will be realised it they are sent to England, which, of course, has the effect of keeping them at home, and only the second or third rate birds come over here. In the town of Si. Andreasberg there are said to be about four hundred families who breed song canaries, and the money valise of the trade was estimated some rawly-etre ago at about £9,000 per annum. Only a portion of the stock bred levee any reputation for Equalities valued by the connoisseur, and fe w people h ve any idea of the amount of education a train•?,d German song canary has gone through. Tae object is to get certain combinations of trills or modulated melody, with deep flute like tones; and ex- cellence consists, not in loudness or length of song, or even quality of mere voice, so mach as in a continuous repetition of certain varied strains. Some birds have a compass of four octaves and will execute various shake e in the must perfect style ; but it is always desired that a bird, whatever strains it has mastered—and a few good songeters have less than three or foer—should and its songs by a succession of soft, flute like, descending tones. Toe most prized melodies are seldom learnt by a young bird in less then six months, and only by quiet birds; the more excitable ones bursting into those detailed, powerful notes which are held to impair the song. Of coarse it requires a vary correct ear and great ex- perience to select the beat performers. div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY 13, 1883.

what later he quarrelled with Cromwell, and engaged him- self in plots, for which he was imprisoned. Fortunately, perhaps, for his family, he died just before the Restoration, but his father lived on till 1673. The elder grandson of the I first Earl, dying without issue, was succeeded by his son, and he by his son, who contracted another advantageous marriage with the daughter and heiress of Booth, the last Earl of Warrington. The Booths had acquired fortune very much in the same iway as the Greys. They were an old Lancashire family, one of whose younger sons had married a Cheshire heiress named Venables. Dunham Massey and other lands in Che- shire, spoils of the Norman Conquest, had passed by suc- cessive marriages to the family of Venables, and: thence in the same manner to the Booths. In the reign of Henry VIII. Sir William Booth married the heiress of the Asshe- tons, the ancient possessors of the valuable manor of Ash- ton-under-Lyne, which is still held by his descendants, During the Civil War, Sir George Booth was a leading member of the Presbyterian party, and gave his support to the Parliament. Towards the close of the Commonwealth period he appeared in arms for Charles 11., but was defeated after a sharp encounter by Lambert, and made his escape disguised as a woman. The following year he acted as one of the deputation to invite Charles back, and received as his reward from the King the title of Lord Delamere, and from the Parliament £lO,OOO. Lord Delamere was accused in the reign of James H. of treasonable correspondence with Mon- mouth, but was acquitted. At the coming of the Prince of Orange he raised Cheshire for William, and gained two steps in the peerage, being 'created Earl of Warrington. He was also awarded a pension of £2,000 a year, which, strange to say, was not paid. At the death of George Booth, second Earl of Warrington, the estates passed to the Earl of Stam- ford, who had married his daughter, and their son and his descendants have since held both titles. -

It will be seen that, though the Greys are an old family, the greater part of their estates are still older, that is, that they have descended by inheritance in unbroken succession from Norman times. The Asshetons, of Ashton-under- Lyne, the Venables an Fittons of Dunham Massey, the Ferrers of Groby, the Lowes of Enville, all of whom were ancient houses, have one by one been merged into the house of Grey. What has not been acquired in this manner has been acquired almost entirely by Royal or Parliamentary grants. Necessarily the wealth of this house has been im- mensely increased by the industry and enterprise of the people of Cheshire and Lancashire. I have given the gross rental of the estates of the Earl of Stamford and Warrington, but I have little doubt that it conveys but an inadequate idea of his wealth. Certainly it gives us no information as to his prospective wealth, seeing that our system of leases in the manufacturing towns secures not only to the landlord a considerable share of the present pro- fits of industry, but is the future an exaction of yet larger sums from those whose capital and labour have, without exertion on his part, given to his lands a value of which his ancestors never dreamed.

div.head: "OUR OLD NOBILIM
div.p: "OUR OLD NOBILIM

[Published by Mr. E. J. Kibbletehite, 81, Tavistock-street London, fr.c., and reprinted by pennission] THE GREYS. (STAMFoRD AND WARRINGTON nniNcn.) There are so many of this fortunate ftmiiv in the English Peerage that I cannot glance at them all, but the Stamford and Warrington branch is of so much importance, both in a territorial and historical point of view' that I cannot pass them by unnoticed. Twice at least has this house played an important part in our history, and, owing in great part to fortunate marriages, its estates are both large and valuable. The Earl of Stamford and Warrington owns in— Cheshire 8,612 acres. Lancashire 5,231 „ Leicestershire q Ol2 „ starford Salop 606 ;, York and Worcester*

Total With a reat''—:;: of £53,395. The late idr, Jt)epla Kay, in his excellent work on the Land Question, says : —"lt would be a most interesting subject of inquiry, had we only the means of following it out, to ascertain how each of the great estates came to be formed. How many were created by the industry and personal efforts of some ancestor; how many were the grants of Sovereigns to their fAvourites; how many were gradually amassed by successive marriages of convenience; how many were obtained by ambitious statesmen, in the troublous times of eur rough island story, by the attainder and death of rivals; how many were either created or im- mensely increased by grants of the vast possessions of the religious houses and of the Roman Church ; how many were the results of our fierce and bloody civil wars and struggles. It would, indeed, be a curious and instructive study." At the time when these words were written I had already com- menced my task, and, indeed, they had not fallen under nay notice tillvery recently; but no words could have more accurately laid down the plan which I have endeavoured to follow. The space and time at my disposal have necessarily left these sketches far from complete ; but had I not imposed upon myself the most severe condensation, my work would have been obviously unfitted for the columns of a newspaper, and I trust that as it is I have placed in the hands of the general reader the most important facts in regard to the agrarian history of each of the houses with which I have dealt. If a more detailed inquiry is desirable, I have made the way easier fer those who shall come after use. After this brief digression, I return to the family whose name stands at the head of this article.

The Greys of Stamford and Warrington owe their estates to several of the circumstances mentioned by Mr. Kay, but chiefly to successive marriages of convenience. The Greys were a Norman family, who rose into prominence in the times of the early Plantagenet Kings. The founder of this branch of the house was a younger son of Lord Grey de Ruthin, who, in the reign of Henry VI., married the grand daughter and heiress of the last Lord Ferrers of Groby. Bradgate and Groby, in Leicestershire, had been acquired by a Norman house at the Conquest, and had passed by successive marriages to the Ferrers family. Since theimar- riage of Edward de Grey into the Ferrers family, these Leicestershire estates have been in the possession of his descendants. The eldest son of this marriage fell in the Lancastrian cause at St. Albans, and Edward IV. married his widow, through whose influence her son, Sir Thomas Grey, was created Marquis of Dorset. His grandson, the third Marquis of Dorset, married the daughter and heiress of Charles Brandon, Duke of Suffolk, whose Duchess was the sister of Henry VIII. The Marquis was elevated to the dukedom of Suffolk in the reign of Edward VI. His three ' daughters, the eldest of whom was the unfortunate Lady Jane -..Grey, died without issue. The Duke himself was beheaded for his share in Wyatt's rebellion. Thus the sudden greatness of the house for a time was eclipsed, but in the reign of James I. it partially regained its prosperity. Lord John Grey, a younger brother of the unhappy Duke of Suffolk, obtained a grant of Pergoe, in F.ssex, which was part of the Royal manor of Havering-Ate-Bower. His son Henry sold the Essex property, but acquired a considerable estate in Staffordshire. Enville had been acquired by the marriage of another offshoot of the Greys with a Stafford- shire heiress, and the last heir of that branch, who was chilflless, sold the property to Henry Grey, who was created Lord Grey of Groby by James I. His grandson married the daughter and co-heiress of Vliam Cecil, Earl of Exeter, through whom he became possessed of the castle, manor, and borough of Stamford. I have already shown in a pre- vious article that the Cecils derived their property almost exclusively from Royal grants. Early in the reign of Charles I. Lord Grey of Groby was created Earl Stamford; from the same monarch he received a grant of lands in Charnwood Forest. The Earl and his eldest son, Lord Grey of Groisy, were ardent supporters of the Parliament during the Civil War, and both of them had military commands. Lord Grey of Groby was especially active, and after the relief of Gloucester and the Battle of Newbury, he received the special thanks of the House of Commons. He is said to have had more to do with Pride's Pure-'e of the Long Parlia- ment than Colonel Pride himself; and his signature appears second, between those of Bradshaw and Cromwell, on the death-warrant of the King. During the Civil War he made great sacrifices in the cause, but he subsequently received large grants from the Parliament, both in land and money. It was voted that laeads in Leicestershire, to the value of £l,OOO per annum, shou7d be settled upon him, and with his pecuniary rewards he male extensive purchases. Some-

The appaintmmt 9f Mr,Naieh, Q.C., to be Solicitor- uerieral fOr Ire Jana is gazetted. A farmer, named Cunnane, was dangerously wounded at Rosskey, near Swinford, when proceeding home. In his depositions Cuunane accuses two men named Casey of being concerned in the attack, and they have been arrested.

The investigation into the Phosnix Park mtuders and the attempted assassination of Mr. Field (who is slowly recovering) is continued in Dublin Castle. It is stated that pro!ec 10n3 for alleged perjury will arise out of the proceedings. ' --

The inquiry into the charge against Timothy Harrington, proprietor of the Kerry Sentinel and secretary of the Irish National League, of using intimidating language towards fa• mrs ins speech at Mullingar, was resumed on Tuesday at Millingar, was again adjourned. "The people" of Ireland were summoned to attend in their thousands, on Sunday, at a rendezvous near Limerick to take part in a Land League Hunt. Mr. Clifford Lloyd prepared a large body of infantry and police near the spat, and nothing was seen of "the people." The exhibition of home manufactures which closed at Dublin, on Saturday, seems to have been a substantial suc- cess. The receipts were nearly £12,000, and the cost of the exhibition building bistween £3,000 and £4,000. The Lord Mayor of Dublin proposed to devote the surplus to the pro- motion of Irish industries.

At the Cork ASSiZ2S, on Tuesday, the hearing of the King Williamstown murder case was resumed. The principal evidence against the prisoner WAS that footmarks near the scene of the murder corresponded with the boots worn by him, and that he was seen lurking about the spot. The jury were locked up at six o'clock, and after four laours failed to arrive at a verdict.

The prosecutions of Messrs. Davitt, Healy, and Quinn are to be proceeded with. TMe following notice was on Tue:.4- day served upon Mr. Quinn, at the office of the National League Take notice that the application on bthalf of Charles Elward Seymour, referred to in my previous notice, and served on you, which came before the court on the sth December, 1882, and was adjourned, will be renewed on Thursday." THE PHCENIX PARK MURDERS: ANOTHER CONFESSION. —A telegram from New York says: Patrick O'Reilly, arias 1114!!. O'Donnell, accuses himself, Peter Tierney, Tim Macdonald, and a fourth, whose name is unknown, all of whom are in the States, of complicity in the Phceuilt Park murders. The details Of the COnfeB3l9l !idd nothing to what is known. The probability is that O'Reilly is a . numesick emigranF. _ _

The resignation of Captain Talbot, Comtnissioner of Police, has created some surprise. It was known, however, that in the reorganisation of the •departments at the Castle connected with the prevention and detection of crime great changes were contemplated. It is stated that the reorganisation will also involve the retirement of Colonel Connolly, who at present holds the reins. He ratites on full pay.

At a meeting held at Mallow, on Saturday, in support of Mr. O'Brien, the Nationalist candidate, a letter was read from Archbishop Croke, of Cashel, who wrote thit he should con- sider it his duty to use every legitimate lilt-the/Ica it; his power to secure the return of " tho leafless and uncompro-, mising editor of ETiaitecl Irdlancl;" and he trusted the eWd, tors woul4 once and for ever rid themselves of the venal biandishnte'.ll; of Whigs and Tories. Mr. Richard Pigott, late proprietor of the Irishnico, in a letter points out that his charges of misappropriation of the Land League funds have bean proved by Mr. Egan's letter to the Irish World. It is admitted that £2,000 was paid for expenses of Irish members of Parliament, and Mr. Pigott thinks it will ultimately transpire that over £20,000 has been spent on Irish Parliamentary agitation, in contra- vention of the condition that not a penny should be used for that purpose.

Ttin SIB&REEN MURDER.-TiMOlby Ryan was indicted at the Cork Assizes, on Tuesday, for the murder of Patrick Sullivan, near Skibbereen, in November, 1881. The prisoner had been convicted at a previous assize of assault, and sen- tenced to seven years' penal servitude. The affair occurred after Skibbereen fair, and a number of men were concerned in the melie. The deceased received serious injuries, and was afterwards ,thrown into the river. The jury now failed to agree, and were discharged. Mr. W. J. Barry, M.P. for Wexford, was entertained at a banquet on Tuesday by his conetituents. The first toast was that of the leader, At. Parnell. In responding to the toast of his health, Mr. Batty remarked that the work of the Irish parliamentary party was one of extreme difficulty. They had to rely upon moral force against a nation which had enormous material resources to meet them. They must return a body of men prepared to give the Government no peace, butaas he had not the time required he must retire from Parliament as their representative. The farm buildings and hay and straw ricks of Thomas Shea, at New Roes, were burned to the ground early on Saturday morning. The dwelling-heuse was saved. -Shea was a prominent Land Leaguer, and took a leading part in getting up the Boyd Murder Defence Fund. He had lately taken a farm from which the previous tenant had been evicted. On the same morning a jar containing gunpowder and a lighted fuse was thrown into the house of Mrs.Jeffares, owner of the farm Shea had taken. No injury was done to any of the inmates, but the furniture and windows were damaged. An exciting scene took place on Monday in the court- house of Castlehar daring the sitting of the Land Sub- Commission. Mr. Denis Duffy, who presided at the Islandeady land meeting, made some grave charges against Mr. James Daly, the proprietor of a local paper. Whereupon it is said he was struck and knocked down by Mr. Daly. The head constable and some of his men were summoned, when, according to Mr. Duffy's statement, Mr. Daly publicly, and in the presence of the police, denounced him assocaiemty. m emberr o. Daffy ftbe gave League and of the Assassination immediate instructions to bring an action in the County Court for the ass cult, and an action in the Superior Court for £5OO for the slander. During the sittings of the Special Commission in Dublin, some of the Irish journals in the Land League interest gave much prominence to a report that an "informer" who had been sent out by the Government to Victoria, had been assassinated. The supposed murder was regarded in the light of a meritorious action, on the whole, because of the "treackery " of the victim to his former confederates. There was the strongest reason for declining to republish the report at the time, the motive for its appearancs being so obvious. It was a kind of threatening letter, addressed through the press of the whole of the witnesses summoned before the Green-street commission, and in some cases it may have had its intended effect. It is now authoritatively stated that the report was a fabrication. It emanated from a town in Ireland which is in a " disturbed " district, and it is rather curious that several of the "correspondents " in that town are now in custody under the Crimes Act. I A MONTH'S AGRARIAN ClaliflL—A return, dated 4th January, is issued by the Deputy Inspector General of Con- stabulary, with reference to the agrarian outrages reported to the Inspector General during the past month. The tetal is 85, of which nine were in Leinster, four in Ulster, 17 in Connaught, and 55 in Manster. The Ulster cases are threatening letters and other intimidation. In addition to cases of this sort, there were in Leinster one aggravated assault, two incendiary fires, two cases of injuring cattle, and one of injuring other property. In Connaught, in addition to threatening letters and intimidation, there were four incendiary fires, one case of injuring cattle, and one case of injuring other property. In Munster, in addition to threatening letters and other intimidation, there were two cases of firing at the person, one aggravated assault, two incendiary fires, three cases of injaring cattle, two of injuring other property, and one case of stealing arms. There was one case of agrarian murder during the month,

and of the 85 cases of outrage 54 were by threatening letters, aad eight by other intimidation. The charge against Mr. Harrington, the proprietor of the Kerry Sentinel, of usiug language inciting to intimidation, at a meeting, was proceeded with on Thursday, at Mullingar, and resulted in his conviction and sentence to two months' imprisonment, without hatd labour. The defendant gave notice of. appeal, and entered into bail. Mr. Harrington was cheered on leaving the court. An action has been instituted against a well-known magistrate, and a member of the Dublin Town Council, for breach of promise to marry. The damages are laid at £lO,OOO. Toth parties are of mature age, and were to have been married in London (where plaintiff has he@t) staying) last Saturday, had the engagement not been broken off a few days before by the defendant, whose reason for taking that step was that his friends objected to the match. A large sum of money offered by the defendant has, it is stated, been refused.

A deputation of the citizens of Dublin, headed by the the Lord Mayor, waited, on Monday, upon Earl Spencer on the subject of the site and arrangement of the projected aneiv national library and museum of art. Mr. Gray, M.P., sup- ported the Lord Mayor in hte objection to the site and es- tablishment of a branch of the English Science and Art Department. Earl Spencer replied that he was desirous that an institution of a national character sheu!d be erected in Dublin. He thought it wonld be against the interests of the country to sever the connection with South Kensington. the site was the most suitable under the circumstances. FIRE IN LIMERICK : A MERCENARY FIRE BRIGADE.—. A fire broke out on Monday night in the old portion of the city of Limerick, which threatened to assume alarming pro- portions. The Corporation Fire Brigade refused to work un- less they were paid for services previously rendered. The fire at this time was making great headwak, and the police, seeing the dangerous condition of things, sent an express messenger to the military barracks, and in a short time the Artillery fire-engine and the engine of the 57th Regiment appeared on the scene, the men working with a will, and succeeding in putting out the fire after two houses had been burned.

A LIVELY &BNB AT A MEETING OF -THE DUBLIN ant- PORATION.—At a meeting of the Dublin Corporation on Monday afternoon, a letter was read from Mr. Gray, M.P., the late high sheriff of the city, offering the gold medal presented to him in commemoration of his imprisonment by Justica Lawson, during his shrievalty, for contempt of eourt, to be permanently attached to the high sheriff's chain. A motion adopting Mr. Gray's proposal was brought for- ward and opposed, the Connservatives maintaining that the inscription on the medal was a subject of controversy and an imputation on Judge Lawson, and denying the accuracy of that portion of the inscription that Mr. Glad- stone had promised to introduce a bill next session to amend the law regarding contempt of court. A Conservative ex- pressed his opinion, irrespectively of Judge Lawson, that the article for which Mr. Gray was committed was danger- ous, and calculated to iaterfere with the administration of Justice. Mr. Sullivan, M.P., interposed, and said if that were allowed it was also allowable to discus* the jury pack- _. . .

ing practised by the uovernment. After some utscua--:‘,7.. the debate was adjourned, the Lard Mayor and other members having to join a deputation to the Lord-Lieu tenant concerning the proposed National Museum.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

The " sliding sae " representative in South Wales has issued a circular to the miners in that district, pointing out that the resolutions as to the restriction of output adopted at the Leeds conference are antagonistic to tha fifty-four hours per Week working scheme.

A conference of Lancashire and Cheshire miners at Wigan, on Tuesday, resolved that the time had arrived for working miners to regulate the production of coal, and that. no collier, except where employed for safety, should work more than fire days or shifts per week. The meeting also decided that the best time for restricting the output of coal would be from the Ist February.

BILLS or SALE AND FAILURES. In the week ending January 6, 1883, there were 209 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 620 over those of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 186, an increase of four. The trAals for portion of year to Jan. 6, 1853, are bills of sale registered for England and Wales. 209, a decrease of 620; the failures gazetted number 186, an increase of four.—Stubbs's Mercantile Gazette. IRONWORKERS —Following the example of the iron- masters of East Worcestershire and South Staffordshire, the ironnaasters of North Stafflrdshire have increased the wages of all classes of ironworkers in their employ 21 per cent This advance, which makes an aggregate increase in wages of 10 per cent, as compared with this time last year, has been conceded for the next three anonths, when prices will be revised, and it is expected the sliding scale will again comae into operation.

REST/ICTION OF TIIR OUTPUT OP COAL.—The proposed general restriction of coal output was considered at a meet- ing of the Fife and Clackmannan Miner's Association, held at Dunfermline, on Saturday, and the resolution passed at the Miners' National Conference held at Leeds on the 19th ult., in favour of a general restriction of the output of coal, was unanimously adopted. Mr. John Weir, secretary of the association, was instructed to Lake the necessary steps to the co-operation of all the Miners' Associations in Scotland, to have the resolution carried into effect.

The Lancashire tinishel ironmakers have, in conformity with the Staffordshire award, which governs wages in this district, given an advance of 211 per cent. to their men. At the commencement of last year the men obtained an advanC of 71 per cent., which 14 Ls since been retained, and the 21 per cent, now conceded represents a total advance in the wages of the finished ironworkers of 10 per cent, during the past twelve months. The last advance of wiges in the coal trade at the commencement of November did not, as a rule, extend beyond the colliers and the daymen engaged under- ground. At many of the Lancashire collieries the topmen are now agitating for an advance. • In a few odd cases this has been given, but in the present state of the coal trade there is no disposition on the part of the colliery proprietors generally to make any further concessions with regard to wages, and where applications have been sent in by the men they have as a rule been declined.

TRH LANCASIIIRt IRON TRA.DR.—There was only a dull I market on Tuesday. aeld a scarcity of orders both for pig and manufactured iron was reported generally. The drop in the ScAch market had no doubt a tendency to check busi I ness, but generally there is a disposition to wait until after the quarterly meetings. In pig iron there was a little giving way. Lancashire makers still ask 478. 61., less 21 for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, but are not gettint orders at this figure, and would be open to offers at less. In Lincolnshire irontnasters announced a reduction of 61. on last week's rates, and present quotation 3 now aver- age 475. to 48e., less 2.1 for forge and foundry delivered. On the basis of these figures a little business was done. Small sales of Derbyshire iron are reported at about 505., less 24 delivered. For finished iron makers still hold out for £6 10s. for bars delivered into the Manchester district, but except a few orders through merchants at under current rates, there is little Cr nothing doing, although there are fair inquiries in the market. LANCASHIRE Coen TruDE.—Although some of the leading colliery firms in the immediate district of Manchester report a fairly steady business doing since the holidays, the coal trade generally throughout Lancashire is only very quiet for the season of the year. The demand both for house fire coals and other classes of fuel for manufacturing purposes is only moderate, and with the orders corning in nothing like sufficient to keep pits on full work a resort to short time, apart from any restriction of the output by the men, is not improbable unless the winter demand improves. The quoted rates at the pit mouth are without alteration, and in the Manchester district the leading coalowners are fully maintaining last mouth's prices. The average prices at the pit moutieremain about as under :—Best coal lOs to lOs 61, seconds 8s to 8s 61, common house coal 63 6d to 7s, steam and forge coals Os to 63 6d, burgy about ss, and good ordinary slack about 3s ad to 4s per ton. There has been 'a fair demand for shipment, but buyers have been able to place out orders at low prices, steam coal delivered at the high level Liverpool or at Garston docks being obtainable at from 74 9d to 8s 3d per ton, and in some classes of house fire coal prices at Crown-street station, Liverpool, have dur- ing the week been reduced is per ton. GREAT MINERS' CONFERENCE.—On Monday, at Walsall, there was opened a two days' special conference of miners of the Federation of the Midland Counties. Its object is to enhance and preserve the prices of coal and wages. All the midlands, including Leicestershire and Derbyshire, were re- presented. The president, Mr. Rust, of West Bromwich, speaking of the present standard of wages in South Stafford- shire, said that correspondence was being conducted be- tween the Federation and Earl Dudley's agent, which was expected to result in an advance before very long. In con- nection with this conference district meetings have been organised throughout the district. On Tuesday resolutions were passed advising miners throughout the country to adopt eight hours as the working day ; approving there com- mendation of the Leeds Conference that all shelving scales be terminated by the end of the year; advising miners to exercise their rights of regulating the output of coal, and recommending them to resist the admission of unskilled workmen into pits in order to reduce the dangers of mining and restrict the output, and to enhance the value of coal in' the markets. At the Conference on Wednesday, the im- provement of organisation was considered, and three resolu- tions were passed. One provided for an increase of contributions from a halfpenny to a penny per member per month. The second recommended a system of exchange of agents between districts and arrangements for apportioning the cost of great demonstrations. The third urged every member to join the local society with a view to the forma- tion of a central association.

The Lailora MAnitur.—The labour market generally shows improvement. The building trade in London is brisk, and several large contracts are about to be placed. Work for navvies is plentiful, and several contracts for new railways in various parts have been decided. At Barnsley iron trade is good and coal trade is brisk. At Barrow-in- Furness the shipbuilders are busy, and steel-makers are also fully employed. In Birmingham the chain trade is good, and makers of fittings for railways and steamship com- panies are well employed. In Bermondsey the tanners and curriera are getting busy. At Darlington the steel-makers are quiet, and coal trade also. At the Hartlepo9ls ship- builders are busy, and at the marine engine establishments and ironworks the workmen are on full time. At Sheffield the steel-makers are fairly busy, and in some branches of the heavy trade overtime is being made. At the mills and forges at Wolverhampton full time is being made, and coal trade is quiet. At Sunderland ship and marine engineering builders are busy. In the textile trades with few exceptions there is little change. At Bradford the Botany wools are in fair demand, and yarns quiet. At Halifax the manufactu-

STANLEY 2:TD V. KNTJTSFORD.--TiliS match was Played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and after a very pleasant game, resulted as follows: Stanley, one goal, four tries, and 6 touches down to their opponents nil. BLUNDELLSANDS V. WIDNES RECREATION.—The return match between these clubs was played on Saturday, on the ground of the former, and resulted in a draw; Blundellsands scoring four minor point.", and Recreation two minor points.

SALE V. -LYMDL—Played at Lymm, and resulted in a win for Sale by two goals, three tries, and three touchdowns. Lymm, one try and two touchdowns. The tries for Sale were obtained by Procter, Howard, Fisher, Taylor, Hardy, and for Lymm by Hamilton.

RUBY COLTS V. NEW BRIGHTON (2ND TEAM). This match was played at New Brighton, on Saturday, the borne team winning by two goals, five tries, and four minor points to two minor points. The tries were obtained by J. H. Pierce (3), R. Barber (2), Manifold, and T. Eskrigge. ST. ANNE'S RANGERS V. LATCHFORD TRUE BLUES.—The return match between these clubs was played on Saturday, on the ground of the former, and after a hour's hard and fast play it ended in a victory for the St. Anne's Rangers by one goal and two minor points to one try and three minor points.

WIDNES v. CREWE BRITANNIA.—A very pleasant game was played between these clubs at Crewe, on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the visitors. The score was as follows :—Widnes, two goals, two tries, and ten minor points, to Crewe nil. McCririe and Goulding scored two fries each.

CHEETHAM 2SI) (12) V. ALTRINCHAM IST (14).— Played on the ground of the former, and resulted as follows: Cheetham, a try (Gaskell) and three touchdowns. Altrin- cham, three touchdowns and three dead balls. For Cheet- ham, Fallows, Dunn, and Sutton played well; and for the visitors, R. Smith and Harrison were the best. LANCASHIRE FOOTBALL ASSOCIATIOIT.The committee of the Lancashire Football Association met at Blackburn, on Thursday night, to make the draw for the fourth round of the challenge cup competition. It was decided that the clubs which had played undecided ties should meet again on the 13th or 20th inst. The protest of Witten against the Lower Darwen goalkeeper was unsuccessful. The draw wan 2CI follAn,a ..__P;ahtnn Rniton Wandarora acrainst Peal

Bank Rovers (Church), Blackburn Park Road against Great Lever or Eagley, Blackburn Rovers against fialdwell, Rossendale against Padiham, Darwen or Irwell Springs against Lower Darwen, St. John's (Darwen) or Livesey Grasshoppers a bye. The round to be completed on the 3rd of February.

RUNCORN TAX O'SHANTERS (20) v. RUNCORN SECOND (15).—A match between these clubs was played on Satur- day, on the ground of the latter club. The ground was sloppy and the fog dense, which made the game far from pleasant. J. Pownall set the ball in motion for the Run- cornians, And being smartly 46010 the Shanters had soon to touch down. After a series of scrimmages in the home 25, the visitors drew near their opponents' goal line, and being dribbled by Farster he succeeded in scoring a touch in goal. The leather was soon ii motion again, and the backs dribbling well, a try by Wilson was quickly made into a goal by Burgess. The efforts of the home team in the latter half to score were unsuccessful. Score : Shanters : 1 goal,l touch in goal, 3 minor points. Runcorn 1 try, 5 minor points.

ST. JAMES'S (HATDOCY) V. 0/IGHTRINGTON.--This match was played at Oughtrington, on Saturday last. Owing to the late arrival of the visitors, only 30 minutes' play each way ensued. Five minutes after starting, St. James's placed the ball through their opponents' upright!, thus securing the first goal. After some very good passing they ' secured a second goal in a very short time. Then the Oughtrington team tried hard to prevent further defeat, and though a misskick by the St. James's goalkeeper secured their first and only goal, the St. James's team completely penned their opponents, and kicked another goal, and also got one which was disputed. They thus won by three goals , and one disputed goal to one goal. Teams :—St. James's: ' J. Ralphs; backs. H. Andefton and J. Pinablet t ; half-backs, R. Rimmer and J. Spencer; forwards, J. Smith, A. Anderton, , M. Arnold, T. Twist, H. Mayer, and J. Barnett. Oughtring- ton : Goal, J. Bolt; backs, T. Thomas and J. Smith; half- backs, J. Wood and A. Riggs; ferwards, H. Thomason, H. Owen, T. Dodson, E. Smith, 0. Smith, and J. Clare. LANCASII iii CRALLICNOR CUP COMPETITION.—The third round of the Lancashire Challenge Cup competition cl ,se on Saturday, and resulted as follows :—Padiham lxat Dar- win Old Wanderers by two goals to one; Rossindale beat Gilnow Rangers (Bolton) by four goals to one; Darwen St. John's and Livesey Grasshoppers (Blackburn) played a drawn game, one goal each; Darwen and Irwell Springs (Bacup) played a drawn game, two goals each; Blackburn Revere beat •A stley Bridge by three goals to none; Hallt,aelj and Darcy Lever, having played two -‘l,nwn Aarnes in the second round were order.ts,',l to met again in the third round, ' and Halliwell beat Darcy Lever by four goals to one ; Blackburn Park Road having been drawn to play the winner of the above tie in the previous round had a bye; Rishton aid Bolton Wanderers played a drawn game, two goals each; Great Lever v. Eagley not played, Eagley being unable to fulfil the engagement upon the date arranged between the clubs; Lower Darwen beat Witton by three goals to two; Peel Bank Rovers a bye. WARRINGTON WANDERERS V. WARRINGTON (2ND TEAM). —This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday. The Warrington team was a strong one, having some first team men within their ranks; the visitors were also well represented. The first scrimmage was formed in the home team's 25. By a combined effort the visitors rushed the bail over the line, touchdown being the result. The home team were obliged to resort to wing tactics four times in succession, which revealed the fact that they were unequally matched against the Wanderers' representatives. Again the visitors rushed the leather down the field, and C. Unsworth pressed to the front and secured the first try. Helsby failed at goal. Shortly afterwards half-time was called. On the game again being renewed, the visitors' for- wards began to play with renewed vigour, completely over- powering their opponents. Saving tactics were again the order of the day. Ultimately, Speakman, picking up sharply, secured the second try. Helsby again essayed the place, but failed. Warburton kicked from behind lines, only to be quickly returned ; the result was another touchdown. Boardman dropped out, and for the first time fortune seemed to favour the home team. It was only of a brief duration, however. A long pass, and alternate runs and kicks by Matthews and H. Boardman relieved tin li4es of the pres- sure; and the leather being gradually worked into the home's 25, Whittle made some fruitless attempts to get away. The game resulted in a defeat for the home team by two tries and eight minors to nil.

RUNCORN v. NEWTON.—These teams met at Newton on Saturday for the second time, when a good game was played, Newton having the assistance of Williams and Eagles of the Salford teams, who proved of great service to them. Hughes, winning the spin, decided to play up hill. When Newton set the oval going, which was charged down, Gat- ley and Wright leading away with a nice dribble into the home 25, where a scrimmage ensued. Lane, moving in another direction, was quickly brought down by the centre flag, from which Andrew and Hughes consecutively emerged into the home 25. Andrews gained possession of the lea...her in centre field, and made a fine dodging run through the home team, grounding the leather over the lino. The place was entrusted to Joule, who made a splendid attempt, the ball sailing outside the post. Williams esayed to run the oval out, but being pressed, punted into touch inside the home 25. On the throw out, J. B. Clarke and Wilkinson led on into the home quarter, when Wright, being handy, picked up and smartly crossed the line, adding another try, from which Mason nicely kicked the major point. Re-starting from centre, the home team tried hard to equalise matters. Scrimmaging ensued for some time, when the home team, playing down hill, at length kicked the ball over the visitors' line, and Egan, falling on it, claimed a try. Williams taking the place, touched down' and ran towards the uprights intending to take his drop, bat was soon arrested, the visitors carrying away the ball. On change of ends, Joule re-started the oval, which, being poorly returned, was carried over the home tine, Lane kick- ing in touch in goal. After the drop out, the ball was seen travelling over the field through the dense fog which pre- vailed. Andrews was again in possession, and was within an ace of the line before he was held. A scrimmage en- sued five yards back, when he grandly crossed the line. Mason, being again entrusted with the place, added the premier point. When no side was called, Runcorn were again the victors, as on the occasion when Newton visited Runcorn, viz., by two goals, one try, one minor point, to Newton one try. Teams—Runcorn: C. Pownall, full back; Lakin, Mason, and Johnson, three-quarter backs • H. Hughes (captain) and H. Andrews, half backs; Gatiey, Wright, Joule, Athertun, Hoffland, J. B. Clarke, J. Clarke, Lewis, and Wilkinson, forwards. Newton: Mee and Boardman, full backs; Massey, McCormick, and S. Williams (Salford F.C.), three-quarter backs: Egan and Lane, half backs; Willis, Fairclougb, Eagles (Salford F.C.), Liptrot, Holt, Emmett. Goff and Hitchen, forwarde.

It has got so now that the papers find Out about every- thing that happens. They also find out some things that don't happen—especially when a man don't happen to pay his debts.— United States Paper. The most patient boy in the world lives in Binghampton, New York. He went to the house of a neighbour for a cup of sour milk. "I haven't anything but sweet milk," said the lady of the house. "The," replied the obliging lad, as he took a seat, "I'll wait till it sours !"
