M ISUELLANEOUS.

Sir Charles W. Dilke, president of the Local Govern- ment Board, was on Thursday re-elected for Chelsea without opposition. An important discovery has been made at Magpie Mines, High Peak of Derbyshire. A vein of clinde (zinc ore) has been cut sft. wide, which premises to be of extra- ordinary value. By the breaking of a chain at Killingvrorth Colliery, near Tipton, three men have been dashed to the bottom of the pit and killed.

A Margate correspondent says that the corporation of that town intend to invite the volunteers to hold the Easter Monday review there. A woman named Flint has been arrested at Leek charged with causing the death of her husband, who was found with his neck broken after a quarrel between the two. The man and woman were married only three months ago. From a return just made up it appears that the number of members and associate members constituting the English Church Union on the Ist instant was 29,917, being, it is stated, a net gain of 1,129 members during the past year. It appears from a report read by the Superintendent of Fisheries, at a meeting of the 'ray District Fishery Board, that the number of diseased salmon taken from the Tay and its tributaries in the past year was only 388, as against 1,773 in 1881.

Several of the Hounslow rioters were brought before the magistrates on Saturday, and punished for their offending. It transpired during the proceedings that the rioting had been most serious and accompanied by great damage to pri- vate property. Mr. Andrew Carneg:e, of New York, a native of Dunferm- line, who founded a free library and public baths in his native town, has sent to the Prince of Wales a donation of £5,000 towards the establishment of the National College of Music.

The suspension is announced of Messrs. Bull, the eminent builders, who constructed the new Courts of Justice. The suspension is attributed to their efforts to prevent the for- feiture clauses of the contract coming into operation. They have a large amount of money to receive from the Govern- ment.

DESTITUTION IN SCOTLAND.—A letter has been received in Edinburgh, from the Free Church at Lewis, stating that there is great suffering there, and that a number of the in- habitants are on the point of starvation. The cause of the destitution is the failure of the crops. The minister appeals for immediate help. The letter has been sent to the Lord Provost, in the hope that public relief will be organised, not for Lewis only, but also other districts of Scotland.

THE MILES PLATTING CASE.—The Bishop of Manchester has sent to the Rev. H. Woods Tindall, in acknowledgment of resolutions passed at a meeting over which he presided, and approving of his Lordship's action in regard to the case of the Church of St. John's, Miles Platting, a letter In which he defines the position which he has taken up in the matter, and in which he says that, whilst not a party man, nor seek- ing popularity with a party, or to win a triumph for one, there are principles which he feels bound by every senti- ment of fealty to his Church and his office to endeavour to maintain.

DOGFIGHTING IN THE MIDLANDS.—A correspondent of the Birmingham. Daily Hail says it is a common thing in certain beerhouses in that town to promote the exhibition of dogfights of a most brutal descriplion. Only the other night upwards of 40 persons assembled in the garret of a public- house, where a pit was constructed of circular boards, fixed with hooks, so as to be capable of dexterous removal in case of a police raid. In this arena two fierce bulldogs, with a stake of £5O depending upon the result, fought with mad tury for 47 minutes to an accompaniment of applause and wild yells of delight. A mere sickening spectacle it would be difficult to conceive. One of the animals was torn literally to pieces and fell dead upon the floor, and the other was carried away in a terribly mangled condition. DARING OUTRAGE AT GORTON.—An outrage of a par- ticularly daring character was committed at Gorton on Saturday. An Irishman, who had been sent to prison for assault, threatened on his release to murder one of the wit- nesses—a woman—who had given evidence against him. Meeting the woman in the street on Saturday night, he fired at her with a revolver. Her brother struck up the pistol, and the ball missed, but the ruffian followed the woman into a shop, and there fired four shots at her, three of which took effect. The poor woman lies in a dangerous state. Her assailant was promptly arrested, and was brought up at the Manchester County Police Court on Monday, and remanded. He denied having had the "least intention' of harming his victim, and said that he'had only acted in self-defence. THE ()RAND CoacurrrEus.—Workmen are at present occupied in fitting up the E room latterly used as the Court of Appeal at Westminster, for the accommodation of one of the Grand Committees. The chairman will be seated at the head of the room, and to his right and left will be three rows of seats for the 80 members constituting the com- mittee. Seats are provided for the press, and the public will be admitted to the discussions. Should the accom- modation be insufficient, the room is capable of being enlarged by 20 feet in length and six in breadth. Provision is made for the second Grand Committee by knocking down the partition dividing rooms ten and eleven, which are at the head of the staircase leading to the committee corridor of the House of Commons. The internal arrangements will be similar to those described above. EXTRAORD INARY CAREER OF A BIRMINGHAM BOY.— James Kelly, a lad of 16, was charged before the Notting- ham borough magistrates, on Saturday, with stealing a purse at the Midland railway station. The case was a very clear one, the purse being taken from a lady's basket as she was going to a train. The stationmaster, however, caught the boy, who, in passing the purse to a companion, let it fall on the platform. The Chief Constable said the prisoner was a very crever thief from Birmingham. Notwithstand- ing his youthful appearance, he bed been seven times in custody for felony, had served various terms of imprison- ment, and had been twice sent to a reformatory. The last time, however, when on the way to the reformatory, he managed to give the policeman the slip, and got clear away. As his accomplice is not yet captured, the magistrates re- manded the prisoner for a week. Boarm OF TRADE RETunNs.—The Board of Trade re- turns for the month and twelve months ending with December 31st was issued on Monday. The exports for the month of December were £18,214, 789 in 1880, £20,182,052 in 1881, and £18,171,551 in 1882: for the last 12 months £223,060,446, £234, 022,678, and £241,477,156 respectively. The imports for the month were £33,216,852 in 1880, £33,235 260 in 1881, £35,369,131 in 1883; and for the 12 months £411,210,056, £396,773.350, and £412,001,683 respectively. The imports of gold and silver for the month were £1,616,066 in 1880, £962,647 in 1881, and £1,529,402 in 1882 ; and for the 12 months £16,287,964, £16,864,918, £23,620,579 respectively. The exports of gold and silver for the month were £2,888,082 in 1880, £1,079,221 in 1881, and £1,418,535 in 1882; and for the 12 months £18,889,503, £22,502,819, and £20,989,258 respectively. The tonnage of British and foreign vessels entered and cleared in the month of December were, in 1880, 2,222,338 and 2,028.837 res- pectively; in 1831, 2.247,294 and 1,968,910; and in 1882, 2.104,586 and 1,846,310. Tor the 12 months the totals were 26,021,236 and 23,736,625 in 1880, 25,839,117 and 23,373001 in 1881, and 26,135,864 and 23,573,011 in 1882, DETERMINED TO KILL HERSELF. The High Bailiff of Douglas has just concluded an inquiry into the death of Elizi Fargher, fifty-five years of age, residing in Athol- street, Douglas. The evidence showed that, having been overworked during the visiiing season last summer, her mind had to a certain extent given way, and she had since. made several very determined attempts to kill herself. On two occasions she had been found sharpening knives with the intention of doing herself or others harm. More recently the deceased had evinced a determination to throw herself from windows placed at a high elevation. The precautioa was taken of nailing the windows down, but on three occa- sions she succeeded in drawing the nails, and had been caught in the act of precipitating herself into the street. Ultimately the deceased succeeded in this determination, and threw herself from the drawing-room window on to the front steps, fracturing her skull. In September last two doctors certified the woman to be a lunatic, but she herself de- stroyed the certificates, and the family did not like incarcer- ating her. The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the evidence.

Mr. GLADSTONE.—Mr. Gladstone is again unwell, and though it is expressly stated that his ailment is not serious, or of a character to occasion alarm, it is impossible not to feel anxiety on the right honourable gentleman's account. 41 he Premier's age renders illness of almost any description a matter of gravitY, and the fact that his present indisposi- tion is believed to result from a chill caught in the Hawarden woods so long ago as Boxing Day is in itself disquieting. On that day Mr. Gladstone indulged in his favourite pastime of tree-felling, and his exposure on that occasion was followed by a slight attack of lumbago. In a few days he was almost quite well again, but his recovery was not complete, and Dr. Andrew Clark, being called in, has pronounced him to be suffering from overwork and in need of rest. As a result, the tour in Midlothian, which has been /looked forward to by the whole country; and especially by Me. Gladstone's constituents, has had to be abandoned. Much as this is to be regretted, it is better tha t the Premier should take his needed rest now than that he should by injudicious exertion disqualify himself fc% the work of the coming session. It may be hoped that More Parliament meets Mr. Gladstone's health will be quite restored.

MR. JOSEPH COMP.': AND HIS CONSTITUENTS. - Mr. Joseph Cowen, MT., addressing his constituents at New- castle, on Monday night, said last session started amidst hopeful assurances and many fair resolves, but its fitful course was strewn with broken promises and baffled pi o- jects. There had been mistakes many and miscalculations not a few. There had been dangerous inroads made into constitutional practices and flagrant violations of Liberal principles committed. The result, although legislatively discouraging, represented a large measure of physical exertion and mental worry, And brought into prominence the parliamentary intrepidity, resource, and endurance of the leader of the House, which all must acknowledge and ad- mire. The distinguishing characteristic of the Cabinet had been its passion for coercion, but the social difficulty in Ireland would never be settled till occupiers were made owners, and the political difficulty would never be settled till we allowed Ireland to govern themselves. Regarding the attire, he said the men now in power might not mean it, but the drift of their policy wag certainly to circum- scribe freedom of action, crush out individuality of charac- ter, and plane down every politician to party pattern. Respecting the future of Egypt, he asserted that, unless a miracle occurred, the Government would be driven to annexation.

div.head: EXAMINER; SATURDAY, JANUARY 13, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER; SATURDAY, JANUARY 13, 1883.
The Marquis of Hartingten will address his constituents f OR the 19th and the 20th inst.

In recognition of the services rendered by the Duke of Cambridge in connection with the Egyptian war, the Queen has appointed his Royal Highness to be personal Aide-de- Camp to her Majesty. On Saturday morning James Farnworth, aged 25 years, a collier, employed at Messrs. Samuel Scrowcroft and Sons' pit, Kearsley, was crushed to death by a fall of earth whilst at work.

The Queen has bestowed the Albert Medal on several members of the exploring party who made such a gallant attempt to rescue the miners imprisoned by a fire which oc- curred at the Baddesley Colliery, in Warwickshire, last May, an exploit which resulted in the death of no fewer than 23 persons. The Bishop of Carlisle has conferred the canonry vacated by the death of Archdeacon Boutflower upon the 'Venerable Archdeacon Cooper, vicar of Kendal. The Arcgdeaconry of Carlisle has been given by his Lordship to Canon Ward, vicar of Kirkby Lonsdale and chaplain to the Bishop. It is understood that the Madagascar question is likely to come more prominently forward in the course of the next few weeks, and will form the subject of serious discussion at the first meeting of the Cabinet. Lord Granville is at present devoting a good deal of attention to the matter, as welt as to the claims put forward by France. COCKFIGHTING IN THE BLACK COUNTRY.—At Halesowen, on Tuesday afternoon, 14 men were charvid with being engaged in cockfights near Hagley. On Boxing Day, about 200 men assembled in a dingle, and sekeral mains of cocks took place. One of the cocks was afterwards, when the police appeared, found dead, and several were spurred and trimmed. The magistrates remanded the prisoners who were then arrested for a fortnight. It is stated that heavy stakes were laid.

ANOTHER SHIP CANAL SOHEIHE.—A scheme has just been set on foot to make a ship canal from the Tyne to the Solway Firth. An eminent engineer is engaged in the necessary survey, and plans and estimates will shortly be made public. Notice of motion in favour of the project has been given by a member of the Newcastle Town Council. The distance from sea to sea is about 80 miles, of which about a dozen are now navigable to large ships.

IMPORTANT DECISION' UNDER THE EMPLOYER AND WORKMAN Aer.—A case of considerable interest to work- men was decided on Tuesday morning at Burslem stipendiary court, when six potters were summoned, under the Employer and Workman Act, for neglect of work. The employer' after the men had gone away from work, dis- charged them. The stipendiary held that the employer's remedy was in the county court, and dismissed the sum- mons with costs. The result was received with great enthusiasm by a crowd of workpeople. THE SALVATION ARMY AND IMMORALITY. - Two work- house nurses at Bristol having been discharged and the con- duct of a third referred to the Visiting Committee, because it was reported to the board that one of the girls was ex- pecting her aacouchement. The governor said a man occu- pying a prominent position in the Salvation Army bad 'ack- nowledged his misconduct with her, and promised her mar- riage. A guardian remarked that the fellow ought to be horsewhipped and exposed. Another guardian said two of theee men went to the workhouse, but the master ordered them oat. The deputy-governor said they would have no all-night services there. An inquiry was ordered. The Bishop of London, in replying to what by implica- tion he styles an impertinent resolution of the Church Association, defends his action in regard to the transference of Mr. Mackonochie. His Lordehip says he is "not aware that the Bishop has the power to require from a duly qualified clergyman, the sufficiency of whose learning he has no reason to doubt, any conditions of admission to a benefice, when presented by the rightful patron, other than the production of testimonials signed by three beneficed clergymen and the oaths and declarations prescribed by law."

PROPOSED TESTIMONIAL TO THE REV. MR. MACSONO- CHIE.—Lord Edward Churchill presided on Tuesday at a meeting of the friends of the Rev. Mr. Mackonochie, in London, the object being to promote a testimonial to him. The Chairman said he had received promises of support from many desirous of taking action in recognition of the twenty years' services of Mr. Mackonochie in the parish of St. Alban's, Holborn.—lt was agreed that a testimonial be presented, and a committee was formed to further the ob- ject. It was agreed that as Mr. Mackonochie had piobably reduced his income by about £l5O a year by the pecuniary support he had given to the parish, the amount obtained be placed entirely at his disposal. A DISMAL CHRISTMAS STORY.—A dismal story of Christ- mas in St. Pancras was told before a coroner's jury on Tuesday. A woman named Baster, aged 50, had died in the Workhouse hospital, having been removed from a room in which she had endured the last extremity of wretchtdness. The poor creature was unable to pay the rent of the room, and, although she was then very ill, her landlord, a perscn named Coxhill, builder, in Seymour-street, Easton-road, caused the doors and windows to be removed. The result was' that Baster died from cold and exposure. The coroner's jury warmly censured Coxhill for his conduct. If this case bad occurred in the West of Ireland there would have been a great outcry. DEATH OP BARON MARTIN.—The Right Hon. Sir Samuel Martin, who was formerly Baron of the Exchequer, died on Tuesday morning at his residence, Piccadilly, London. He had latterly been attended by Sir William Gull and Mr. George Pollock. The deceased jadge was the son of Mr. Samuel Martin, of Caimore, county Londonderry, and entered as a student at Gray's Inn and subsequently at Middle Temple. He was called to the bar in 1830, and made Q.C. in 1843, and was elected in 1847 member for Pontefract. He was appointed Baron of the Exchequer in 1850, and held that position till 1874.

THE EASTER MOLIDAY REVIEW. ^ A meeting of the metropolitan commanding officers was held on Tuesday at the offices of the National Rifle Association, in Pall Mall East. Lieutenant-Colonel Ranelagh presided. On the motion of the chairman it was unanimously agreed that a review of the volunteers should be held on Easter Monday. Letters were then read from the Town Clerk of Dover and the president of the Local Board of Aldershot, offering Dover and Aldershot as available places for the review, and the deputy-mayor of Brighton, Mr. Alderman Davey, stating that that town would be very glad to receive the volunteers at Easter. A committee of officers was appointed to select the locality they might consider the most suitable, and to report to an adjourned meeting. The meeting was then ad- journed until the 23rd inst. SHOCKING CASE OF BABY-FARMING.—Mr. William Carter, East Surrey coroner, held an inquest on Monday. at Dept- ford, as to the cause of death of an infant named Albert Blackman, aged six months, recently under the care of a woman named Amelia Evans. The evidence showed that Evans had had the care of the child for some time at a re- muneration of ss. per week. In Christmas week the mother received two letters urging her to go and look after her child. She bad to go twice to the house before she could get admittance, and then it was only got by means of a neighbour's doorkey. On entering the house on the evening of the 30th ult., Evans was found lying on a bed, and the deceased was in his cradle in a horrible condition of filth, and scarcely alive. He was removed to Rotherhithe Infirmary, where he died in six hours, and the woman Evans was given into custody. Mr. Robert Shepherd, medical officer of the Infirmary, said that the child when admitted was in a filthy and dying condition, and was too weak to permit of being washed. He had made a post-moi tem ex- amination, and was of opinion that death was accelerated by neglect. There was a number of bruises on its body, but he could not say they were caused by blows; they probably resulted from the child's struggles and the neglect. The jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against Amelia Evans.

A LEARNED COSTERMONGER.—Two costermongers were summoned at the London City Police Summons Court, be- fore Sir Thomas Gabriel, on Saturday, for causing an ob- struction with their barrows in Lower Thames-street, by Billingsgate Market. The defendant in one case, upon being called upon, said, "Yes, here I am; I'm corning to give you an explanation of this." He then raved an Act of Parliament before the Alderman, and shouted in a loud voice, "I admit'it as far as the monopoly of the Corporation is concerned, and I apply for a summons against the Cor- poration of the city of London for receiving unlawful tolls, and preventaily it'll bring provisions up to a guinea an ounce." (Loud laughter.) The Alderman: Stop a minute; lam not going to bear this nonsense. You are charged with blocking the traffic.—The defendant; I didn't do it; let's fight it legally, my lord. (Renewed laughter.)—The Alderman: You will not do yourself any good, you know, by going on in this way. Defendant: Won't Imy lord? We shall see. Here's the Act of Parliament; now let's fight it, and I shall appeal against it —The Alderman : Yes, that's all right, and in the meanwhile you are fined 2s. 6. and costs or three days' imprisonment. The defendant: I shan't pay. I'll go to prison, and I shall take proceedings against the Col poration and the chairman of committee for monopoly. (Laughter.) Now, then, justice may take me to my new residence, but let the Corporation kn)yr I intend to upset them. I'll show them the meaning of this at Westminster Sessions before a jury.—The defendant was then removed to the cells.

D. BENSON AND TRH BURIALS QUESTION.—Mr. Thos. Rowe, chairman of the Burial Board, Newlyn East, Corn- wall, writing to the Daily News to urge the repeal of the Burials Act from 1852 to 1871, says :—" The report of Sir A. Gordon's committee has led the way, and Mr. Richard's bill, which will be re-introduced into Parliament next ses- sion seems drawn on the lines of that report. It does not go beyond the views of the late archbishop, and other high authorities of the church, but unfortunately Dr. Benson does ' not take the fallen mantle. He has within the last month appealed to the Home Secretary to urge the Burial Board of this parish to divide the cemetery and consecrate a part. Au inspector ha a been sent here to urge us, as he said, to do our duty. The cemetery has been open nine months. Twelve funeral services have been perforrhed—three by the vicar and nine by the Wesleyan minister. Ninety-nine per cent. of the people are against such division, yet the Burial Board are threatened with the utmost rigour of the law. This is hard on the eve of its repeal. I know of five cases near this parish where the burial boards are waitincr for legislation, after which they will complete their cemeteries satisfactorily. When the Act of 1880 was passed, the division of the cemetery and consecration at the cost of the rate ,should have been no longer legal. This would have prevented the unseemly rush which the clergy have made to close the old churchyards, so as to create for themselves in the consecrated part of the cemeteries now endowments, which will not cease until death, resignation, or removal. This contest over the grave is painful. The best Church people here object to division, as well as to the fees which in consecrated ground the incumbent charges in addition to fees charged by the Burial Board."

IWednesday way the anniversary of the commencement of the penny postage eystorn, which took place in 1840. There is reason to believe that a club called the Constitu- tional, to embrace all classes, on a very lsrge scale, will shortly be started with the approval of the leaders of the Conservative party. John Cumber, a labourer, was put upon his trial on Tuesday, at the Central Criminal Court, on the charge of writing a letter threatening to murder the Prince of Wales and Mr. Gladstene. Mr. Justice Hawkins ruled that the letter contained no such threat, and the jury acquitted the prisoner. _ _ _ _ _ _

The Queen has granted Professor Palmer's widow a pen- sion of £2OO per annum. As there are four children to pro- vide for, the Admiralty, however, have been applied to in the matter, and are considering the advisability of appropri- ating a sum of the vote of credit towards educating the younger children and affording them a comfortable start in life on their coming of age. SERIOUS CUE; EXPLOSION.—A serious gas explosion occurred at Dunfermline on;Wednesday evening, The mana- gers of the United Presbyterian Church intended holding a meeting in the sessions house, and on one of the officials entering and striking a light a terrific explosion occurred. The sessions house and part of the church were wrecked. Coventry, the official, had a narrow escape. The escape of gas was caused by the fall of a lustre suspended from the roof.

On Thursday morning, shortly before two o'clock, a destructive fire cccurred at the extensive linen manufactory of Messrs. Richardson and Nevin, Lambeg, near Lisburn. Information was at once conveyed to Lisburn, and the fire brigade turned out, but the efforts to check the fire were fruitless, and the entire mill known as the Beetling Mill was destroyed. The damages are estimated ot £30,000, and is c,,vered by insurance. ~ The cause of the fire is unknown. No accidents are reported. Judgment was given on Thursday in the Queen's Bench Division in the case of Bradlaugh v. Erskine, which was an action brought by the junior member for Northampton against the Deputy Sergeant-at-Arms, for assault upon the occasion of his attempting to enter the House of Commons after a resolution had been passed prohibiting him from so doing. Mr. Justice Field cited a large number of precedents showing the power of the House to exercise its control over its own proceedings, and gave judgment for the defendant, with costs.

A Lloyds telegram received on Thursday morning states that the brig Elaine, of Newport, 233 tons register, which left Liverpool a few days ago for Para, North Brazil, was discovered ashore on the Wicklow coast yesterday. When first seen she was fast breaking up, and has since gone to pieces. Three bodies have already washed ashore, one of which is that of the captain. The remaining five men are all supposed to have been drowned. From the appearance of the wreck she appears to have been in col- lision.

The Lord Chief Justice, on taking his seat on Thursd ty, for the first time, in the New Law Courts, remarked that the Judges had left Westminster Hari, but that he trusted they had not left behind them the traditions of that great and illustrious building. Especially he hoped the traditions of mutual dependence between bench and bar would continue unbroken traditions, without which, the bar probably and the bench certainly, would find it impossible to discharge their important functions. A man, named Enoch Hill, is in custody at Wednesbury on the charge of causing the death of a boy named Enoch Pickering. The deceased and the prisoner worked in a manufactory, and it is alleged that in consequence of Pickering calling Hill offensive names he struck 'him on the right temple with a pair of pliers, inflicting a large wound, which immediately caused death. Prisoner says he had no intention of killing the deceased, but only to severely chastise him.

A general strike of the Caledonian Railway servants in Glasgow, Edinburgh, Stirling, Motherwell, and Greenock is threatened. At a meeting of the Central Committee held in Glasgow late on Wednesday night, it was resolved to hold an idle day on Monday next in the event of the directors refusing to comply with their request for shorter hours. A general strike will be proclaimed in the event of any of their numbers being dismissed for taking part in the agita- tion.

ANOTHER Plasm WARDER ATTACKED. A murderous assaalt on a warder is reported from the convict establish- ment at Princetown, on Wednesday. A gang of convicts, who had been engaged in drainage and reclamation work, were mustered for the purpose of having dry stockings served out to those who might require them. A convict, named Jones, applied for, but was refused a pair, his own being dry, whereupon he struck Staddon, the officer in charge, a fearful blow on the head with his shovel, laying open his skull and exposing the brain. Staddon was removed to the infirmary, and lies in a precarious condition. Jones was manacled and placed in solitary confinement. IMPROVED INLAND MAIL SERVICES.—The Press Associa- tion has reason to believe that Her Majesty's Government have accepted the tender of the London and North-Western Railway Company for the conveyance of mails between London and Kingstown or Dublin after October Ist next. By the acceptance of this tender the Government have secured a reduction in cost to the public of this service of nearly £30,000 a year and an acceleration of service, coupled with a contemplated earlier despatch of the night mail from Dublin. This acceleration will prepare the way for improved services between Dublin and many provincial towns. In addition to the improvement of the Irish mail servic?, an acceleration of the postal communications between England and Scotland and South Wales is also in contemplation. THE GREAT ROBBERY OF HUMAN HAIR. At the Bir- mingham Quarter Sessions, on Wednesday, the Recorder, Mr, Stratford Dugdale, Q.C., sentenced Henry White, one of the leading hairdressers in the town, to five months' impri- sonment with hard labour for feloniously receiving from a clerk named Ernest Lotze £lOO worth of human hair, a por- tion of £4OO which he had stolen from his employer, Mr. Schlette, merchant, and Italian vice-consul in Birmingham. —Ernest Lotze, who is now undergoing a sentence of im- prisonment, testified to selling the hair, which was all fine Swedish, to the prisoner, for only £l5 on credit, whereas it would realise 14 times that amount in the market.

On the opening of the Irish Law Courts in Dublin, on Thursday, for Hilary term, the State prosecution of Messrs. Healy, M.P., Davitt, and Quinn, was again brought forward in the Queen's Bench, which was crowded. The Crown applies that the defendants should be ordered to find securities to be of good behaviour, or in default to be im- prisoned. The proceedings are taken under tenth and eleventh Charles 1., in consequence of certain speeches de- livered by the defendants at different meetings held in con- nection with the land agitation in Ireland. In one speech Mr. Davitt said they would compel the landlords to support the starving people; and Mr. Healy advised the people not to pay rent under certain conditions, and said the Govern- ment of the country were simply so many brigands. On the cases being called on before the Lord Chief Justice and Mr. Justice Lawson they were again postponed in order that they might be heard before a full court of judges. No other day was fixed for the trials.

The quarterly meeting of the ironmasters of Birming- ham and the Midlands was held in Birmingham, on Thursday, and was attended by merchants and producers from the Metropolis, Liverpool, and the north of England. There was a quieter feeling in all branches as compared with three months ago, and though the standard quota- tions for iron were nominally unaltered, the actual prices obtained showed a declining tendency all round; and the impreesion produced was that unless a change for the better speedily occurs trade will be seriously depressed. List bars remained at £7 103. £B, and £8 12s. 6d., but only the lower priced bars sold with any freedom. Com- mon bars were down to £6 55., with ss. mere for medium qualities, or about 10s. below last quarter day's rates. Common sheets (singles) realised £8 a ton, as against £8 108. in October, and nail rods and other classes of iron were similarly affected, In pig iron there was a drop of ss. a ton on all mine qualities, hot air selling freely at £3 55., and cold blast at £4, though quotations nominally are ss. and 103. more. Common pig cinder was quoted at £2 against £2 ss. Ernerast PATENTS.—The following patents amongst others published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal were sealed during the week ending January 6th, 1883 : Miles Settle, Bolton, mining engineer and colliery pro- prietor, for improvements in the means of blasting or rending coal, rock, and other minerals or substances, the same being applicable to other useful purposes; John Roberts, Oldham, and George Travis, Failsworth, for im- proved means for preventing the radiation of heat from steam boilers or pipes; John Myers and Benjamin Berry, Bradford, for improvements in spinning and twisting, and in apparatus connected therewith; Enoch Heppenstall, Huddersfield, for improvements in apparatus for dyeing cotton and other fibres; James Johnson and Richard Talbot, Blackburn, for improved apparatus for regulating the trans- mission of power for operating the bellows of organs; John Ashworth, Rochdale, machinist, for improvements in or applicable to machines for tentering, stretching, and other- wise treating fabrics, parts of which improvements are applicable for other purposes; James Carr, Hulme Man- chester, for improvements in the production of tape ;adders. —List supplied by George Davies, CE., Patent Solicitor, 4, St. Ann's Square, Manchester. THE CREMATION SOCIRTY.—A correspondence has passed between the Cremation Society of England and Sir William Vernon Harcourt. In a letter addressed to the Hon. Sir A. P. 0. Liddell, the secretary of the Cremation Society asks —" Supposing I were to die now, directing my executors to have my body burnt in our crematory at Woking, would my executors be liable to prosecution ? As the council of the Cremation Society of England are extremely unwilling to proceeed with any cremation without the knowledge of the Home Secretary, and under conditions which shall ensure the legality of the proceedings, I am desired to ask yoa to favour the council with his decision as to the legality of cremation as proposed by them. lam also instructed to ask if you will allow the council to submit to you for approval regulations in the practice of cremation intended'to prevent the destruction of evidence of poisoning." The Permanent Under-Secretary for State, in reply, writes as follows :—" I am directed by Secretary Sir William Vernon Harcourt to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 28th ult., inquiring in behalf of the Cremation Society as to the lega- lity of their proposed method of disposing of the remains of the dead by process of burning. And lam to acquaint you, for the information of the gentlemen forming the above society, that Sir William Harcourt can give no opinion in matters which belong to the jurisdiction and decisions in courts of law. fu Sir William. Harcourt's opinion the prac- tice of cremation ought not to be sanctioned except under the authority and regulation of an Act of Parliament. It is the duty of those who desire, to pursue such a practice to obtain such an authority, and until it it granted, Sir William Harcourt must adhere to the view expressed by his prede- cessor in office."

div.head: DISTRIBUTION OF THE BRITISH ARMY.
div.p: DISTRIBUTION OF THE BRITISH ARMY.

Though the strength of the military forces in Ireland has been considerably td aced, there are still about 30,000 men in the island, under the command of General Sir T. Steele, K.C.B. This number is, with the exception of 1881, the greatest that has been reached in any of the years from 1861 up to the present time. In 1861, the strength of the Irish establishment was slightly over 25,000, from which it gradually decreased to 21,000 in 1865, rose again to 24,000 in 1866, and in 1869 had got down again to less than 22,000. In 1870 and 1872 the total was as high as 27,000, after which it decreased again till 1877, when there were 22,000 troops in the island. The total rose to nearly 24,000 in 1878, but in 1879 sank to 18,684. At the present time there are in the three military districts :—Belfast (Major-General Sayer) Dublin (Lord Clarina), and Cork (Major- General Terrens), seven regiments of cavalry, 15 bat- teries of artillery (besides depots), three com- panies of enginers five companies of commissariat and transport, and 24 battalions of infantry. The army of occupation in Egypt absorbs two regiments of cavalry ' six batteries of artillery, three companies of engineers, three of commissariat and transport, one of the ordnance etors corps, and 11i battalions of infantry. In India Sir D. M. Stewart has nine regiments of cavalry, 77 batteries of artillery, three companies of engineers, and 50 battalions of infantry. In the Dominion there are three batteries of artillery, one company of engineers, and two battalions of infantry; in Malta, eight batteries of artillery, bne company of engineers, and three battalions of infantrr; at Gibraltar, seven batteries of artillery, four companies Of engineers, and four battalions of infantry; in South Africa, one regiment of cavalry, three batteries of artillery, two companies of en- gineers, and two battalions of infantry; in Ceylon. two bat- teries and a battalion of infantry; and on the Chinese and Straits stations, two batteries and two battalions of infantry. Besides this there are small detachments in the West Indies, Bermuda, and Mauritius. At home—that is, in the ten com- mands of Great Britain and the Channel Islands—there are 12 regiments of cavalry, 72 batteries of artillery, 21 com- panies of engineers, and 39 battalions of infantry, exclusive of commissariat, transport and ordnance corps, and depot troops.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A GIRL.
div.p: MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A GIRL.
STRANGE CONDUCT OF A CLERGYMAN.

An inquiry was resumed at West Mailing, Rent, on Wed- nesday, as to the .death of a young woman named Sarah Ann Wright, who had died suddenly. Mr. E. Clarke, Q.C., M.P., watched the case on behalf ot the Rev. J. H. Timins, vicar of the parish. Great interest was manifested in the case.—Mrs. Emma Ralph, nurse, who was attending a fever patient in the house of the deceased's parents. stated that on the 14th December last she saw deceased leaning on Mr. Timins' shoulder, and Timins took her hand, remarking that she was weak. After that the girl became sick, and after- wards her mother remarked, "Oh, Mr. Timing, you have murdered my child ! " and he then endeavoured to ad- minister some brandy and water. At the request of Timing, Dr. Pope was fetched, but the girl was dead before he arrived. Professor Heaton gave the result of the analysis. He stated that the vomit contained a strong smell of bitter almonds, and prussic acid was also found. He added that the repetition of the experiments showed poison, ten days after death, which was unusual, and if analysis had been made sooner more prausic acid and oil of bitter almonds would certainly have been found. Mr. Pound, surgeon, Snowdland, who made the post-mortem examination, said in his opinion death did not occur from natural causes, but from a nerve or narcotic poison. Dr. Pope corroborated. An order given by Timing to a chemist named Stedman for the essential oil was put in, Timins having stated that he required it for outward application. Mr. Timing was then sworn, and, after having been cautioned, said he had been through a regular course of instruction in chemistry at St. Thomas's Hospital, and had used the knowledge thus obtained for his parishioners. He obtained some medicine for the deceased, as she had a swelling in her throat, and the application of the oil of almonds outwardly had been beneficial to his son. The oil got from Stedman resembled in colour the innocent ex- pressed oil, and he had no idea that he had been supplied with the poisonous oil. He found afterwards he had made a mistake. He still had the bottle with the oil got from Stedman in his possession. The mother of the deceased having given some further evidence, the chemist Stedman was called, and he stated that the essential oil supplied to Mr. Timing was labelled and marked "Poison." The inquiry was then adjourned for a fortnight.

LADIES AND RAILWAY CARRIAGES. The following correspondence appeared in the Daily News :—Sir,—Will you kindly allow me space to give an instance of how.ladies are liable to be treated when travel- ling? I was journeying last Saturday in a first-class carriage alone, from Manchester to Newtown' in Wales. On arriving at Crewe my part of the train ran beyond the cover of the station, wheu shortly the guard (asl suppose) and another man came to my carriage where I was com- fortably seated wrapped up in a rug, for it was a bitterly cold day, and it was raining heavily at the time. I was questioned as to what place I was going. On wishing to know why the inquiry was made, the reply was, would I object to change my carriage, as five gentlemen wished to be together to smoke. I replied, "And do you expect me to step out into this rain to oblige five gentlemen to smoke ?" Immediately the answer came, "Oh, never mind, we will put on another carriage." QUery ; have not men of every, class already enough space allotted them for smoking with- out ladies being asked to step out of a carriage which is not set apart ,for such a purpose? Of course I have no idea what the fee would be to an official seeking to grant this extra indulgence; I leave this to your readers who are initiated into these mysteries. But I would like to inquire how much longer the comfort of the women of our country is to be considered of less importance than that of the men. —I am, dic., MARGARET BRIGHT LUCAS, 7, Charlotte-street, Bedford-square, Jan. 5. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me space to give an instance of how gentlemen are liable to be treated when travelling. I was coming to town on Friday week from Peterborough in the last compartment of a floe-composite first-class carriage; and, like your correspondent of the sth inst , was alone. At Hitchin the guard, surrounded with a number of ladies, came to the door, and asked me if I would have any objec- tion to change my carriage, has these ladies wished to be to- gether during the remainder of the journey. Although I had my things—books, newspapers, traps, &c.—all lying about, I immediately assented, and gathering all together, went into another compartment without a murmur. A gentleman who had seen "the move" on the platform took the next seat beside ma when the train was about starting, and told me that he had been curious enough to watch whether the guard had been feed by the ladies for his attention; and haying seen no sign of it, he (knowing the guard personally) asked him if he had been "tipped." His reply was, "Not a farthing—barely thanks." I leave the above circumstances, by no means unusual, to be placed by your readers alongside of the cases reported in your's of to-day ; and in conclusion must say that in more senses than one your correspondent "begs the question "when she asks " How much longer the comfort of the women of our country is to be considered of less importance than that of the men ?" To all who are so misled as to think that such a view is anywhere entertained, the simplest answer would be, just so long as there are persons going about advocating the lowering of the status of women in the land. By a time-honoured chivalry, gentlemen look up to women as the superior sex, and consequently defer to them, give pre- cedence to them, protect them; and so long as women are satisfied with their distinguished position, and do not give heed to unfemine counsellors, so long only will their pre- sent comfort continue.—l am, (Irc., G. B. BRODIE, M.D. Connaught-square, Jan. 6.

div.head: MYSTERY AT GLOSSOP.
div.p: A MYSTERY AT GLOSSOP.

On Sunday morning a shocking calamity occurred in the family of the Rev. G. Sadler, pastor of the Littlemoor Independent chapel, Glossop, when the two servant girls were found dead in bed. The names of the deceased are Catherine Smith, 20 years of age, a native of Sheffield, and Hannah Raley, 17, of Madeley, near Shiffnal, Shropshire. The former .has been in the service of Mr. Sadler for over two years, and the latter about two months, and both bore the best of characters. They retired to rest on Saturday night in good health. No sound was heard in their room during the night, and when Mrs. Sadler entered the room on Sunday morning with the intention of awakening them, thinking they had overslept themselves, they appeared to be in peaceful slumber. On Dr. Rhodes arriving he pronounced both to be dead. No cause could be traced, but on the police arriving they took away several bottles, though they did not appear to have been recently used, and what they contained has yet to be revealed. The whole neighbourhood was thrown into a state of excitement, and when the congrega- tion assembled for worship at the adjoining chapel the deepest gloom prevailed. • On Monday, Drs. Mackenzie and Rhodes made a post-mortem examination of the bodies, and the contents of the stomachs were sent to Manchester for analysis, and until the analyst's report is received, not ex- planation of the tragic event can be given. An inquest has been opened on the bodies. In the course of the proceedings it transpired that the chapel joined the house, and on Mon- day morning, when layers of paper were stripped from the wall of the attic in which the girls slept, it was discovered that a quantity of sulphurous gas from the coke used for healing the chapel had passed into the bedroom, and Dr. Rhodes expressed an opinion that the gisls had died from asphyxia.

We (Morning Post) understand that the Government have received several addresses from political and religious associations in the kingdom protesting against the idea of re-establishing diplomatic negotiations with the Vatican. Several among these addresses point to the fact that, the King of Italy being in virtue of the Roman plebiscite the legitimate sovereign of Rome, the English Government have no justification for sending a representative to the Court of the Vatican, which is now an essentially spiritual Power. Mrs. Gladstone, who left Hawarden on Wednesday night for the purpose of fulfilling the engagement, on Thursday performed the ceremony of christening Sir Donald Currie and Co.'s steamer " Hawarden Castle,' on the occasion of its being launched from one of the Glasgow shipyards. At a luncheon which followed a telegram was read in which Mr. Gladstone said that, though confined to his bed by cold, L he already felt better for the prescribed rest.

div.head: DISASTROUS COLLISION OFF LIVERPOOL. TEN LIVES LOST.
div.p: DISASTROUS COLLISION OFF LIVERPOOL. TEN LIVES LOST.

A terrible and fatal collision occurred off the bar of Liverpool on Sunday morning, during a dense fog. The inward-bound Inman steamer City of Brussels, one of the finest aud fastest of the transatlantic fleet, was overtaken by the fog when nearing the north-west lightship, and Captain Land stopped the engines and allowed the ship to alrift to- wards the light vessel. The usual sound signals were given to announce the position of the ship, but after a short time another steamer was heard approaching. This proved to be the Kirby Hall, on her trial trip from the Clyde. She ran stem on into the City of Brussels, smashine! in her side to such an extent as to render useless several of the water- tight compartments, and she went down in a few minutes. The passengers and crew, to the number of nearly 200, were nearly all got off in the boats in safety through the admir- able arrangements of the captain and the good discipline of the crew. Eight of the crewe, however, were either carried , down with the steamer or died from exposure. Captain , Land and some of his officers were the last to leave the ship, and they were picked up after floating about for some time on wreckage. Two Italians, passengers on the mail steamer, sprang into the water in a panic, and were lost. It is impossible to describe exactly all the circumstances of the collision, the accounts given by those in charge of the respective vessels being in important respects very conflict- ing. That there was a dense fog is athnitted on both sides, but here agreement ends. The commander of the City of Brussels maintains that on hearing the bell of the North- West Lightship his vessel was allowed to drift towards the bar, and was eventually brought to a dead stop, in which condition it remained for 41 minutes, the steam whistle be- ing kept going. Then the Kirby Hall's whistle was heard, and the commander of the City of Brussels, concluding that the approaching steamer intended to pass his vessel, did not start the engines. The collision followed. The commander of the Kirby Hall, on the other hand', says his engines were going "dead slow," •and he was feeling for an anchorage when they came upon the City of Brussels, which atteinp- ted to cross the bows of the Kirby Hall; that both vessels were under way; and that as soon as he saw that a collision was inevitable he reversed his engines. Both these accounts are no doubt given in perfect good faith, it being difficult to see with exactitude what is going on in a dense fog, but they cannot both be according to facts. After the collision every effort was made to save life, and in this particnlar too high praise cannot be given. The sunken steamer lies ia a position which impedes navigation, and prompt steps are being taken with a view to clearing the waterway. The City of Brussels, it is stated, was chiefly covered by iasurance against risk of collision only. The loss falls on the different insurance offices to the extent of £lOO,OOO. The cargo, which consisted of cheese, bacon, lard, and other produce, was worth £50,000. The owners of the Kirby Hall have lodged a claim of £6,000 for damage clone to their vessel, while the Inman Company claim £160,000 for the less of the City of Brussels, leaving out of consideration all claims for cargo lost, and those which may be lodged by the families of those whose lives were lost in the steamer.

Little has yet been done towards removing the wreck of the City of Brussels from the channel at the mouth of the Mersey, the weather so far having been unfavourable for the operation. The coroner's inquiry was concluded on Wednesday. The chief engineer of the City of Brussels said the engines had been stopped some time before the collision, but the steamer drifted with the rising tide. Wit- ness and the captain left the last before she sank. Just before he received a signal to go astern full speed, which was done immediately. Captain Land said he could see about a ship's length. He first saw a light, and ordered the enginel.to be put back, but the steamer strucklefore she could get under way. They sounded a powerful steam whistle every 15 or 20 seconds, which could be heard a mile off. Captain Ham- bery, of the Kirby Hall, was afterwards examined, and stated that when the fog set in he reduced speed from eleven knots to " slow," and on hearing the other steamer's whistle he ordered the engines " dead slow." At the seconi whistle he stopped the engines. The third officer reported a light on the port bow, and his vessel was immediately put astern. The collision occurred three minutes afterwards. The Jury returned a verdict of accidental death. The Coroner oom- mended the conduct of the captain and officers of the City of Brussels.

div.head: WINSFORD SALT TRADE.
div.p: THE WINSFORD SALT TRADE.

The marked feature in the past year is the unanimous de- termination of the trade to regulate the supply, with the re- sult that there has been for nine months a continuous stop- page of a large proportion of all the pans and that the ex- isting winter stecks are the smallest on record for very many years. The fact that the trade has been less by at least half a million tons is worthy of special attention, as it must have an important influence on the future. Prices were fairly maintained till the scarcity of ships, height of freights, and very small demand, created some weakness, due only to the action of one or two short-sighted individuals. The afore- said facts form as solid a basis for a rood future as any Itrade ever had the fortune to make by careful and united control, and it must be patent to all cbservers that the tem- porary folly of a few cannot frustrate the patient determina- tion of the many to reap the sure fruits of long self-restraint. In fine the large spring demand, which must follow on the restricted export combined with the larger shipments to Cal- cutta will have a much stronger influence upon prices than may be commonly e.apected. The Au..rican markets ha, e taken rather less on account of the very high freights pre- valent, there having recently been a large fall. Shipments mAy be reasonably expected to increase. There is, moreover, fair reason for assuming that a reduction, if not a repeal of the United States duty will be achieved. The effect of this will be obvious. The Calcutta market has been a perfect paradox to all, but as we now know that it is due to the skil- ful management of their position under the reduced duty by the clever natives, and not to a decrease of consumption, and more especially as the last quarters, shipments have been very small, there is a fair certainty in the demand it will give rise to. The Baltic has had a good average, buyers there will not make such bargains for this year as were offered them before the Association was formed last year.— The chemical trade has been so much depressed that (under a special exception of the Association) contractors were enabled to take figures below those fixed for other trades. This will naturally increase their desire to secure remunera- tive 'prices elsewhere. Prices for contract deliveries of 1883 are as follows :—Shipped f.o.b. Liverpool per ton of 20 cwts. (Small craft loading at Weston Dock, will have a rebate of is. per ton from Liverpool quotations). Common white lie., butter 12s. 6d., Calcutta (half and half) 135., chute stoved 145., factory tilled 265. 6d.,handed squares 175., fishery, first quality: 145.; ditto second 135., picked lump rock 9s. 6d., Prussian rock 6s ,rock riddlings 63. 6d., ground rock (rough) is., ditto (fine) Bs., soiled agricultural 75., sacks (with cartage and labour of filling) common sd. to 6d., 'striped 6.1. to q-1., corn sacks Bd. to 10d. Freights to America, Galveston 103., Baltimore (steam) 55., New York (sail) 4s. 61, (steam) Sc., Boston (steam) is. 61, Calcutta 13s.61,without consignment. Baltic no fixtures yet. The amount exported from the river Mersey during Decem- ber, 1882, to the chief centres of distribution are as follows : —United States, 223,620 tons, which is below the same month in the last three years, but in excess of the previous eight years, 1871 to 1878, for December. To British North America, 81,716, which for the Decembers of previous 11 years has never been exceeded but in 1880, when it reached 109,836 tons, and 1871, when it attained 94,332. To West Indies and South America, 23,935, which is the highest for 12 years. To Africa, 34,287, which stands second to that for December, 1880, at 35,475. To East Indies, 274,866, or a less amount than in 1875, 1879, 1880-1. To Australian Colonies, 17,342, which was exceeded in 1875-7, 1880-1, by lots. To Prussian ports, 34.464, exceeded in 1871-6, and 1880. Russia has taken 46,973, which quantity was sur- passed in 1872-3-4-5-6-7, but not since, till 1882. Other Baltic and North Sea ports, 33,072, which surpasses any December for 12 years. To France and Mediterranean, 5,001, to which the last remark ales applies. To our coast : Newcastle, 6,561, not a half of that for many Decembers, and but one-fifth of what it has often been, as in 1876, &c. Rest of England, 2,733, which is above that for 1881 and 1879, but below with these exceptions, every year from 1870. To Scotland, 21,604, which compares 'favourably with last year, and is much in excess of 1880, 1879, 1878, 1877, and 1876, but below, much, 1870 to 1875. To Ireland, 1,564, which is in excess of 1879, but below every other from 1871. Holland, 21,070 which has never been higher since 1876, while Belgium had 45,358, exceeded in 1881, but never before. Making the total shipped from Liverpool, 876,062, and from Weston and Runcorn, 214,863; or a grand total from the Mersey of 1,091,825 for December, 1382.

The Bishop of Gloucesttr and Bristol, in his annual pastoral, says that party spirit and party societies are largely countervailing the work of the Church, and, unless the present bitterness be allayed, great changes must come. He advises union as a remedy for this state •of things. Mr. Parnell has received a telegram from America requesting that Mr. Sexton, M.P., should attend the conven- tion there next month for the purpose of reorganising the Land League of America into the national league. Mr. Sexton sails at once. The Bolton coroner on Thursday morning inquired into the death of Robert Stanley, a paper pattern maker, who had died at his lodgings in Queen-street. Deceased, who was partially intoxicated, whilst eating his supper attempted to swallow a piece of pork, but it lodged in his windpipe and choked him. The piece was afterwards extracted, and found to be over an ounce in weight. A verdict of acci- dental death was returned. On Wednesday night an inspector at the Bullfield Sidtng, near Bolton, on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, named James France, was cut to pieces by the express from Fleetwood to Manchester due at Bolton at 7-7 p.m. Deceased had been•employed on the line all his life, and was giving instructions to the driver of a goods train when he was struck down by the express.

In the Lord Chief Justice's Court, at the New Law Courts on Thursday, before Lord Coleridge, Baron Pollock, and Justice Manisty, the Attorney-General moved on behalf of the plaintiff, in the action of Chamberlain versus Eoyd, for a rule calling upon Mr. Goodlake, the publisher of the Times, to show cause why he should not be dealt with as their Lordships thought fit for having committed contempt of eourt in publishing certain correspondence in connection with ,the case when it came before Mr. Justice Field recently on technical grounds, and subsequently allowing a leading article on the subject to appear. Their Lordships granted a rule' and also a similar application against the publisher of the Observer. Co-comm.—Cement for Broken Articles, 6d,is. 2s; postage 26.. Bold everywhere. OBVERSE AND REVERSE. EBY " ANGLO-SCOTE'S."3

As the origin, source, or explanation of some of tlis matters mentioned and expressions used in the letters of " Anglo-Scotus" may be of interest or use to young readers of The Examiner, he has supplied the following The entire poem about Whittington hailing from Lanca- shire, from which I quoted in the letter published in The Exarnintr of June 10th, 18.82, will be found in the collec- tion entitled "Poems of Places."

The explanations of the phrases "selling the cat" or "bving the rabbit "(July 1, 18820 are to be found in the story anent the countryman who put cats into pokes or sacks, and sold them in the market-place as rabbits, hares, or sucking pigs, as opportunity served. " Letting the cat out of the beg" derives its origin from the same circum- stance.•

The bagpipe (July 22, 1882,) is an ancient Greek and Roman instrument. On a piece of ancient Grecian eeulp. ture, now in Rome, a beg-piper is represented dressed like a modern Highlander. Nero is also said to have played upca a bag-pipe. Again, Mr. Lowther, in his " Wayside Notes in Scandinavia," says "it is a curious fast that bag-pipes were invented in Norway, and thence imported into Scotland during the period when a portion of the country fell into Scandinavian hands." But I have no wish to make fun cf the bagpipe, since it is recorded of the grandfather of Professor Clerk Maxwell—a naval captain in the service of the East India Company, and an expert player on the bagpipes, a set of which he always kept with him on board ship, and which, on one occasion, was the means of saving his life from a double danger, that of being wrecked in the Hooghly—he used the bag of his pipes to keep him afloat while swimming ashore. When he landed he played an unco fit" to cheer the survivors, and succeeded at the same time in frightening away some tigers which were stalking the party., lhe accounts of the apotheosis of the bees arid ants (Aug. 5, 1882) will be found in " Ovid's Metamorphoses." The story with which the letter concludes is a parody of that of the " Kilkenny Cats." the true origin of which is supposed to be as follows :—" During the re- bellion in Ireland in 1303, Kilkenny was garrisoned by a troop of Hessian soldiers, who amused themselves in barracks by tying two cats together by their tails and throwing them across a clothes • line to fight. The officers hearing of the cruel practice resolved to stop it, and deputed one of their number to watch. The soldiers, on their part, set a man to watch for the comity, officer. One day the sentinel neglected his duty, and the heavy tramp of the officer was heard ascending the stairs. One of the troopers, seizing a sword, cut the tails in two as the animals hung across the line. The two cats escaped, minus their tails, through the open window, and when the officer en- quired the meaning of the two bleeding tails being left in the room, he was coolly told that two cats had been fight- ing and had devoured each other—all but the tails." The particulars anent the ea-communicated ants (August 12th, 1882) will be found in " Credulities, Past and Pre- sent." For an account of Peter Wilkins (September 23rd, 1882) his adventures, his marriage with the gawrey. named Youwarkee, and their honeymoon in Nosmnbdsgrsutt (I cannot give a key to the pronunciation of this last word), see Pultock's " Life and Adventures of a Cornishman." In case reader,s should imagine lam quot- ing from or alluding to books of a stupid or frivaous nature, I would remind them that Coleridge said of the " History of Peter Wilkins" that "it is a work of uncommon beauty." See "Table Talk "(1335).

As to the Haggis (October 7th, 1882), it is quite evident that Scotchmen are net the inventors of what Burns apostrophises as tho "great chieftain o' the puddin' race." A perusal of the "Animal Products" of Mr. P. L. Simmonds, prepared by order of the Lords of the Committee of Council on Education in sonnection with the Food and Economic Exhibition at South Ikensington, wilt show that the Esquimau' or the North American Indians are the real inventors of the haggis. Every part of the carcase of the reindeer " serves the natives who people its habitat for food. The entire stomach, with its contents of lichens and other vegetables, is also eaten just as it is taken from the animal, sometimes raw, sometimes cookA— the vegetable substances being much more easily digested by human beings after they have partially undergone that process by the gastric juice of a ruminating animal. Some Indians and Canadians leave this savoury mixture to ferment or season for a fem. days before they cook or eat it." The English "marrow. bone course " is also borrowcd from a savage custom. Being dyspeptic, I an no admirer of the haggis; I would only add that if the Scotch—or any other nationality, for that matter—must cook sontething in a portion of the " innards" of a ruminant aliimal, let thetn stuff a spring chicken with oysters and boil it in a dried bullock's bladder. When properly cooked, I think they will admit the dish has mo,e claim to be considered a "chieftain of the puddin' race" than a so called haggis. In connection with Scotch hab'ts and expressions, it may be of interest to point out that the last word in the following line,

The cock may craw. the day may daw is neither a colloquialism nor a " poetic.licence." Anciently the day was said to daw. Drayton says, "morning claws," and in "Reliq. Antiq." are two examples—" Day daweth," p. 7, and 'The daye wenne hit daw," p. 244. " Newtonian " may possibly have something to say upon this subj(ct. Again, a " cutty pipe" is not necessarily a short one. As Kutaieh is the name of the city in Asia Minor where the soft whlto stone Is found, Of which the Germans manutac- ture the much-prized pipes, " cutty " applied to the pipe is most probably a corruption of the name of the ancient Coticeum, and was originally meant to express quality, not size.
A description or account of "pigeon's milk," the indivi- dual who writes the household pets column could no doubt supply. If he cannot, then I will.
. . A good maxim for young people to bear in mind at the commencement of a new year is "to do all they have to do with all their energy, whether at work or play."

div.head: BUILDING ON EXPECTATIONS.
div.p: BUILDING ON EXPECTATIONS.

At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Henry Morecroft, of Parr Moss, whose name is familiar in St. Helens as that of the hero of a long and eventful litigation, in connection with the common rights of Parr Moss and the enclosure of the Moss by Mr. Evans, -the reputed lord of the manor of Parr, was defendant in an action whereby Luke ,Kirkham, joiner, St. Helens, sought to. recover from. him for work done in repairing certain property belong- ing to him at Kirkby.—Mr. Massey, who appeared for the plaintiff, said he understood the defendant was working, and had three sons wl:o lived with him, were in full work, and contributed to the support of the family. Moreover, the defendant was at the present time receiving the rents of the property which the plaintiff had repaired. Ire had also been plaintiff in the great action of Morecroft v. Evans, which had been tried in the Chancery of Lancaster, and was now being carried by him t.. the Court of Appeal. That action was one involving a large suns of money, and by it Morecroft claimed a considerable property at Parr. The judg- ment of Vice-Chancellor Bristowe had gone against him, and he was now carrying the case to a higher court. Therefore he (Mr. Massey) submitted it was evident that if defendant could find funds to carry on the litigation referred to he could not but be in a position to pay the small sum claimed by the plaintiff Kirkham.—Evidence having been given in support of the claim, Mrs. Morecroft, who appeared on be- half of her husband, stated that defendant had not worked for three years, and at the present time he was at home ill and unable to leave the house. He had not sixpence of his own, but was entirely dependent upon what his children 'chose to give him. The law proceedings to which Mr. Massey had referred were being carried on by friends, and as to the property at Kirkby in question, in the present case the rents were received by a Mr Dutton, and defendant would not receive any money from them for three years.— His Honour : What can you pay ? Mrs. Morecroft replied that defendant could pay nothing. He had other debts, but they were due to gentlemen who knew how he had been robbed, and therefore did not press for payment., He had been dreadfully ill used, but if he got the property which was the subject of the appeal he would pay everything he owed. He had given a bill of sale for law costs amount- ing to £2,700, but witness was unable to produce the docu- ment as it had been sent up to the Court of Appeal.--ffis Honour made an order for the amount claimed and costs payable by instalments of is per month.

On Thursday, a man named James Arnold, brother of the landlord, committed suicide in the Dane Mill Tavern at Ilicester. The man, it appears, had been away for a few weeks, and returning on Thursday, went into the house and shot himself with a revolver, death being instan- taneous. The affair caused a great sensation in the neigh- bourhood. _ _ _

Mr. Thomss.,Brosklehurst, a colliery proprietor of Deane, near Bolton, was, on Thursday morning, fined 20s and costs by the Bolton magistrates, for having in Use at one of his coalyards a pair of scales 71b3. against the purchaser. - It It was proved that the yard was in charge of a servant, and that the Corporation inspector had had an opportunity of adjusting the scale% The dead body of a woman, shockingly m tile ad, wPa found, on Thursday, in a field at Tullyvan, near Dungan- non. The body was nearly naked, and a terrible struggTe had evidently taken place, nearly all the woman's bait having been torn away. A later telegram states that a, farmer, named Lamb, has been arrested, who it is suppozed committed the murder on his return from Aughnarchy market, on Wednesday night. The woman had obtained a decree at the Quarter Sessions, on Monday, for £l6 wages due by Lamb. div.head: TILE EXAMINER.
div.p: TILE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 13, 1883.

kern E Political utterances during the ParHa- le* "ar3r recess have been so far comparatively 4,0r:14 Unimportant; and there have been Josk;:fve dare say, so bitter as that of Mr. `keNs -p' COWEN, the senior member for ar—Qm. upon-Tyne. The breech which kldes the hon. member from the rank- 'lie of the Liberal party is becoming ate iht. at every turn he takes, and so isolated 11,11Ve POSitions he assumes that it is not qithltlently hinted he niust be a Tory in 14. 1-hise. Mr. COWEN claims to be a Radical ,tekse first water, and while we have no 41,t0 douLt the sincerity of his political "risid,.;"t may be open to us to question the k10,—,41 of the course he so systematically ! 11(ri.`8,0fabusing alike Liberal Governments :iberal measures. There is no dis- i ,;q,ortle, ,the fact that the hon. member s ' IVR-eglY independent; he has the courage '4441- °Pinions, and he gives expression to kseoWlithout fear, favour, or affection. He i Pri4j. his yet the public as a martyr to s ifl)tetPles ; yet in doing this he ought not to it'lldi:e-,"l',at even his periodical exhibitions of d'e -e,,tl°ll have their advantages, for if at ileN, lcier, of them he happens to be con- „ltle ,r, his Liberal friends, he at the same .14,41atTutninands the applause and fulsome sV -,;(41 of his Conservative opponents. ZNeeeh he delivered to his constitueats l'tAbi,"Qeastle on Monday is a perfect tirade -"b„,(1 etCde of the Government from beginning tice„,.' and were it not that Mr. COWEN'S inilia-:reS to ,catch the popular ear are now tC) everyone, the addrees would cer- -4_-"t e Mistaken for that of a member of tlbt tsPosition. Indeed, we very iniich eith,,"ether a member of the Opposition the Upper or the Lower House 1„-4 1111, still less surpass, Mr. COWEN in et.-el)itig denunciations of the Govern- abefllivßN, -Collectively they have, in Mr. cliss''t. pas°Yinion, been false to their pledges, insizliguish'ilon for coercion has been their 41zates ,ing characteristic, individually, he th "Qat they changed tlir doc..rines ci-lanwed their ceats. ILS is a •

description which few, if any, will accept as accurate, and we assert it is not borne out by the facts. The doctrines or principles the members of the Government advocated in Opposition, they have consistently adhered to in office, though it has been their ill-luck to deal with a state of affairs, both at home and abroad, which might have tempted them to deviate. Coercion is still with them a "hateful incident," and if they have adopted such a policy in Parliament, in Ireland, or in Egypt, it is either because they have them- selves been coerced into it, or because they felt it was the only course left open for them to pursue. Mr. COWEN is mortally offended at the Closure being intro- duced into Parliament, and he enters into what is, to him at any rate, a most instructive analysis, showing the time which the Government and private members occupy at the present time when Parliament is sitting, as compared with the time occupied in previous years. For instance, he shows that in 1872 the House sat r2o days, and out of these private members had the initiative of the business on 70 days and the Govern- ment on so. In 1877 the House sat 122 days, of which Government had control of 4.2 days and private members of So. But the order was reversed in 1880. In that year the Session lasted 87 days; the Government had 70 and private members only 17 of those days. In 188 i the House sat T 54. days, of , which the Government had control of z. 4.4. ' and private members of 40. Last Session the House sat 162 days, and the Govern- ment had the initiative of business on 127 days and private members on 35. To our mind this analysis would be of some value were the Sessions compared an all fours, but that is not the case. In 1872 there were no Irish or Egyptian troubles on hand, and we are not Avare that there were any disturbing elements during the Session of 1877 ; but in the Sessions of rBgo, 1881, and rBB2, there was nothing but turmoil in Ireland or difficulties somewhere else with which the Government had to contend, and in addition the wilful obstruction in St. Stephen's was a great hindrance to legislation. When we consider these things, Mr. COWEN'S statistics are worthless. When the member for Newcastle complains so bitterly of the Government policy in Ireland, he ought at the same time to give the Administration credit for endeavouring to rule Ireland without force, and also .to remember that they have not been unmindful of remedial legislation. He cannot have forgotten how much the Government were condemned by the Opposition for allowing the Peace Preservation Act to expire, nor should he close his eyes to the fact that the Land and the Arrears Acts were passed amid torrents of abuse from the Conservative benches. During the past three years we have made rapid strides towards bringing the government of Ireland into closer harmony with Irish ideas, and we hope to succeed still more in this direction. It is no longer intended that the Irish people shall be "ruled by a corps of English bureaucrats fulminating edicts from Dublin Castle," as Mr. COWEN elegantly expressed it. This very system is now under revision, but we fear it will be some time before the objects of the Government are attained if gentlemen of the position and influence of the member for Newcastle keep alive, by their indiscreet utterances, the flame of Irish discontent. Mr. COWEN is altogether wide of the Mark in assuming .that the sympathy of the Government with struggling nationalities has in the slightest degree abated; and he does them an injustice by declaring "they have beaten down by bombs and bayonets one of the most interesting and hopeful efforts after national life that modern times has seen." If there is one thing above another which the Govern- ment is, anxious for in the settlement of the Egyptian embroglio, it is that whatever is of a national character in the country shall have the fullest and freest scope for develop- ment. The movement, however, led by ARABI Pasha was a national one in a very limited sense. He represented what has been very properly described as- a " military despotism," though, we doubt not, its ultimate outcome will be that the Egyptian people will very soon enjoy the blessings of self-government. It is very desirable that the actions of the Government should be freely criticised from an independent stand- point; and the criticism of Mr. COWEN would be very acceptable but for the vindic- tiveness which accompanies it. In playing the part of the " candid friend," he betrays a desire to inflict an injury which robs his remarks of the value which would otherwise attach to them.
PROPOSED ACCIDENT HOSPITAL FOR RUNCORN.

The response to the invitations issued by Dr. Steele, to consider the necessity of establishing an Accident Hospital for Runcorn, was not such as the importance of the subject demanded, or the philanthropy of the project merited. Per- haps the hour at which the meeting was called was not a suitable one; for it would be hard to explain the apparent apathy—for real we sincerely think it could be—on any other assumption. Accidents may be few and far between in Runcorn, but it is nevertheless a-duty, which is recognised in almost every town, to provide a place where the unfor- tunate victims of any catastrophe which may occur can be professionally treated at the least possible cost and with the least possible pain. The project as at present explained is a very modest one, and would not involve, at the highest estimation, an annual expenditure of over £l5O. Were the hospital to be supported from the rates, this amount would mean an additional burden of about a penny in the upon the taxpayer. But Dr. Steele is very decided in his opinion that the charge for maintain- ing an Accident Hospital cannot be levied on the rates, al- though we may point out that Widnes Local Board provides in every way for the by no means pretentious but very valuable Accident Hospital, which that town possesses. We believe too, that the local authority at Garston acts in a similar manner. Generally, however, accident hospitals, or infirmaries, are eustained by subscriptions which is perhaps the best method, as every person has them an opportunity of contributing to the funds of an institution, of whose aid he may sometime be in need. He could then enter with a kind of prescriptive right. That there is sufficient public spirit in Runcorn to voluttarily establish and sustain a hospital, will hardly be questioned. The heaviest expense will be at the outset in furnishing and fitting up whatever premises may be selected, and the most important question for the promoters to consider, is the raanner in which the money has to be raised. And in this respect they could not well follow a better example than that set by the governors of Warrington Infirmary, who would, we are sure, be glad to supply every information.
