ALLEGED OUTRAGE ON A FARNWORTH SCHOOLMISTRESS.— An outrage of an extraordinary nature was perpetrated on Thursday evening week, upon a young lady named Miss Davies, who is a teacher at Fainwortb Church schools' and resides in that village. About half-past seven, as Miss Davies was passing along Derby-road, she was accosted by a tramp, who solicited alms. She was about to give the man some coppers, when he snatched them from her, and put his arm round her neck. In her terror the young lady screamed, and her assailant, either accidentally or intentionally pushed her into a pool of water near by. He then decamped, but another man !pass- ing a short time afterwards rescued Miss Davies from her alarming position, and aided her to reach her home. The fright the unfortunate young lady received has told seriously upon her health, and she has since been confined to the house. In the hope of capturing the ruffian, the police kept the matter a profound secret for some days, but he has succeeded BO far in baffling all their efforts. A WATARMAN KILLED AT WID2EI.—On Thursday, Thomas Tomlinson, a waterman, who resided in Church- lane, Northwich, was killed at Widnes under the following circumstances :—Tomlinson was employed on the flat "Jessie," which is at present lying in Widnes Docks on Widnes Old Marsh. About a quarter to nine on Thursday morning he left the flat with the intention of proceeding to the town to buy a quantity of bread. At that time a small locomotive belonging to the London and North-Western

Railway Company Was at a standstill on the Billing near the docks. The driver, George Mort, put the engine in motion, but it had not travelled many yards when it was felt to "jump." The break was quickly applied, and Mort jumped to the ground. He discovered Tomlinson lying in the " four-foot," behind his engine, in a state of inseniibility. The poor man was removed to a hut not many yards dis- tant, and Dr. McDonnell's assistant quickly came to his aid, but he died a few minutes after the doctor's arrival. The deceased, besides receiving internal injuries, was much bruised about the body, and the ankle of his right foot was , badly cut. A DRUNKEN PAUPER FROM DUTTON.—At RIIIICO2II Police Court, on Monday, William Baker, an old man, who 1 is an inmate of Dutton Workhouee, was brought up in custody on a charge of being drunk in Halton on the 7th inst. It seemed P.S. Laundes saw the prisoner in Halton in a state of intoxication, and he took him a considerable distance on the way to Dutton. A short time afterwards, however, he again found him in Halton in such a condition that he thought it advisable to lock him up for safety. Whenever the prisoner got out of the House, it was stated, be never reurned for several days. The prisoner, in a sorrowful tone, informed the Bench that his was "a deplor- able case," he having had to enter the Workhouee through , a sen's ingratitude. He narrated a long story of how he ! came to get drunk, and pleaded that he might be allowed to I return to the Workhouse, hinting that if he were sent to gaol he would probably shuffle off this mortal coil.—Mr. Bankes (the chairman) pointed out to the prisoner that drink, which had been his ruin, would lead him into further trouble, and warned him of the consequence that would ensue if he again appeared before the court.—The prisoner was discharged, and ordered to al. once proceed to Dutton Workhouse. He left the court with some alacrity. r FREE BREAKFAST TO CHILDREN AT RUNCORN. About eight o'clock on Sunday morning 2,100 children were pro- vided with a free breakfast by the Committee of the Yeung Men's Christian Association. Its cost was defrayed by the surplus left after the old folks' treat on the previous Friday. The committee had not anticipated so great a demand upon their resources, and it was no light task to meet all the claims upon the accommodation and provisions. By seven o'clock children of all descriptions clustered round the door- way to obtain admission to the hall, and when the doors were opened at eight o'clock every seat was rapidly filled, , while hundreds still waited outside. It had only been ' intended to give the children of the poorer class a meal, but • many whose parents were in comfortable positions put in lan appearance, and the committee felt they could not turn 'them away. It would be well to provide against such a contingency on any future occasion when a similar treat is organised. Fortunately the supply of provisions proved ample, and each boy or girl received a good meal. The wants of the host of children *ere supplied by about 100 young men and young ladies, who had attended, no doubt, ,at some inconvenience to themselves. Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst 1 was present, and before the . meal was commenced he addressed a few appropriate words to the youngsters. There was a balance in the treasurer's hands of £1,838 3s sd.—The re- port was adopted.—This was all the business of importance TREATING STRANGERS AND WHAT CAME OF IT.—Darby Bohan was charged, at Warrington Police Court, yesterday, before Captain Reynolds and Mr. Ziba Armitage, with stealing about 12s. from John Hellwood.—lt appears that the prosecutor is a clerk and lives at 11, Angel-street, Manchester. He came to Warrington on Thursday after- upon to see some friends at the Barracks, and he spent a few hours there. He left about 10 o'clock, and when pass- ing through one of the Principal streets in the town he was met by the prisonerand others who asked for a "treat." They went into a public-house and had some beer, for which prosecutot paid. He left the house and went to several places in search of lodgings, but was unable to get any. He again met the prisoner, and asked where he could get lodgings, and he said "Oh, come and sleep with me." They went to the prisoner's house in Union-street and slept together, but before undressing, the prosecutor took about 128. from his trousers' pockets, and put it into his waistcoat pocket, and then placed the waistcoat on the bed near the wall in order to lie on it. The following morning, about five o'clock, he awoke and found that the prisoner had gone, and that the money was also missing. He went downstairs, and saw a man wrapping up some- thing, and apparently getting ready to go out to work, but he did not mention the robbery to him. He then went out, and informed the first policeman he met. The prisoner was apprehended during the day in a public-house, and he was taken to the police station where about Bs. was found upon him.—The prosecutor, on being questioned, admitted that some females were with them at the publichouse, and that he was under the influence of drink. He was not sure whether the bedroom door was locked.—The prisoner, when asked what he had to say, replied he had plenty to say. The prosecutor had promised to give him a sovereign if he would find him a "wife," but he had not done so. ' DEATH OF FATHER MAGI:UHF, LATE OF RUNCORN.—Our readers will hear with regret of the death of the Rev. Father Maguire, which took place on Sunday morning, at Shifnal, Salop. F.or a period of 18 years the reverend gentle- man, who had attained the age of 60 years, was the priest at St. Edward's Catholic Chapel, Runcorn. During that time his Christian philanthropy and high moral character won the respect and regard of the public at large, while his parishioners, to whom he was indeed a friend, had for him a sincere affection.

LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE BINE, LIMITED.—The directors Of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Bank, Limited, state in their annual report that the net profits of the bank including balance brought forward, amount to £36,771 Os. 3d. An interim dividend of Bs. per share was paid in July last, and it is now proposed to pay a further dividend of 10s. per share, making for the year a total division of 9 per cent, clear of income tax. A sum of £5,880 will be added to the reserve fund, raising its total to £lOO,OOO, leaving £4,076 Bs. 3d. to carry forward.

THE ETIRATTER AND A WEST ON BOY. - An incident which shows very clearly one of the characteristic of Eng- land's Premier has lately occurred. Master Richard Clark Rosenberg, of Weston Point, forwarded a New Year's card to Mr. Gladstone, and he enclosed a note which ended with the words "From a little boy who loves you." A few mornings ago a letter containitig the following, which is in Mr. Gladstone's handwriting, was received by the little fellow, who is only nine years of age Hawarden Castle, Chester. Pray accept my thanks and best wishes. W. E. Gladstone. January 4th, 1883." Although not one of Mr. Gladstone's disciples, Mr. Rosenberg considers the letter to his son of so much value that he intends to have it mounted and framed. .

AN OLD OFFENCE. —At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, an elderly man named John Smith was charged, under a warrant, with having on the 28th June last assaulted Robert Jeffries, con- tractor. From the plaintiff's statement it seemed the prisoner at the time stated was employed by the prosecutor, who a few days previous to the assault paid him his wages. The prisoner alleged that he had not received them, and on the date named be met the posecutor in the street, an seiz- ing him by the throat threatened to use violence towards him. The prisoner gave a blank denial to the prosecutor's charge, but the Bench fined him 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days' imprisonment—The prisoner was .then charged with being drunk in Church-street on the sth inst., and on the evidence of P.C. Noden and P.S. McMichael, he was fined Hs. and costs.

BUTTER ADULTERATION AT WESTON.—Bfore Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn Petty Sessions. on Monday, Edward Jones, grocer, of Weston, was summoned to answer a charge of having, on the 24th November, un- lawfully sold to the prejudice of James Bossons a pound of butter not of the substance and quality demanded.—P.C. Bossons said on the date named he went to the defendant's shop and purchased a pound of butter, for which be paid is. 4d. It was divided into three parts ; one part was retained by the defendsnt, one banded to Mr. Superintendent Williamson, and the third forwarded to the public analyst, who certified that the butter was adulterated with 80 per cent of foreign fat. Mr. Superintendent Williamson said be might state that the price of best salt butter was is. 4d. per lb. • but in this case a most inferior article was received for that price. Other samples of butter were purchased in the same neighbourhood, and were found pure.—Defendant said he had only been in business six or seven months, and he was ignorant of the quality of the butter.—He was fined 103. and costs. ROBBERY FROM A WIDNES CHEMICAL WORKS. At Widnes Police Court, yesterday, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, junr., a young man named Thomas Smith, was charged with stealing 90Ibs. of scrap lead of the value of us. 3d., the property of Messrs. James Muspratt and Sons. —John Junor, receiving clerk, who resided at 30, Milton- street, said that on the 10th January, from something that was said to him he went to examine some scrap lead, which was concealed near the footbridge at the works. It was in a corner, and covered with two pieces of old timber. He recognised the lead pro- duced. It was taken from the side of a melting pot in the centre of the chemical yard. It was not missed until it was discovered in its place of concealment. The lead had formed part of a chlorate absorber. There was a portion of the refuse of the chlorate upon the lead produced, which was part of that he had found. The prisoner was not em- ployed by the prosecutors.—Wm. Turton, foreman plumber, also identified the lead.—P.C. Murray deposed that he watched the lead on the night of the 10th inst. After the men had left work he saw the prisoner come out of the prosecutor's yard, and go into the corner where the lead was concealed. He went towards the prisoner, and found near him a piece of lead which had been concealed,-and the other pieces had been evidently disturbed. He took the prisoner into custody.—The prisoner, who had been previously conflicted, was committed to the Liverpool Sessions for trial.

ALLEGED ROBBERY AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, before Mr. S. B. Chadwick, two men named Charles Price and William Johnson were charged with having, on the Bth Japuary, stolen a shirt of the value of ss, the property of Edward Withington.—lnspector Hollingworth said from information received he appre- hended the prisoners in Mersey-street on the present charge, but they strictly denied committing the offence.—Samuel Hodgkinson, a youth, residing in Dover-street, stated that he saw the prisoner Price take the shirt from a clothes line os a piece of ground near John-street. RAILWAY SERVANTS' SUPPER AT WIDNES.—The railway officials of the Widnes London and North-Western passengtr station had their annual supper at Anderson's Hotel, Victoria-road. The caterivg was all that could be desited, and the 25 persons who were present thoroughly enjoyed the repast. The traffic department was represented by Mr. Carter, and the locomotive department by Mr. Turnbull. After the cloth had been drawn, Mr. Smith, the station- master, took the chair, and Mr. Carter occupied the vice- chair. The Chairman gave the usual loyal and patriotic toasts, and these were followed by the health of the chair- man, proposed by Mr. Ashton, to which Mr. Smith responded in a suitable speech; the officers of the railway company, proposed by Mr. Smith; the donors, by Mr. Ashton; &c. The proceedings were rendered of a highly entertaining character by a number of songs and recitations, which were given by Messrs. Lambert, Howard, and Dugan. Mr. Smith created much amusement by a recitation of a comical nature. The party broke up at midnight. In an article on "Lancashire Proverbs," in Satu:- slay's Manchester Guardian, appears the following satirical allusions to this distritt t--
" Preston for pinmugs, Huyton for pride, Childwall for toiling. And playing beside."
Another version runs:—
Presec,t, Huyton, and merry Childow, Three p trish churches all in a row ; Prescot for mugs. Huyton for ploydes. Childow for ringing and singing besides,"

LITAMFOIiI) b t.TNSELL.—The funeral of Lord Stamford took place on Tuesday, at Enfield Churchyard, near Stourbridge, in the presence of a large assemblage of persons from the surrounding district. Cheshire, Lanca- siiire;and Leicestershire also sent representatives. In the procession were Lord Ormathwaite, the Earl of Lanes- borough, Lord Colville, of Culross, Sir Robert Peel, Dr. Quain, and others. The Rev. A. Phillimore and the Rev. Robert Sayers conducted the services. The coffin, on which were placed rich floral tributes, was of oak, with brass mountings, and bore only a simple inscription, with the name of deceased and the date of his birth and death. The tenants preceded the coffin as it was borne from Enville Hall to the village church, and a large number of mourners fol- lowed. The coffin was placed in a new vault, which had been prepared for its reception.

BRICK-STREET AND FRIARS' GREEN BAND OF HOPE SOCIETX.—Last Tuesday evening this society recommenced the winter series of entertainments, which the Christmas and New Year holidays had retarded. The chair was taken by Mr. John Critchley: There was a large and attentive audience. The chairman, in his opening remarks, referred to the objects of this and other kindred societies for the young. In the Sabbath school, he said, the children read the Scriptures and were admonished from the same, leaving little room for temperance. Therefore, what the Sunday schools lacked in that direction the Bands of Hope supple- mented, training the children in the paths of truth and sobriety. A programme, both instructing and amusing, consisting of songs, recitations, solo, round, and dialogues, was rendered in an acceptable manner. A pleasant even- ing's enjoyment was brought to a conclusion by a humorous temperance dialogue entitled "Dr. Quack and his patients," the characters being well sustained. Mr. Joseph Critchley presided at the harmonium with his usual ability.

• A WARRINGTON AII.LINK STORE DEALER FINED.— William Plinston, licensed marine store dealer, was sum- moned before the Mayor, Major Cartwright, and Mr. Fair- dough, at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, for having failed to enter the description and price of 112ibs. of tea lead. Defendant pleaded that he had been unable to obtain a book for the purpose.—The Town Clerk (Mr. W. H. Brook) prosecuted, and said the summons was biought under the bye-laws relating to marine stone dealers. De- fendant took out a license on the 16th November, but he had taken no steps whatever to bring himself under the 'provisions of the bye-laws. Books had been printed a long time and he might have got one. One of the provisions of the bye-laws was that a marine store dealer should write the description and price of every article acquired by him, and the name of the person from whom they were purchased. When defendant got his license a sheet was given to him showing exactly what the kind of book was, and he was told where he could get it.—P.S. Bowen proved that he visited defendant's premises and found he bad not entered 112Ibs. of lead which he bad purchased from a grocer and sold to another marine store dealer.—The Bench fined the defendant 20s. and costs, and considered be was let off very easily. If he came again the fine would be £5 it least. OXFORD AND CAMBRIDGE SCIIOOLS EXAMINATION. The Oxford and Cambridge Schools Examination Board have arranged for a general examination for the lower forms of schools suited to boys of the age of 16, and for granting certificates to the successful candidates. These certificates give exemption from the preliminary examination for ad- mission to the medical profession, and from the preliminary examination of the Pharmaceutical Society. Full informa- tion respecting this examination can be obtained on applica- tion to the secretaries at Oxford and Cambridge. The report of the Board has just been presented to the Convoca- tion of Oxford and the Syndicate of Cambridge. Daring the past year examinations have been conducted at 60 of the principal high schools for boye, and 23 for girls. The boys' schools examined included the Warrington Grammar School. In the examinations for certificates there were 734 candidates, of whom 709 were boys and 23 girls, of whom 385 obtained certificates and 140 obtained distinction in one or more subjects. Out of the 734 candidates 140 had already obtained certificates in a former examination ; and of these 70 gained a certificate with distinction in the present year. Out of the 385 certificates 254 were such as would exempt from Responsions at _Oxford, 238 from Part 1., 140 from Part 11., and 69 from the additional subjects of the previous examinations at Cambridge. The examina- tions were conducted by 116 examiners, of whom 51 were members ef the University of Cambridge, 55 of the University of Oxford, and 10 others. SOcIAL GATHERING.—The second annual dinner of the inspectors and foremen in the engineers' department of the Cheshire Lines works, Warrington, has been held at the house of Mrs. Butterworth, Ram's Head, HersEmarket-street. After ample justice had been done to a most substantial re- past, served up in the hostess' best manner, Mr. Stephen Dale was unanimously called to the chair. In the course of a few introductory remarks he spoke of the pleasure it afforded him to meet and enjoy a social evening with all present at the close of another year. He concluded by pro- posing the health of "The Queen," which was loyally re- ceived, and drunk with musical honours. Other loyal and patriotic toasts followed, the toast of "The Cheshire Lines Committee Railway Engineers' Department" being ably re- sponded to by Inspector Hemingway. Songs were !sung at intervals by Messrs. Ward, Everett, Evans, Hemingway, Walker, Dixon, Foster, and Devine. Messrs. Whittaker, on the concertina, and Bolsworth, on the harp, played several choice selections, which were greatly appreciated. After the usual vote of thanks to the hostess a most enjoyable even- ;.ng was brought to a dose by the singing of the National Anthem. The company broke up sympathising with In- spector Porter, ani regretting his unavoidable absence.

LATEST NEWS.
We undsrstand that Lord Alcester will succeed Vice Admiral Lord John Hay, as second sea lord at the Admiralty.

Marwo-od arrived on Thursday evening at Kingstown, and proceeded, escorted by four constables in plain clothes, cn route for Galway. Mr. Sexton and Mr. T. D. Sullivan yesterday accompanied Mr. William O'Brien to Mallow, and will remain there to assist him in his election campaign. In connection with the elopement of Lady Macnaghton proceedings have been instituted in the Irish Divorce Court, and eminent counsel have been engaged. The Hon., Evelyn Ashley, Mr. 'Samuel Pope, and Mr. Robertson, M.P., are tiie Liberal candidates for Merioneth- shire on the retirement of Mr. Holland. A conference will make the final selection.

Steps are being taken in Cornwall to promote a memorial to the Archbishop-designate, irrrecognition of his connection with the county and the important services he has rendered to the church in the diocese.

It the army medical and transport inquiry, held at the War Office, yesterday, one of the medical officers of the Malabar emphatically denied that the invalids returning from Egypt had not been treated well. _ _

Lord—gdmond Fitzmaurice, replying to a resolution of congratulation from the Caine Liberal Associgtion ow his new appointment, says it will be his earnest endeavour to prove himself worthy of the position. A Parliamentary return issued yesterday. regarding Irish agriculture, states that the harvest of 1882, though un- favourable, did not approar:h that of the disastrous year 1879, nor that of 1872. Depreciation in money value of crops amounted in the aggregate to £5,818,167, compared with 1881, the great bulk of the money loss being on the potato crop, which showed diminution in value of £4,317,687 compared with the previous year. The Freeman's Journal is informed that Dr. Kinnear is about to resign the representation of Donegal, and that a distinguished Catholic gentleman, whe was not successful in securing re-election in 1880, will be put forward as the Government candidate.

An inquest was held at Dungannon yesterday upon Rose Quinn, housekeeper to a farmer, who was supposed to have been murdered. It was, however, proved that she died from exposure having lain on a mudheap all night. A verdict in accordance with these facts was returned.

The Dukes of Edinburgh, Connaught, and Cambridge, will accompany the Prince of Wales to Woolwich to-day to unvail the statue of Prince Imperial. Their Royal Highness's will remain at Woolwich three hours. r,t bifibbereen, yesterday, Mr. Mo lloy, Q.C., heard three claims for compensation under the Crimes'Act. The father of Downey, the murdered driver of Mr. Hutchins, landlord, claimed eight hundred pounds; Mr. Swanton, landlord, who received several gunshot wounds, fifteen hundred pounds; and a process server named Nelvan, two hundred hounds. The police gave the district a bad character.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 13, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 13, 1883.
MR: GLA-DSTONE'S CONDITION.

On inquiry at Hawarden Cattle yesterday morning, our Chester correspondent was informed that Mr. Gladstone passed another fairly good night, and that the cold and cough which are confining him to his room are better. If his health permits, he will leave Hawarden on Mon- day, and will probably proceed to the South of France.
THE CHESHIRE RECTOR AND HIS PARISHIONERS.

A Chester correspondent states that the Rector of Worles- ton, Cheshire, who was recently censured by the Education Department for insisting that a boy named tiump'areys, the son of the local station master (a Noncomformist), should attend divine service at the parish church during school hours or leave the school, has re-admitted the child, the Education Department having threatened to take away the school grant if he persisted in his determination.

DARING JEWELLERY ROBBERY AT GLASGOW. John Hall, who sated that he belonged to Liverpool, was remitted to the Sheriff, at the Central Court, Glasgow, yesterday morning, on a charge of having stolen diamond bracelets, of the value of £2,000, from a jeweller's shop in Bucliaman-street, Glasgow. Hall smashed the jeweller's window with a brick on Thursday afternoon, and made off wlt'a a case containing the diamonds. After a short run, he was apprehended with the case in his possession.

div.head: SHOCKING DISCOVERY IN MANCHESTER.
div.p: SHOCKING DISCOVERY IN MANCHESTER.

A shocking discovery has been made at Manchester. In St. George's churchyard, which is in the centre .of the busi- ness portion of the city, two men saw a suspicious looking parcel inside the railings, and on the police being com- municated with the parcel was found to contain the body of a fu!ly-developed male child. The head and front part of the body was much bruised, but it is as yet impossible to say whether the injuries were caused before or after death.

div.head: HOTEL FIRE IN AMERICA.: NINETY
div.p: THE HOTEL FIRE IN AMERICA.: NINETY

PER.SON-S STILL MISSING. Accordiig. to the latest reports received at New York re- gardiog the Milwaukie disaster, there were 110 visitors and 67 emplovei in the Newhall House Hotel at the tirne of the fire. Twenty dead bodies have been identified, and 67 per- sons are known to have been saved. The remaining 90 are missing' and most of them are believed to b 3 buried in the ruins. General Tom Thumb and his wife are amongst those who escaped.

div.head: RUMOURED MINISTERIAL CHANGES IN FRANCE. ,
div.p: RUMOURED MINISTERIAL CHANGES IN FRANCE. ,

An Exchange Company's telegram from Paris, Yesterday, states :—The rumours of Ministerial changes are unfounded, but the general opinion prevails in and out of Parliament that the Duclerc Cabinet will soon be defeated. A leading member of the Left said last night that it was too early yet to think of changing the Ministry, but the death of M. Gam- betta must lead to the partial reconstitution of the Left and Left Centre fractions. Then a Cabinet more in unison with the majority would be formed.

div.head: MRS. GLADSTONE IN EDINBURGH.
div.p: MRS. GLADSTONE IN EDINBURGH.

Mrs. Gladstone, accompanied by Mr. Herbert Gladstone, arrived in Edinburgh yesterday from Glasgow, on a short visit to Mr. John Cowan, of Beeslack, chairman of the Mid- lothian Liberal Association. At the Waverley station Mrs. Gladstone, who was received with cheers by a considerable crowd, was presented by Mr. Cowan with an address from the association giving her a cordial welcome and expressing the horSe that Mr. Gladstone would soon be restored to health. The party proceeded to the Council Chambers, where they were received by .Lord Provost Harrison, and several members of the Town Council. Mrs. Gladstone, in course of a conversation with his Lordship, spoke of the Prime Minister's great regret at his inability to sleet his constituents at the present time. The arduous session, the changes in the Cabinet, and the vacancy in the see of Can- terbury had created a large amount of extra work. Mrs. Gladstone afterwards drove to Dalmeny.

div.head: SHIPWRECKED SAILORS LEFT ON AN ISLAND.
div.p: SHIPWRECKED SAILORS LEFT ON AN ISLAND.

Information received from London yesterday morning I states that the four-masted iron ship Shakespfre, of Liver- pool. 1,812 tons, en a voyage from Cardiff to Calcutta, ran on a reef at Inaccessible Island, an uninhabited rock in the South Atlantic, during foggy weather, and foundered, but the whole of the crew and several passengers who were on board got away safely in the boats and reached the neigh- bouring island of Tristan d'Acunha, where they remained for eight days. when their signals of distress were seen by the emigrant ship Abbey Holme, bound for New Zealand, which sent off and tool; the master and nine men on board, and landed them at the Cape of Good Hope. Twenty per- sons were left on the island, but assistance will be sent as soon as possible.

FIER AT WARIZINGTON.—On Wednesday morning, a fire broke out in a shed over the boiler-house on the premises of Mr. H. Miller, corn and flour dealer, Academy- street. An alarm was immediately given, and Sergeant Rowbottom was speedily on the scene, and with the assist- ance of Messrs. Collin and Son, builders, whose prstnises adjoin, and several ethers, the fire was extinguished before the fire brigade arrived. It is supposed the tire originated from the overheating of the boiler. The shed, which was unoccupied, was not insured, and the damage is estimated at about £lO.

THr Snip Cum.—At a meeting of the Provisional .Com- mittee, it has been resolved that a call of 20 per cent. be mane upon each subscriber to the Parliamentary fund of £lOO,OOO upon the amount guaranteed by him. A circular has been issued, which states that the Wants and book of re- ference, together with the Bill, have been duly deposited, and that arrangements have been concluded for the Parlia- mentary deposit of £229,905. The committee add that they have found it necessary, in consequence of the considerable expense already incurred, to call upon the subscribers for !t percentage of their contribution. The first stage in opposi- tion to this measure has commenced by the London and North-Western Railway Company, the Mersey and Irwell and,Bridgewater Navigation Companies, the Upper Mersey Navigation Commissioners, and the Mersey Docks and llar- hour Board, who have lodged memorials at the private HI , office of the House of Commons, complaining of nen-corn- I pliance with the standing orders of Parliament.

div.head: %titer t* tht (Editor.
div.p: %titer t* tht (Editor.
" ANGLO-SCOTUS" TO "NEWTONIAN."

am afraid " Newtonian" has got his "monkey up," or he is too Scotch in temper for the English climate. I attempted to make a joke in my letter of Christmas Day in connection with the asserted plimness of a portion of ' that bridge; but he will not have it so. Well, if he insists that my augur is blunt, and the material I attempted to pierce impenetrable, I must submit. He gives me another opportunity for a joke or banter in his letter of the 6th January, where he states that he intended to be poetical. It is very kind of him to confirm my recent assertion that there were a lot of capital P's knocking about. And in this connection "'Newtonian" has himself unconsciously made a good joke, only it has the disadvantage of being against him. It is, however, none the less enjoyable on that account. Plimnese in individuals very often induces the poetic feeling, sometimes of a boisterous and noisy kind; it often also creates pugnacity, and a disposition to prance. But I will not be too hard upon him. A person who makes jokes unconsciously has my respedt. He has admitted that there is a reverse as well as an obverse side, and I presume that must be set down as one score to me. If he will read my letter again, he will see that I did not assert that my definition of "Pig and Whistle" was the only correct one. In fact, I gave him two to choose from, and merely stated that I preferred the religious reading— , i.e., the Scotch, or practical one. But "Newtonian," for a "dictionary man," has an unfortunate habit of impaling himself on his own prongs. Surely he knows the meaning of religion, as applied to habits. If he will turn to any manual on trade tokens or signs, he will find lots of definitions. For instance, to meet a sow and its young ones is considered lucky; and so it may be a corruption of "Pig and Litter." And surely " Newtonian " might pause be- fore he inflicts upon your readers at a festive season dry extracts from dictionaries in an attempt to prove so little. If it is allowable for him to transpose, add to, or subtract from the letters of a word or sentence, you may ultimately translate "Pig and Whistle" into almost anything—for instance, "Tea in Darkness," or "Mauling in Mud! And what on earth does he mean to prove or disprovetby the quotation from Butler? The lines read all right, but the author's meaning might be made clearer by the insertion of a comma in the first and in the last lines. " Newtonian " confesses to have been recently studying platos and muge, 41.111 thinking" while writtnis• Of the pipes of wine drunk in England in the olden time." Possibly the natare of the study accounts for the mixture" apparent in the last paragraph of his letter. I can assure "Newtonian" that what with his letter and the Newton news, I enjoyed the perusal of The Examiner last night more than the eight pantomimes, the whole or portion of which I had been com- pelled to witness or sit out during the previous fortnight. So I will forgive him his " hard " words. Will the com- positor do so? Take that New Year's gathering, for instance. The "venerable liquid" the company partook of must-have been strong. I had an explosion in my hoase on Christmas Day, but it was not caused by tea, although that beverage is brewed pretty often (I am partaking of a cup of it now with a cigarrette). Nor did it put the gas out, or evoke pug- nacity. It was, to my neighbours and ourselves, startling, amusing, and instructive. Colley Cibber makes one of the nharacters in "The Lady's Last Stake," say: "Tea, thou soft, thou sober, sage, and venerable liquid; thou female tongme-running,smile-smootlaing,heart-opening,wink-tipping cordial, to whose glorious insipidity I owe the happiest mo- ment of my life, let me fall prostrate!" What kind of tea do they brew at Newton, that it conduces to mischievous prac- tical joking, leading up to wrangling and struggling be- tween clergy and laity, culminating in • a roll in the mud during a downpour of rain? Glorious insipidity indeed! If that is the way in which the teetotallers of the district "prostrate" themselves before their idol as a symbol that they are passing a "happy 'moment in their lives," then, as I have said before, iievrtnn has not only got a fair share of "peculiar people," but has also furnished a practical defini- tion of the term "tea-fight " that should be at once sent on to the editor of the "Slang Dictionary." The circumstance recalls Pope's lines:—

What dire offence from amorous causes springs, What mighty contests rise from trivial things. It is just possible that some frisky lovers broeight about the annoying state of darkness with a view to stealing a few kisses, just as Lamb's Chinaman is said to have burnt down a house to secure a dish of roast pork. The incident would form another subject for " Newtonian's " fork, now that he admits there are two sides to a question. Bacon, I think, says, "Children fear the dark as men fear death." Do they really, at a certain age? Otway, again, asserts that— Children blessings .‘eam, but torments are; When young our folly, and when old-our far. . . . . . . .

I commend the syllogism which the incident and the quota- tions suggest to those who may choose to propound it. Verily there is nothing new under the sun. I will conclude with two more quotations : When to mischief mortals bend their will. How soon they find fit instruments of ill An though I have treated the incident in a jocular manner, I would earnestly entreat all those interested in the case to bear in mind that— To mourn a m'scitief that is past and gone, Is the next way to draw new _mischief on.
Wishing you, sir, "Newtonian," and the readers of The Examixer, a happy and prosperous new year,—! remain, .sir, ANGLO-SCO rus. Newington, London, January 7.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND LOCAL TAXATION. - A Welsh correspondent has received the following reply to a repre- sentation made by him to Mr. Chamberlain respecting local taxation :—" I am directed by Mr. Chamberlain to acknow- ledge the receipt of your letter of the 4th instant, and to say, in reply, that he does not think it would be proper for him to "offer any advice as to the action which you or others should take in regard to an agitation for reform in local taxation. All questions connected with this subject will have to be carefully considered by the Government before it makes any proposal to Parliament; but the manner in whicl. the discussion should be carried on, and the views of the country brought to the knowledge of Government, is entirely a matter for your own determination."

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Mr. G. Blackhurst (chairman) presided at the meeting of the Board, on Wednesday. Present—Rev. Yonge, Rev. G. F. Roberts, Major Cartwright, Messrs. Darbyshire, Long- shaw, Wallington, Appleton, Houghton, Greenall, Burn, Caldwell, Woolfall, Cooper, Humphreys, Marsh, Owen, Gibson, Taylor, Brown, and J. C. Sutton (clerk).

div.head: NEW SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE NEW SCHOOLS.

Major CARTWRIORT asked what likelihood there was of a removal to the new schools, and reminded the Board they would have to give a month's notice to the county of their intention to remove.—Mr. DA.RBYSIIIRB said the members of the Schools Committee had been trying to induce the Gae and Lighting Committee of the Corporation to lay gas in the neighbourhood of the schools at Padgate. • Applica- tions had been made by the church authorities, the station authorities, and others in the neighbourhood for gas to be taken there. He saw Mr. Paterson, manager of the gas- works, the previous day, and he said he had laid the matter before the committee, who had gone into it carefully. They, however, found there would be a loss of something like £4O or £5O a year, and the com- mittee decided it was not desirable to carry the mains to Padgate. Therefore the Schools Committee would have to adopt other means for lighting the schools, and he supposed the Board would consent to the purchase of lamps. The fixtures were being erected as rapidly as possible, and he hoped to be able to report very soon when they would be able to take the children to the new schools.
INSPECTION OF THE HOUSE.

The CLERK read the following report of the Inspector : "I have inspected the workhouse to-day, and I find it gene- rally in a very clean state; the only exception will have the officer's attention, and is where men are, employed as scrubbers in the sick hospital. The area of the washhouse and laundry seem barely sufficient, and I ant told that the baker's oven has had to be resorted to for drying clothes ii."

div.head: MATRON AND THE BOARD.
div.p: THE MATRON AND THE BOARD.

The CHAIRMAN informed the Board that he had received a communication from the Matron about her application for remuneration for extra services at the Barracks. He ex- plained that the matter had been considered by the Barracks Committee, whose decision the Board had confirmed, and that he, therefore, considered the present letter an insult to the Board.—Major CARTwitiGHT objected to the Chairman making such remarks before the letter had been read; and, after a passage-at-arms between the Chairman and the Major, the communication was read as follows :—" To the Chairman and Guardians of the Warrington Union.— Gentlemer,—l applied personally to the Barracks Commit- tee a few days since far remuneration which was promised me for extra services rendered during nine months whilst I had the management there; also for continuous supervision in regard tdtheir washing since that time, as well as for pre- paring, kc., their Christmas dinner. There were remarks made by one or two,especially Mr. Longshaw, which were most in- sulting. It was quite clear that the extent and character of my work vies not understood. In order, however, to answer any enquiries that may be made, and to avoid going into any disagreeable details, if you will kindly depute any of your number I will gladly furnish them with any infor- matien they may require to satisfy them of the justice of my claim. I am at all times most wishful, as is well known, to do whatever is within my power to carry out efficiently your wishes, and to help them out of their diffi- culties at the Barracks; but it is manifestly unfair to put this work upon me in addition to my arduous duties here without having some acknowledgment thereof, 1 am, etc., SARAH A. MACKEY."—The CLERIC stated that after the last meeting he wrote the Master to this effect : "The committee considered Mrs. Mackey's application, and could not concur therewith. Their minutes thereon are ap- proved by the Board. It was not pointed out to the com- mittee or the Board, but I may explain that the Guardians and the Local Government Board are by statute prohibited from making payments in respect of services determined over a year back; and that, therefore, the nine months' services following upon the removal of the children to the schools, oould not as a matter,oi law be entertained. Then the for- mer decision thereon, if it were otherwise, must have been rescinded. The committee, however, came to their decision apart from the difficulties I name, which are not, of course, applicable to the other grounds on which the matron based her application."—Mr. LONGSHAW, speaking with consider- able warmth, pointed out that for three weeks the matron did not go to the Barracks.—Major CastwetParrr here interposed, but Mr. LONGSHAW retorted : You hold your noise. (Laughter.) She has been your (the Board's) master, and she has said she would not do what you told her to do, and you had to go to the Local Government Board to compel her. Does she want compen- sation for breaking the orders of the Board? I think it is a perfect disgrace to ask for compensation, when Mrs. Mackey thinks that her family is kept in the Workhouse at ' an expense of nearly £lOO a year, and she does not pay a halfpenny of it. What compensation does she want? Does she want all the ratepayers have in their pockets? I think it is a perfect disgrace that such things should go on.— Major Caerrvertrour (to the reporters) : Report it verbatim. —Mr. LONGSHAW : Yes, report it. I think the ratepayers ought to rise as a body, and put down such an expenditure.—Mr. BURN said as to Mr. Mackey's children being at the house the Board were perfectly well acquainted with the circumstance. The Board knew they had the children there, as the master had told him he wanted the Board to give him an increae of salary, and he would pay for his children. Unasked if that was not so.-. The CLERK said the law was if any provisions that catne into the house for the supply of pauper inmates and the supply of the officers were used for any other purpose, it should be with the direct sanction of the Board, approved by the Local Go- vernment Board, because otherwise he was every week of his life signing a false return. He was every week in his life certifying the previsions were consumed by the officers entitled to food, and no other officers except those the Board directly stipulated oughfunder any circumstances to partake of food in that house supplied for the use of officers and in- mates.--Mr. BURN said the clerk was throwing duet in his eyes. Did not the clerk know of his own knowledge that these children were kept in the workhouse 2—The CLERK : No. I have not seen a child of Mr. Mackey's for the last four years.—The CHAIRMAN: If there is any arrangement with Mr. Mackey in regard to those children I do not know of it.—Major CARTWRIGHT remarked it was not a question as to whether the clerk knew who was on the premises. It was not the duty of the clerk to know. The man who was responsible was the master of the house, and therefore it was no use appealing to the clerk. Did the clerk recollect, when an increase of salary was applied for by the Master, what remarks wore made at the time 2—The CLERK: I have no recollection.—Major CARTWRIGHT : And you have been clerk of this Board 14 or 15 years 2—The CLERK: More than that. He remarked that the Master's salary had been increased from £BO to £9O, 90 to £lOO, and £lOO to £l2O, and he ventured to say that from the time of the latter increase no application for an increase of the Master's salary had been made to the Board.-. The Rev. J. YONGR : How long is that 2—The CLERK: When Mr. Woods was chairman.—Mr. HOUGHTON: What age are the children ?—The CLIRK : I tell you candidly I have not see a child of Mr. Mackey's for four years. It is quite true these children's being on these premises has been the subject of discussion and complaint over and over again; but I have always advised, as I have advised you now, children cannot be maintained here when they arrive at such an age as that they need food to keep them in a proper state of health. You must have the ap- proval of the Board and the Local Government Board as to the terms upon which children are to be kept.—Major CARTWRIGHT : Do you know these children are supported out of the ratepayers' pockets 2—The CLERK: I do not know.—Major CARTWRIGHT : And you say you don't know there was an arrangement come to that the master was not to make an application because the Board would make an arrangement about the children.— The CLERK: No.—Mr. DARZYSHIRE hoped the Board would confirm the minutes passed a fortnight ago. He did not think there was one word then said which could be con- strued into an insult by any reasonable thinking person. If a Guardian in the discharge of his duty from any cause did not use the choicest words perhaps it was to be regretted ; but there was nothing said in the discharge of the duties of the members of the School Committee which could be con- strued to be an insult. They plainly stated a few facts in the presence of Mrs. Mackey why they could not entertain her application. He considered if a Guardian was to be rounded upon in such a manner it was an insult to the Board, and the sooner it was pat an end to the better, for it was not the first time a Guardian had been grossly insulted by an officer of that Board.—Mr. BROWN thought it could not be truthfully contradicted that the matron had had additional labour, and he pointed cut that the medical officer had had an increase of salary for his extra services at the Barracks.— The eßev. J. Yonge thought it unfortunate a matter of this kind could not be discussed without such a display of heat. (Hear, hear.) Nearly every discussion on a matter of this kind created an amount of temper and party spirit which might be very amusing to the ratepayers, but was rather offensive to any one whose mind was at all filled with proper feelings. He reminded the Board that he was present at the committee meeting when the apiaication was made, and he hoped his presence in the chair was a sufficient guarantee that nothing of the nature of an insult would be allowed to pass. Mr. Longshaw certainly did speak with a degree of warmth, but he did not say any- thing approaching an insult. (Hear, hear.) He believed it was correct Mrs. Mackey did not present herself at the Barracks for the first few weeks the children were there. It was possible during the first few months the Master and Matron had placed upon their shoulders extra work, but supposing their labours were increased during that time Mrs. Mackey's labours since then had decreased; and if Mrs. Mackey was to be remunerated for extra services dur- ing the first nine months then her salary ought to be docked in consequence of the reduction of work during the last two years or 18 months—Major CARTWRIGHT said Mr. Yonge fds oeorewg the e tt hheer time whole mw eeo rfethewhena ll sixesl lr s . aMackey went to the Barracks to • one against the other; and washingtnhdewr aes es wypearnsosp:ieortlhyheeycal oanweoe. were et hThefiegehsstitiaanbffg. l lishment, but the committee came to the conclusion to . debar Mrs. Mackey going down there at all. What was the result? The exhibition they saw at that Board in regard to the washing. He exposed the whole of the mismanage- ment, and then Mr. Yonge took the opportunity of removing him from the committee. Why? Because he did not approve of his (the Major's) method—he exposed too much' but the result of the exhibition was that there was con- siderably better management afterwards. When the matron at the barracks asked for remuneration not long ago. was the question raised in the manner it had been that morning? It was all very well for Mr. Yonge to say he did not think

Mr. Longshaw spoke pointedly in the remarks he made. He wanted to know if Mr. Longshaw gave an exhibition of feeling similar to that that morning.—The Rev. J. loamit : Certainly not —Major CARTWRIGHT said he had it from a private member that the treatment was anything but what it ought to be. It was only fair and just that they should treat every application to that Board in a gentlemanly man- ner. (Hear, hear.) The chairman, whose duty it was to take an independent part, never same near the house, and did not see the way in which it was conducted. He was sorry to say Mr. Blackhurst was the only chairman he had known who had taken so little interest in the welfare of the House. Independent of the feeling the chairman might have against Mr. and Mrs. Mackey—which he had shown that morning deliberately—it had nothing to do with the busi- ness of the House.—The CHAIRMAN: I must object to Major Cartwright. It is very unfair.—Major CARTWRIGHT: It is not.—The CHAIRMAN: As long as I am chairman of the Board—Major CARTWRIGHT: I shall not support this ap- plication at all. I have no feeling in it. I will not say one single word about it, but I do say this, a more unfair remark at the commencement of the reading of an application by the chairman I have never heard.—The CHAIRMAN : As long as I am chairman of this Board I shall act independently of what he may say. I have a duty to perform, and I shall do it fearlessly. As to my not going to the House, I have my reasons for not going, and I tell you I shall not go to the House.—Major CARTWRIGHT: I tell you it is quite true.— Mr. LONGSHAW rose to speak, but the Chairman said unless there was a resolution proposed by some gentleman there was an end of the business altogether. Mr. GREENING: It's a waste of time.—Mr. OWEN : It has been a waste of time all morning.—Major CARTWRIGHT: I beg to give notice of motion tbat the letter be taken into con- sideration this'day fortnight.—Mr. CALDWELL moved that such notice be not nceived.—Mr. BURN: You can't do that.—The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Baru, independent of your eight years services at York, I must take the clerk's advice. —Mr. BURN: Mr. Chairman, allow me—(load cries of " chair.")—l rise to a point of order. (Cries of "chair.")— Mr. Caldwell then rose, and was greeted with cries of "chair."—Mr. GREENING: Mr. Burn has not spoken on this subject.—Mr. BURN : No, I have not —Major CART- WRIGHT: I think you ought to give way on account of his large experience. (Laughter.)—The CHAIRMAN: I must put this to the vote.—Mr. BURN: Oh, no. The Rev. J. YONGE : I rise to order. Who is the ruling authority of this Board? If the chairman has ruled against Mr. Burn, the latter ought to submit. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Bunk: If I produce the Orders.—The CHAIRMAN: I rule you out of order.—Mr. BURN: You don't know what I am going to say. He then read an extract to show that Major Cartwright's course was the right one. The vote was then taken, with the result that 11 members supported the pre- vious decision and 6 opposed. Major Cartwright did not vote.—The CHAIRMAN: I think that is decisive ensugh.—. Major CARTWRIGHT: Then I beg leave to give notice that the application of Mrs. Mackey be taken into consideration this day fortnight.—After a brief discussion it was decided that the clerk should not send out the usual circulars of notice of motion.

div.head: CHILDREN'S TREAT.
div.p: CHILDREN'S TREAT.

_ Mr. MINES (superintendent of the schools) reported as follows:—" On bekalf of the children I have to thank the numerous subscribe 7 to their Christmas tree fund. The prizes were distributed by the Rev. J. Yonge, chairman ef the Schools Committee, on Tuesday evening last, in the girls' day room, which had been tastefully decorated for the occasion. Many subscribers and other friends were present to witness the distribution. The band was in attendance and played a selection of popular music during the evening. The Rev. J. Yongs and Mr. William Darbyshire made suit- able addresses to the children at the commencement and close of the proceedings. The total amount of money subscribed was £7 2s, total expenditure in the purchase of toys .£5 17s, leaving a balance of £1 ss. Every child received a prize." It was further stated that the Rev. S. Wilkinson sent a small Christmas tree for the children, which was ordered to be ac- knowledged with thanks.

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST THE PORTER.
div.p: CHARGE AGAINST THE PORTER.

The MASTER reported under date sth inst. :—" Police- constable Clianiivr brought Mathima Ward, and informed me he had applied to the justices for a summons against Mr. Curry, the porter' for perjury, arising out of the charge he preferred against him the week previous, and they referred him to the Guardians. I told Ward if he had any complaint or charge to make, the committee would meet at half-past two o'clock to-day, and he could appear before them, but when I sent for Ward he had gone and could not be Nand."

div.head: MASTER'S REPORT.
div.p: MASTER'S REPORT.

The MASTER reported under date Bth inst.: Mr. Sheridan kindly invited the old people and the children from here and the Barracks to the mid-day performance of the panto- mime at the Prince of Wales Theatre, a treat which they all greatly enjoyed. The Guardians will be pleased to hear the profit on the keeping of pigs is £lO5 14s 21 during the year.

div.head: MOTIONS.
div.p: MOTIONS.

On the propasition of Major CASTRIZIGHT, the following motion, of which he had given notice, was adopted: "That medicines hereafter used at the Workhouse be supplied at the cost of the Guardians, and not, as hitherto, at the cost of the Workhouse medical officer."—Mr. BURN moved "that except as prohibited by the Consolidated Orders tradesmens' bills and officers' salaries be paid monthiy instead of quarterly," but after some conversation the motion was withdrawn.

div.head: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH TEA PARTY.
div.p: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH TEA PARTY.

The annual tea party and entertainment in connection with Holy Trinity and St. Mary's churches was held in the Public Hall, Warrington, on Monday, when about 300 per- sons partook of tea. A sale of ladies' work was held during the interval between the tea and entertainment and realised about £l3. This sum is to be devoted to the foreign mis- sion cause, the tea party being in aid of the Sunday schools. Mr. Robert Pierpoint presided at the entertainment, which was given by the united choirs with the assistance of Mr. Levison Myatt (tenor), of Chester Cathedral, and under the direction of Mr. Johnson (organist). There were also on the platform the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, and A. H. Jones, Messr. W. Burgess, Brundret, and Hatton.—The CHAIRMAN, in addressing the rneeting,said that they would.all be aware of the object of their meeting together that night. It was, be might say, in the 11:st place, in honour of Holy Trinity Church, and in the second place, for the promation of edu- cation through the means of that Church. But what he would say would be more with respect to general education than the object of the meeting. Pope had said about two hundred years ago,
'flu education forms the common mind: Just as the twig is bent the tree's inclined. _ _ _

He (the chairman) wished to speak of the education of the poor little boys and girls who were to he met with in the streets of our great towns. Take for instance the little boys belonging to the training ships and similar establishments and institutions.— these showed that they had had the benefits of education conferred upon them. He remembered once meeting in Pall Mall a number of boys who belonged to a training ship, and the Prince and Princess of Wales were passing at the time. As soon as the boys became aware of the fact they instantly turned round and the band played "God bless the Prince of Wales." He mentioned such an incident to show what education could do. But let them look at the other extreme. He thought there could not be a sight more heartrending to either man or woman than the sight that one might meet with in any large town in England—to see the little waifs and strays of life eking out a miserable existence in the streets, perhaps selling newspapers, or pre- tending to sell matches. It was a terrible thing to think that these children had no prospect before them; if educa- tion stepped in then they had, and he hoped it would. They had not got a school board in Warrington and he hoped they never would. He for one would be the last to speak against national education, but he would mention a few of the various advantages they would have from having no school board in the town. They would refrain from quarrelling among themselves, and each denomination would go on doing what it could for the education of the people. Then they would avoid the necessity for a school board rate • but perhaps the greatest gain they would have for putting themselves forward for education in denominational schools would be that they would not have that education that was devoid of religion. Still he would say that in those towns where they had school boards any education was better than none at all. He would close his remarks on this question with what Sir Thomas Moore had said. If they suffered their people to be ill-educated, and their manners to be corrupted from infancy, and then punish them for those crimes their education had given them, they made of them thieves and then punished them afterwards. The speaker then referred to the bazaar and its object, and stated that they had the promise of a very munificent gift from Sir Gilbert Greenall. (Applause.)—The united choirs then sung the part-song "The sea king," after which Mr. Myatt sang " Once again" in such a pleasing manner that the audience insisted on an encore, to which he responded with" The anchor's weighed." —The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON then addressed the meeting. After some remarks with regard to the parsons and the lay- men, he said, as those present would be aware, there was now the prospect of their obtaining a Sunday school for that part of the parish—(applause)—and of course he must mention the name of the gentleman to whom they were everlastingly indebted for placing that within the range of possibility. As they would know, they owed it to the muni- ficmce of Sir Gilbert Greenall. (Applause.) He had come forward and offered them £5OO if they would take the matter in hand. He (the speaker) hal simply called upon him to inform him of their annual tea party, and to ask him to preside, and, after hearing of the difficulties with which they were beset, he, with all that interest they knew he showed in the welfare of the church, freely and sponta- neously offered that sum if they would take the matter up at once. With due respect to the shareholders of that hall, he would say that he hoped it would be the very last time they would hold their tea meetings there. He then referred to the bazaar which the society intend to hold, and said they would want the assistance of every one of them to make it a success. He was sure it would not only have the support of the people in the par;sh but the people in the district. He might say that the building they intended to erect would be used as a day school, and would, therefore,snpplement the dLy schools of the town, and in doing that they would be making the entrance of the school board into the town as remote as possible. He did not think that those who introduced school boards looked up m them with the same degree of affection that they once did. Although a school board might look very well at a distance, and be nice to read about, yet to have the real living thing among them he was sure they :had no desire. He again reminded them of the donation by Sir Gilbert Green-

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
TUESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffonllces, judge. INTERESTING CASE TO LANDLORDS AND TENANTS.

John Yapp claimed from Thomas Bate, of Aston, the sum of £lO 108 6d, for damages caused through breach of agree- ment. Mr. Radon represented the plaintiff, and Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the defendant. A jury, of which Mr. Joseph Jeffs was foreman, was empannelled to decide the case. The particulars of the claim were £8 for painting, £2 108 cost of re-papering, £1 10s damage to blue satin couch, and lOs 6d damage to curtains.—Mr. Hitchen, in opening the case, said the plaintiff was the tenant of a house owned by the defendant at Overton, near Frodshame On the 29th September, 1880, a lease was entered into between the parties, in which the plaintiff undertook to keep the inside of the house in good, substantial repair and condition, while the defendant was to repair the outside walls. According to an agreement previously entered into, the defendant allowed the plaintiff £5 out of his first half year's rent towards the expense of re-papering and re-painting the house, which at the time the plaintiff entered was in a very unfinished state. The plaintiff had, however, spent considerably more than that sum in decorating. After the tenancy had been run on for some time, it was found that tie house became very damp, although the outside walls had been covered with cement. He had no complaint to make of the manner in which the cement had been put on, but it was "rough faced," and con- sequently would not keep out damp so well as "smooth- faced "cement. In the drawing-room water drove in under the roof at a point where the cement did not join the roof of the bay window. There was some lead " flashing "of come kind put in, but it did not seem to cause any improve- ment, and the paper began to come off. The dampness was so great that some varnished paper on the top of the stair- case Wai, Constantly CoVerect With a blue mould. 'lne porosity of the cement was shown by the fact that when a shower of rain took place it became black, in consequence of the water it had absorbed. under any circumstances there must be some difficulty in keeping the house dry owing to its exposed position, and only having 9-inch walls and a covering of rough cement. In November, 1881, the plain- tiff complained to the defendant of the dapapness of the house, and the former suggested that the house should be painted. The result of the conversation which then took place, was that the defendant instructed the plaintiff to get a tender for the painting, the latter undertaking to paint the back side of the house. Plaintiff received a tender for the painting from Mr. 011iver, of Run- corn, on November 8, IEBI, and on November 24th the defendant's wife instructed hine to accept the tender, which he did on the following day. In that tender Mr. 011iver agreed to paint the front and gable end of the' house, which the defendant undertook to pay for, for £6. On December 3rd the defendant and another man supposed to be Mr. Gleave, the builder, went to the house, and the former said he understood that his wife had given an order for the painting, but he should like some guarantee that the paint would cure the damp, and the builder stated that in a few months' time the paint would be running down the gutter like whitewash. However, on the 12th December the paint- ing was carried out according to contract, and it had stood twelye montbs' wear and tear, and that through a very damp and trying season.—The plaintiff was then called, and said he was manager to the Old Qaay Mill Co., Runcorn, and resided at Rock Villa, Overton, Frodsham. His evi- dence bore out his advocate's statements, and, speaking of the damage to his furniture, said a blue satin couch had been bleached white by the lime. It would cost £4 or £5 to re-cover it. Three pairs ef curtains had been injured, and he had had to re-paper at a cost of £2 10s.—Benja- min 011iver, painter, Parker-street, Runcorn, gave evidence as to painting the outside and papering a portion of the in- side .of the house. He deposed that the walla were very damp.—Mr. H. Heywood, chemical manufacturer, Runcorn, said he had frequently visited the plaintiff's house during the last 18 months, and he corroborated the statement of the plaintiff in regard to the damages caused by the damp- ness of the property.—Mr. James Kirkham, builder, Run- corn, 20 years' experience of building trade, said the house was in a very exposed situation. It had nine inch brick walls, and was cemented at the front and gable ends. He did not think that "rough-faced cement" and nine inch walls would keep out the damp without paint.—Mr. Linaker, in defence, submitted that there was no case to go to the jury in reference to the claim of .26 for painting.—His Honour said there was no evidence to show that the wife, had authority to make that contract. That claim had faind. —Mr. Linaker also submitted that there was no case to go to the jury on the claim for £2 101. for repairs to walls. His Honour did not concur, and Mr. Linaker addressed the jury for the defence at some length. He said the jury had to determine now whether the defendant had been guilty of a breach of covenant of his lease and become responsible to the plaintiff for the damage to curtains 103. 6d., cost of re-papering £2 10s., and damage to a satin couch £1 10s. He drew attention to the fact that the lease was not signed for nearly 19 months after the plaintiff had become a tenant of the house. In that lease provision was made that the defendant should allow the plaintiff £5 if he satisfied the defendant that he had spent that amount on good and substantial repairs to the property. The plaintiff admitted on cross- examination that if the £5 had been expended on painting the external wall, there would have been no need for the jury to hold that inquiry that day. The plaintiff's witness, Mr. Heywood, said that three months after Mr. Yapp took possession his attention was drawn to the fact that damp was coming through the walls, and that cloths had to be laid ta catch the water, but the plaintiff executed the lease six months afterwards. Directly that was done he went to the defendant and said he should like the outside wall painted. If Mr. Yapp bad thought that by signing the lease Mr. Bate was to exoend money upon any repairs to the property—upon painting the outside wall—should he not have insisted upon having something done to it when there was allowed £5 towards the repair of the property? He asked the jury to put themselves in Mr. Yapp's position. If they had sustained the damage Mr. Yapp said he bad six months before the lease was signed, would not they have said to Mr. Bate, "I cannot sign this lease. There is a provision that you shall maintain the outside walls and main beams in repair, and I must have something done before I sign my name to that piece of paper." The understanding was that Mr. Yapp was to accept the house in its then condition. He had examined it, and knew the cement was not pointed. Mr. Linaker called no witnesses, an 4 His Honour, in directing the jury, impressed upon them that they could not take cognizance of any agreement outside the lease. It at the time the lease was signed the outside walls were merely cemented and not painted the covenant with respect to keeping the outside walls in good and substantial repair, would not, as a matter of law, oblige the lessor to paint the walls, because it was not part of the building when it was let. The house was let as-a house with cemented walls, and as such the lessee was willing to take it. There was no doubt that damp dith•come through the walls. The question was whether the damp came through the wall and damaged the furniture owing to some neglect on the part of the defendant to keep the outside walls in repair. Mr. Yapp was well aware of the dampness when he signed the lease, when there was no paper on the walls, but there was nothing then to indicate that there was a de- fect in the wall. He could sympathise with Mr. Yapp as he had no doubt suffered a good deal, but he could only point out one defect in the wall, a small aperture over the bay window. The only damage traceable to that was really the , damage to the couch, and it might be some damage to the curtains. That, however, was not quite clear.—The jury, after about fifteen minutes' consideration, returned a verdict for the plaintiff, 303. damages.

A RUNCORN PUBLICAN CHARGED WITH FELONY,

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Walker was charged with having, on the 16th ult., feloni- ously stolen and led away a mare, the property of George Meek, a boatman, residing at 45, Surrey-Btre6t Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich, appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Burton for the defendant. —From the complainant's ad- vocate's statement it appeared that in the month of August last the defendant, who is landlord of the Navigation Inn, sold the complainant a horse for £7. A memorandum was drawn up setting forth the bargain between the parties, the arrangement being that the plaintiff should pay ss. for each trip he made with his boat. The complainant proceeded to carry out the arrangement strictly. He only made eight trips, and be had paid £9. Everything went on right until the lekh December. On that day, about four o'clock in the afternoon, the defendant met the complainant on the canal bank, where he forcibly took possession of the horse, using considerable violence to the complainant in doing so.—Mr. Fletcher remarked that he believed it would be contended that because he (the defendant) did this outrageous thing openly he was not guilty of felony, but it seemed to him (Mr. Fletcher) that the rights of property in Runcorn must be vastly different to what they were in other places if such a state of things was to be allowed. The clerk would I advise their worships that after the horse was delivered into the custody of the complainant, the property was vested in him, and the defendant, if he had...any claim at all, ought to have pursued the orderly way in which good citizens asserted their claims, and taken action in the County Court.—The complainant gave evidence confirming this statethent, and alleged that the defendant whilst seizing the horse tried to "throttle " him (the complainant), and with his finger nails pulled bits of flesh from his hands. —ln cross-examination by Mr. Burton, the plaintiff admitted that he had "swopped" the horse with another man, but he afterwards had it returned to him.—P.C. Kelly was called, and deposed to seeing the dispute about the horse, but declined to interfere as it was a matter for the County Court.—. Without hearing the case for the defence, the Bench gave their decision that there was no felonious intent, and Mr. Fletcher announced that be would take action in the County Court, where Mr. Burton said he was quite prepared to meet him.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Mr. John Ashton (vice-Chairman) presided at the fort- nightly meeting of this Board, held on Tuesday, at the Workhouse, Dutton. There were also present—Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. J. Lockwood; Messrs. Thomas Massey, Joseph Stokes, Thomas Andrews, George Whitlow, Peter Hall, John Davies, Wm. Jackson, James Darbyshire, Robert Ashton, Wm. Pickering, Wm. div.head: RESIGNATION OF AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER.
div.p: THE RESIGNATION OF AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER.

A copy of a letter from the Local Government Board to the assistant overseer for the townships ef Halton, Walton Superior, and Walton Inferior, was read, acknowledging the receipt of his letter on the 6th inst., respecting his proceed- ings as assistant overseer for those townships. The letter stated that the Board, having c.3mmunicated with the over- seers of the several townships on the subject, had decided, under the circumstances of the case, not to press for his immediate resignation, but to allow him to retain office until 25th of March next.

div.head: ALLEGED NEGLECT BY A MEDICAL OFFICER.
div.p: ALLEGED NEGLECT BY A MEDICAL OFFICER.

Thomas Clark, an elderly man, was called into the Board Room and questioned respecting the accident which he had met with, and the alleged neglect of Dr. Willett to attend him. Clark stated that he broke his leg one dark foggy night by slipping on the pavement, and on the following day was taken to the Warrington Infirmary. On coming out of that institution he applied for an order for medical attendance, but Dr.Willett refused to attend him, and he had never seen his leg..—A committee, consisting of five mem- bers, was appointed to investigate the matter.

div.head: INCREASE OF SALARY.
div.p: INCREASE OF SALARY.

Mr. Tuozcsa Nos.(AN, in the absence of Mr. Mclntyre, moved the motion of which that gentleman had given notice with respect to the increase of the salary of Dr. Robinson. He said the committee had carefully considered the increased work of Dr. Robinson since he took the office 18 years ago. At first he had 30 beds in the hospital, and now there were 80, all of which he believed were nearly filled. In the earlier years of the office it took him something like half- an-hour to do his work, while now it took him an hour and a half or two hours. Taking into account his long servi- tude and the distance he travelled four times a week, he greatly deserved the increased salary. Since November he had had to come half-a-dozen times in the night, and his medicine cost him nearly LEO out of the MO. The com- mittee recommended that the doctor's salary be increased to £9O, that was an increase of £3O, and he did not think it was a penny too much for the work he had to do.—Mr. ROBERT ASHTON seconded the proposition, and fully endorsed everything Mr. Norman had said. The committee were unanimously of opinion that they would not be giving him too much if they gave him £9O, and half of that would be paid by the Local Government Board.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said it was a question with the committee whether £9O WdS sufficient. The doctor was present, and it was understood that he would accept Nortmes : Mr. Jones informs the committee there has not been in the 18 years one single complaint about Dr. Robinson's work. (Hear, hear.)—The motion was unanimously carried.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday. Mr. S. Marsh presided, and there were also pre- sent the Rev. .1. Barnacle, Messrs. Fidler, Dobai!, Swift, Lowe, Syder, Gerard, P. Longton, Hall, Birchall, Leather- barrow, Newsome, Hughes, and Hartley (clerk.)

A letter was read foom the Local Government Board ap- proving of the appointment of Dr. Edward Casey, to ths office of medical officer for Sutton district at a salary of £45 per aanum.

div.head: WDOLTON AND HALL
div.p: WDOLTON AND HALL

A letter was read from the Local Government Board acknowledging receipt of a letter from the clerk,, as to the agpointment of Dr. T. A. Wood, medical officer for Wootton district, to act as medical officer for Hale district. The Board stated that the representations of the Guardians should receive due consideration, but they wished to be furnished with information as to whether it was not in the power of the Guardians to appoint a medical practitioner for Hale who did not already hold the office of district medical officer.—The CLERK said it had been customary for one person to hold the dual appointment of medical officer for Hale and Wootton, and with regard to vaccination, the Local Government Board had themselves suggested the joining of the two districts. In answer to the chairman, he stated that the salary of the medical officer for Hale was DI a year.—The clerk was instructed to reply to the Local Government Board in the terms of his statement.

'VAGRANCY. A letter was read from Mr. Brewig, town clerk, St. Helens, and magistrate's clerk, suggesting the advisability of the Guardians providing " casual " wards for vagrants at St. Helens.—On the motion of Mr. HALL, seconded by Mr. NEWSOME, the subject was referred to the Building Committee.

The CLERK read a letter from Dr. Cooper, medical officer for Widnes, calling attention to the fact that the present Vaccination Station, at 00, Victoria-road, Wines, was un- suitable and insufficient for the requirements of the town. Mr. FIDLER announced the receipt of a handscfme present of woollen goods to inmates of the Workhouse by the Hon. Miss St. Clair and the Hon. Mrs. Feilden, of Knowsley. The present bad been made through Mr. Syder, the Guar- dian of that townshin. Mr. Fidler moved a vote of thanks to the donors, and it was seconded by Mr. NEWSOME, and agreed to.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY EXPENSES,
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY EXPENSES,
