div.head: ST. HELENS LITEIIARY & SCIENTIFIC ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ST. HELENS LITEIIARY & SCIENTIFIC ASSOCIATION.

A meeting of this association was held on Tuesday even- ing to Fear a paper by Mr. E. R. Russell, of Liverpool, on " Character created by Art." The president (Mr. R. Pilking- ton) occupied the chair. The paper, which was enriched with numerous and well-chosex literary illustrations, was chiefly directed to the application of the arts, plastic, pictorial, and literary in the formation of moral character. Summing up the conclusions deduced from the premises laid down in the paper, Mr. Russell said that whether or not it might be possible to alter the face of the world or the face of our own character in the short time that was allowed to us, we were bound, however little our prospect of Success, to try to do it. In the whole history of art, philosophy, and moral suasion we saw that principle at work, and the effect of it had been to peo- ple the world with forms of beauty, images of thought and treasures of literature which, even if it were a mere question of enjoyment would be price- less and would make the creations of human art and imagination perfectly collossal and beautiful in our estima- tion. But beyond that there was moral art to which the other arts greatly contributed, but which must have its real basis and strength in the control of our own nature, and in this way he urged that our endeavour should be to create that noblest result of art, and approach to a perfect moral character, undisturbed by the vicissitudes of time, the troubles of life, or the gusts of temptation, so that we might take credit to ourselves for having used to the best advantage those great gifts which the progress of the world had offered to us, and which we believed to be not lass truly connected with the triumphs of art and moral control than with the resources of nature and the progress of the universe.—The reading of the paper was followed by a short discussion, in which the Rev. J. P. Ritchie, Mr. C. C. White, the president, ,and Dr. McNicoll took part, and a vote of thanks was given to Mr. Russell.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.

LYMM. LYMM CHURCH TEA PARTY. About 300 persons attended the annual tea and entertainment in connection with Lymm Church, held on Monday evening, in the parochial schools. Trays were given by the following : Mesdames Norris, Swanwick, Brabazon, Bayley, Guest, Battersby, Stubs, Williamson, T. Ardern, Brazendale, M. Crosfield, R. Smith, Henshall, Fox, Pearson, Hoult, Schwabe, Pearse, and the Misses Robinson and Browning. At the entertainment the vicar, the Rev. G. W. Guest, pre- sided, and gave a summary of the work done in the parish during the year. The Rev. J. Cullen, of Oughtrington, the Rev. J. Lomas, curate of Lymm, Mrs. G. Hall, Mrs. Addenbrook, Miss Pearson, Colonel Godfrey, Mr. Pearse, and Mr. Mitchell, also took part in the entertainment, the proceeds of which were in aid of the parish clothing club.

div.head: LEIGH.
div.p: LEIGH.

The Rev. Richard Nicholson, vicar of Christ Church, Pennington, Leigh, died on Saturday evening. Mr. Nichol- son, who was educated at St. Bees, was ordained at Chester in 1846, and he held the living of St. Paul's, Burnley, from 1851 until August, 1879, when he exchanged benefices with the Rev. I. W. Milner. The patronage of Christ Church is vested in the Simeon Trustees,

• Two MEN KILLED NEAR LEIGII.—On Sunday night the bodies a two men belonging to Bolton were recovered from the ruins of a mill at Chowbent, near Leigh, which was burned down some time ago. The deceased were engaged last Wednesday in removing the machinery, and were evidently killed by a fall of debris. They were not missed for some days, and the search for them was only made on Sunday evening.

div.head: ROBY.
div.p: ROBY.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT ROBY.--All inquest was held on Tuesday, by Mr. Clarke Aspinall, coroner of Liverpool, on the -body of Michael John Rylance, aged thirteen years, son of a farmer's carter, who lives at Crouton, near Rainhill. The father came to Liverpool on New Year's Day with a waggon and three horses, in order to take back to Crouton a load of manure. Upon passing through Roby he met the deceased, whom he placed on one of the shafts with his legs hanging down the side, while he himself walked on the other side of the vehicle. He had told the deceased not to attempt to get down without letting him know, but after proceeding about a quarter of a mile he saw the lad lying on the road, just in advance of the front wheel. Before the horses could be stopped the wheel went over the deceased's shoulder and injured the side of his head. A doctor was sent for, who ordered the boy's removal to the Royal In- firmary. Deceased died in that institution on Sunday. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." . SANDBACH.

SHOCKING ACCIDBNT IN CREWE WORIS.—John Shaw, of Sandbach, was on Tuesday walking near a vat of boiling caustic fluid in the London* and North-Western Railway Company's works at Crewe, when he stumbled and fell into it, being frightfully scalded and otherwise injured. He was removed to the company's hospital, where he was attended by Dr. Atkinson. His condition is precarious.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

PAROCHIAL TEA AT WHARTON:The annual tea con- nected with Christ Church, Wharton, was held on Tuesday last, and as in previous years was well attended, and very popular. The genial and kind-hearted vicar having the hearty co-operation of the neighbouring clergy and laymen of his congregation, together with a number of ladies, and a good choir under the organist, Mr. Singleton, all rendered good service. An ex-parishiener from America gave his short experience of American life, to the delight of many. The whole affair passed off well. The speeches of the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, M.A., Rev. E. Nixon, M.A., and Mr. C. Cross pleased, as did the songs of Mr. Timperley, THE SALVATION ARMY.—The Army has been dealing out slaughter with a high hand during the week. Fire and blood, war and carnage, noise and tumult, as if from Edom, and with dyed garments from Bozrah. There has certainly been an unsabbath-like noise in the great drum and other instruments which the Army has added to the great detri- ment of more orderly and babbath-keeping people. It utay he their policy to draw out some who will only come out for such parade, but in so doing many think the Army noisier than discreet.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

TERRIBLE SUICIDE IN • Can.—A tragic event occurred at Wigan on Monday night. A young man, about half-past five, hailed a cab on the Wigan railway stand and requested the driver to take him to a house in Dower Ince, about a mile distant. He had with him a small paper parcel, and he informed Bannister, one of the best known among the local cab drivers, that he w(ts not so well. On arriving at his destinaticn Bannister opened the door of the cab, but his fare did not make any movement, and, the driver thinking that perhaps he had been taken seriously unwell, proceeded to carry him into the house. It was then found that he was dead, and further examination showed that he had com- mitted suicide by shooting himself down his mouth. On the floor of the cab were found a packet of cartridges and a loaded six-chambered revolver, one barrel only having been discharged. There was no blood about, and the young fellow lay across the seat. The cabman states that he never heard any firing, and his consternation was quite as great 38 that of the occupants of the house. The deceased was a puddler at a neighbouring ironworks, and was lodging at the address given, but for the past few days he had not been working, owing to an attack of pleurisy.

div.head: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
div.p: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

At the annual meeting of the Wirral Farmers' Club, on Tuesday, several resolutions were passed, after some discus- sion, affirming the right of the farmer to compensation for improvements, to freedom of cropping, to a year's notice to quit, to the abolition of the law of distress, and to an amend- ment of the Ground Game Act.

DEPRESSION IN THM CHESHIRII SALT TRADE.—The salt pruprietors are looking forward hopefully to the spring for a renewal of activity in the salt trade. In order to revive business and induce more remunerative prices, the winter stocks have been decreased by half a million tons, and this has been accomplished by shutting off pans. The trade is dull throughout the whole salt district of Cheshire. The total exports for December, just'completed, were 1,091,823 tons.

SWINE FEVER IN CHISIIIRE.-At a special sitting, on Thursday, under the provisions of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, the Hyde magistrates issued an order declar- ing a large portion of the township of Tintwistle to be an infected arena, swine fever having broken out on the pre- mises of Thomas Farrand, James Wilde, John Buckley, and others. The district has been singularly free from infectious diseases of late.

DIE STOPPAGE OF A CANAL IN CHESHIRE. A large body of men are still at work upon the canal locks which a short time ago collapsed opposite Beeston Castle station. Owing to the quicksands the loek is cased with sheets of iron about an inch thick, and these have been displaced on both sides of the lock. The work of repairs has gone on uninter- ruptedly night and day since the occurrence, and is still likely to last another week or 10 days. The work is most difficult, the excavations having to extend some distance round the iron sides in all directions, and this is a treacher- ous bottom. A number of boats are waiting the opening of the traffic.

DEATH FROM VIOLENCE AT CWBSTER.—The Chester city coroner held an adjourned inquest, on Tuesday afternoon, on the body of James Douglas, 27, moulder, who died on Saturday, the 30th December. The deceased was heard quarreling with a woman named Bebbington, who threw a mug at hira which hit him a violent blow on the left temple from which blood spurted. The man was treated at the in- firmary, and was subsequently removed to his home, where he died, according to the medical evidence, from erysipelas arising from the wound in the temple. There was some con- tradictory evidence as to the identity of the man at whom the woman was seen to direct the missile, and the coroner accordingly'adjourned the investigation for a week in order to obtain the evidence of a material witness. CHEsram FARMERS' CLUE.—The annual dinner of this club was held on Saturday at the Blossoms Hotel, Chester; Mr. John Roberts, of Saltney, presiding. Captain Cotton, the Conservative candidate for West Cheshire. responding to the toast of "The landed interest," expressed the hope that the club, which tended to keep up a good understand- ing between landlords and tenants and was the means of laying before the public important information on dairy farming and other subjects, would long continuo to exist. There could be no doubt that the efforts made of late in connection with the newly-established kindred organisation, the Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Association, had tended greatly to improve the sale and raise the price of Cheshire cheese by reason of the establishment of new fairs and new regula- tions for the fairs. He attributed success to two things, the support which had been given to the Dairy Associations by the landed interest in the country, and the determined efforts of the farmers themselves. Various other toasts were proposed, and the suggestion that the club and the Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Association should amalgamate was very warmly received. _

THE -MALAGASY ENVOYS AT CREWE WORICS.—The envoys from Madagascar and their suite arrived at Crewe station from Liverpool on Wednesday morning by the 9-15 train, and were received by the superintendent of the London and North-Western Railway (Mr. F. W. Webb) and the manager of the Crewe Works (Mr. C. Dick). Entering Mr. Webb's private saloon, they were taken to the steel works, where they watched with evident interest the interesting process connected with the manufacture of Bessemer steel. The rough ingots were shown and the several stages of manipu- lation were traced until the metal was brought to the rolling mill from the huge steam. hammer, and the steel rails were produced. The large new foundry recently erected at a cost of £23,000 was inspected, and several castings were made in the presence of the distinguished visitors.. The Envoys seemed astonished at the skill displayed in the various departments of the works, which are regarded as the finest of the kind in the world, and through their interpreter ex- pressed great satisfaction with their visit. Their Excellen- cies left in the afternoon for the Potteries. During their visit they were photographed by an official from the London and North-Western Railway Company's laboratory. CRESHIRE RIFLE ASSOCIATION.—The annual meeting of the Cheshire Rifle Association was held on Tuesday, at Chester Castle, the Duke of Westminster presiding. Among those present were Calonel Humbertson, Colonel France- Hayhurst, Colonel Marshall, Colonel Walker, Majors Fox, Johnsen and Dickson, Lieutenant S. Whalley, Messrs. A. Potts and J. E. Edwards. Colonel Marshall read the annual report, which referred with regret to the death of Lieut.- Colonel Vincent Ashfield King. It also alluded with satisfaction to the character of the competitions at the twenty•aecond prize meeting at Altcar. The total number of competitors who fired during the last two days of the meeting was 2,199, against 2,209 who competed in 1881, showing a decrease of 10, The entries for the three princi-

Ipal competitions were—Volunteers 264, agaitVk . ._ 507, all all-comers 377, against 407 in 1831; sweethean. •,tiott ; against 489 in 1881. The total receipts of the aStfoitu- • I were .£1,130 17s. 7d. ; total expenditure. £l,lBO 16s. 01.. I exceeding the receipts by over £49. The expenses for Ili ducting the meeting bad been £165 17s. id, against X _ 14s. 9d. for 1881. During the year 1882 the subscriptiou amounted to £297 13s. 6d., against 315 18s., or a decrrage of £lB ss.
EXTRAORDINARY ELOPEMENT OF A

PUBLICAN'S WIFE. Though many persons are inclined to question the salll3g of the poet Southey that— Three things a wise man will mot trust. The wind, the sunshine of an April dab And woman's plighted faith. 'le3 —au event which has recently occurred not many mid. from Earlestown and Newton is sufficient to show that wise man" cannot trust the "plighted faith " of woman. The affair has given rise to an almost elld170": amount of talk in the neighbourhood, and the local gessif,-, have not been slow to avail themselves of the opportuall thus afforded of spreading the scandal far wide. In brief, the facts are that a Cer,,Ted- well-known wrestler, residing within one ben:the miles of Ashton has joined "hand and heart' ce wife of a prominent publican residing within a like diStantbe of Golborne. The elopement has in it a tinge romantic. The publican had not been very long present premises before a robust and strong•looking took up his quarters at the public-house. He came b, tc with the avowed intention of training for a wrestling and for that purpose was accompanied by another Pe into whose hands he had placed himself. He went thrletli his accustomed exercises with all the care necessarn..oB evidently unknown to the landlord he was at the sarne exercising himself in winning the affections of the landl7b The wrestling match came off about a 111°-0 ago, and the individual in question succeededoei winning. Whether this in any way Wee ti the mind of the woman is not known, but it is a certlll_l_,i that she was not afterwards very long " halting betel; • two opinions." She at once threw in her lot with‘ter successful wrestler, It is now known that the parties wards met on several occasions, but not content with liPeo meeting her new "lord and master," the fickle and fait,hloo woman deserted her husband, and for home days Palo been residing with the wrestler at his house. Since by the wrestler has been unwell, and has had to be attend 0 a medical gentleman—though let the thought be far frfoo the mind that it is the fault of the woman. She to declared her innocence, but still is firm in her intention or remain true to her newly found partner. Whether.o not the lonely publican mourns or rejoices at the loss of 110 faithless wife is not known. Additional interest is takeso the elopement owing to the statement that the wonlee,io already two " husbands " living, and that if she,eigo through or has gone through a form of marriage wit", bet present protector, he will make the third " partner elbst bosom." She is evidently a believer in having 111011 t one string to her bow.

Though the actors were tas amateurs, and, in fact, made their first appearance °eel stage, it did not in the least detract from the excelleuctasi the performance, but on the contrary that fact only show° 00 more credit and honour is due to the performers. div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, klforde Chambers, on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage, the chairman, presided, an there were also present Dr. Booth, Messrs. W. H. Kershaw, E. Carey, T. Handley, D. Wright, J. Midwood, S. Sadler, T. Shuttleworth, R. Webster, J. E. Johnson, and J. T. Allen (clerk). PETITION TO DITIDII THE TOWN INTO WARDS. It was intimated to the Board that a deputation desired an interview, and it was decided to give the gentlemen who formed it a hearing. The deputation consisted of Mr. S. Owen, Mr. T. Sadler, and Mr. J. Beech.—The CHAIRMAN said he supposed they represented the Ratepayers' Associa- tion' but Mr. OWES replied that they were a deputation from the ratepayers who had signed the memorial, which he banded to the chairman. It read as follows "The Chairman, and Members of the Widnes Local Board. Gentlemen,—We, the undersigned ratepayers, resident within the district of Widnes Local Board, hereby request you to con- sider the advisability of dividing the town into wards as here- unto annexed, and that you do receive a depuatiou thereon : No. 1, Wbst Bank Ward: Commencing at the junction of Mersey-road, with the r.ver Mersey; thence along Mersey- read, Waterloo-road, 'Victoria-road, to the bridge of the Cheshire Lines Railway in a westerly direction to the Local Board boundary; thence along the Local Board boundary in a southerly direction to the river Mersey; thence along the river Mersey township t mndary to Mei-my-road. No. 2, or Mersey Ward: Commencing at the junction of Mersey-road, with the river Mersey, thence alo-ig Mersey-road, Waterloo-road, and Victoria-road, to the bridge of the Cheshire Lines Railway; thence along the Cheshire Lines Railway in an easterly direc- tion to the Local Board boundary; thence along the Local Board boundary in a southerly directim to the river Mersey; thenee along the river Mersey to Mersey-road. No. 3, or Appleton Ward; Cemrcencing at the bridge of the Cheshire Lines Railway, Alforde-st; thence r long Alforde-st,Widnes-road, Albert-road, and Peeihouse-lane, to the bridge of the Cheshire Lines Railway, thence in a westerly direction along the said railway to the township boundary; then turning in a southerly direction al mg the township boundary to the Cheshire Lines Railway, Widnes Branch, then along the mkt railway to the bridge, Alforde-street, including Newtown, Moss Bank, and Os-ow Wood. No. 4, or Lugsdale Ward: Commewing at the bridge of the Cheshire Lines Railway, Alforde-street, thence along Alfora-street, Widnes-road, Albert-road, anci Peelhouse- laue, terminating at the bridge of the Cheshire Lines Railway, then turning in an easterly direction along the said railway, to Ma township boundary, then turning in a southerly direction along the township boundary, termir -.Ong at the Cheshire Lines Railway, Widnes Branch, and then in a westerly direc- tion along the said railway, terminating at Alforde-street bridge. No. 5, or Farnworth Ward; Commencing at the township boundary, at the junction of the Cheshire Lines Bail way, thence a'ong the Cheshire Lines Railway in an easterly direction to the township boundary, to the junction of Onerdley and Bold; then in a north-easterly direction along the said township boundary to the junction of the township of Crouton; thence along the said boundary in a southerly direction to the Dittoa town..hip boundary, thence 'turning in a south-easterly directfon alor:: the said boundary, and terminating at the junction of the Cheshire Lines Rail- way." Then follow about 80 signatures.

—Mr. T. SADLER said the following towns, similar to Wid- nes, had divided their districts into wards :—Heywood, population 24,000; Farnworth, near Bolton, 20,000; North- wich, 13,000; Eccles, 20,000; Littleborough 12,000; Tod- morden, 23,000; Bacup, 24,000; Leigh, 32,000. The Board would see that, with one exception, Widnes had as large a population as any of these towns, and it seemed desirable to a good many ratepayers that Widnes should be divided into wards. They thought such a division would cheapen and simplify elections. It was quite probable that in some, if not all the wards, the ratepayers might agree in their choice of candidates at an election. Thus an election for the whole of the town would be obviated, and expense would be saved in that way. There were other reasons why the division should be made. They all knew that when Use Board was about to make improvements in the town there was money borrowed for the purpose, and the memo- rialists thought that if the town was represented in wards, each ward representative would see that the money would not be spent for any other purpose than that for which it was obtained.—CHAlßMAN: I suppose you are not making an accuation in that remark ?—Mr. SADLER: No, air. The memorialists were of opinion the town would be better repre- sented if divided into wards, and they hoped the Board would give the matter their consideration, and if possible carryout the wish of the ratepayers.—The CHAIRMiN said the Board would of course give so important a memorial as that their careful consideration, but they were not pre- pared to discuss the matter that day. The deputation would have to leave the matter wilh the Board for the present.— Mr. nenser.e.w wondered if there would be any saving in expense if only one ward was contested.—The CHAIRMAN observed that all the machinery would have to be put in motion.—Mr. T. SADLER: There would not be so much printing. If an extraordinary vacancy occurred on the Board, the election will only apply to one ward.—The CrternitAN said the Beard could fill such a vacancy up.— Mr. SADLER: The Board might not perhaps see their way to do so.—The CHAIRMAN : They cannot help themselves. —Mr. S. SADLER said a poll of 5,000 could not cost as much as a poll of 25,000.—Mr. T. SADLER (deputation) remarked that there were many ways in which the division of the town into wards would be agreeable to the ratepayers, and if there was not something beneficial in such a system the iowns he had mentioned would not have been anxious to adopt it.—The CHAIRMAN said the Board had on a previous occasion unofficially discussed the question, and at the con- clusion of the debate,tlae gentleman who suggested the altera- tion admitted that if the division were made the Boar I would be jumping from the frying pan into the fire—that the system would entail more expense instead of less. He did not really see himself that there was any advantage in election by the whole township.—Mr. OWEN said the township was now so large that no individual member could be cognisant of all the wants of each neighbourhood, and he thought that was a very strong reason with many people in favour of the di- vision of the town. For instance, West Bank would have three representatives, and the inhabitants of that neighbour- hood would require their representatives to see that they had improvements carried out commensurate with their rates and taxes. They wonld aloe know that the improvements were not centralised, and that they had a fair share of representa- tion.—Mr. CAREY remarlecd that there were two different ways of dividing the duties of the Local Board. In one, certain members devoted themselves to one neighbourhood, and in the other to one subject, such as highways, gas, water, tkc. The question was, which was the best way to do. The members of the Board at present devoted themselves to par- ticular subjects, and tried to do their beat for the whole township in regard to those particular subjects; but if each member devoted himself to a certain neighbourhood and endeavoured to learn the matters in con- nection with each department, he would be Jack of all trades and master of none, and he was afraid every department would be in a worse condition than it was now. —Mr. OWEN said the deputation were not going to argue the subject with the Board. They considered they had done their duty in bringing the memorial before the members, but they asked them to give the subject their sincere con- sideration.—A short discussion took place as to with whom rested the responsibility of taking action in the matter, and divided opinions were expressed, the chairman and Mr. Handley contending that the ratepeyers had the power be their own hands. After thanking the Board for their recep- tion, the deputation withdrew, and the ordinary business was proceeded with.

div.p: GA.S AND WATIAR COMMITTER

The ENGINEER reported that the water in stock December 20th, 1882, was 6,472,754 gallons. The rainfall for the mouth had been—per gas yard gauge 4,205 inches, per Pem Hill gauge 4,000 inches; mean, 4,102 inches. The water pumped during four weeks ending December 20th, 1812, bad been :—Stock's Well, 26,961,372 gals.; corresponding period, 1881, 24,930,714 gals.; increase per cent., 8.14. Netberley. 15,675,729 gals.; 1881, 13,913,453 gals.; increase, 12.66. Total, 42,637,101 gals.; 1181, 38,844,167 gals.; in- crease, 9 76. Water delivered, 41,501,693 gals.; 1881, 40,260,078 gals.; increase, 308. Gas made during four weeks ending December 20th, 1882, 8,333,090 cubic feet; corresponding period, 1881, 3,582,000 cubic feet ; decrease, 290. Gas delivered, 8,477,000 cubic feet; 1831, 8,557,000 cubic feet; decrease, .93. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 15.85 candles. With regard to the gas yard, Ditton-road, the conveyance of land exchanged between the Board and the Sheffield and Man- chester Railway Company was read. The Board received 6,030 square yards, in exchange for 1,190 square yards. The committee decided to defer consideration of the matter to next meeting,—The minutes were passed, on the motion of Mr. PANKHURST, seconded by Mr. WEBSTER.

div.head: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.-lINMADE STREETS.
div.p: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.-lINMADE STREETS.

At a meeting of this committee, held on the 28th Decem- ber, a letter was read from Mr. Shaw (L. and N.-W. R. Co.) respecting windows in the huts at the Appleton and Plumpton crossing, as suggested by Dr. Booth, and the clerk was instructed to ask if the suggestion would be car- ried out. A letter was read from the Newton Building Society, asking for levels in Bank-street. The surveyor was instructed to reply declining to comply with the request. Mr. A. Shelmerdine wrote respecting drain connections in Widnes-road. The surveyor was instructed to reply that the Board would not make branch drains, but would be glad to give a connection. The surveyor estimated the damage to roads caused through the carrying out of the Vyonwy water scheme at 145, and the clerk was instructed to apply to the Liverpool Corporation and to the contrac- tor for payment.—Mr. KERSHAW moved, and Mr. SADLER seconded the confirmation of the minutes.— ?tr. CARET asked foran explanation of the minutes respect- ing levels. He said the members of the Health Committee weut round a good many of the streets yesterday, and they would once more like to call the attention of the Highway Committee to the state of some of them such as Elizabeth- street: The Health Committee had on several former occasions asked the Highway Committee to take some measures, either to have the streets prved or to have them cleansed, but they were in their old condition. They again pressed upon the committee tlie!.t they pay some attention to the subject.—Mr. JOHNSON directed attention to the bad state of the footpath at Appleton yields.--Mr. KERSHAW, in reply, sail it was not in the province of the Board to give levels of unadopted streets, and if any owner put down a parapet, it was at his own risk. The Highway Committee were aware that there were numerous etreets in Widnes that required making, and he, as a property owner: should be glad for any street be had to be made; but be stio.uld not be prepared to pay the expense entailed in doing so 17 the pre- sent state of Widnes. If the committee had to tae action it this inatter they would have to obtain an irnprcvement in the office. They found it impossible to get anything done. At the present time the highways were neglected very much, and it secraed to him that the committee would not get attention given to them until they had a larger steff. "The committee were fast be- tween two." They did not see their way to progressing at present. With regard to the footpath at Appleton, it ought to be the duty of the surveyor to see that these things were attended to. He did not think it was the

province of the committee to see te every little thing, and if they paid the surveyor a salary they expected him to do the work.—Mr. CA.RET said he knew several instances where the parapets had had to be taken up because they were not put down at the proper level through the committee with- holding information.—The minutes were adopted.

div.head: HOSPITAL COM3IITTRE.
div.p: HOSPITAL COM3IITTRE.
The minutes of thii-c-Oin—n-liti;;;W-hiCl7-contained no item of public interest, were passed on the motion of Mr. SADLER, seconded by Mr. JOHNSON.
THE SEWERAGE SCHEME.-MR. IHRIIfAW ON ornau.Ls AND " NEW " MEMBERS.

At a meeting of this committee, held on the 3rd jest., the I resident Engineer's summary of report was read as fellows : "I beg to report that during the past month the weather , has caused considerable delay to the contractor, and there I has been very little work done. The ground has given way ! in two places and seriously damaged the culverts of the ! Marsh Brook in each case; these slips have been caused by the length of time the trench has been kept open. The 1 bottom of the brick sewer trench, which was fairly firm when the ground was first opened ont, has become very treacherous, and I consider that it will now be unsafe to trust to the slag foundation alone. I, therefore, recom- mend that in addition to the slag an artificial foundation be formed by boards, carried on sills, laid over the bottom i of the trench, and that this be continued until the bad ground is passe!, as provided for in the bill of quantities. I have called upon the contractor to keep the brickwork of the invert of the sewer dry during con- struction (as required by the specification) and he has stated his inability to do so : as this is a very important matter, I desire your instructions as to what course I am to take. The formation of the founda- tion in the bad ground for the brick sewer requires very close supervision, as it cannot afterwards be inspected, and there should be a man standing in the bottom watching the work during the whole time that the Contractor is engaged upon it. The amount that I have certified as due to the Contractor on the 20th ultimo is £176 12s. 6d.; this, with the sums already paid to Messrs. Kirk and Jeffreys, amount to ,£1,889 16s. 6d." Recommended, that the boards for artifi- cial foundation for sewer be used as per Engineer's report, and that when the contractor was prepared to proceed with the foundation a man be employed as suggested. —Mr. KERSHAW moved the adoption of the minutes with the exception of that relating to the em- ployment of a man. Mr. HANDLEY seconded. Mr. Minwoon, referring to the damaged culverts, said if the contractor was allowed to do the things described by the engineer, a large sum of money would be required to put the work right. e He thought they could do very well without employing another man to superintend the setting of the brick work if the surveyor, Mr. Higginson, "would go down when he should do," and assist Mr. Copeland to look after the work. They had too many men now for the work, and he should oppose at any time the employment of another man upon this work. He considered it was not going on at all—it was just creeping—and there was not sufficient work for the two surveyors they had upon the job at the present time.—Mr. CAREY said it was a great disadvantage to have these sub- jects discussed over again. He heard all the discussion at the committee meeting, and he came to the conclusion that for a short time, while the brick work was being put in, for reasons which the engineer clearly stated, a man ought to be employed. He thought it would be well in future if the engineer was asked to attend and explain particulars to the Board as well as the committee. He must demur strongly ' indeed from the statement that fir. Higginson had time to ! superintend the details of the sewer, while he was attending to the general surveyor's business for the township. It would be impossible for him to do so efficiently, and go over any detail work of the sewers. He could see the sewer in a general way, but he could not stop there whole days looking over brickwork of this kind without neglecting his duties in other parts of the township. He (Mr. Carey) should support the original recommendation of the oom- mittee, and he hoped the Board would not be so pound wise and penny foolish as not to see this work properly done.— Mr. KERSHAW said Mr. Johnson had observed that the staff was sufficient in the office. Heewas surprised at the Board, and also at the ratepayers of Widnes sitting down so quietly as they did and nay the salary of a surveyor who was simply in th 3 office without being of any use. He (the -surveyor) took no interest in the sewer, and it would not affect him if the bottom was covered with clog soles or anything else. And yet the members of the Board came there and saw this work being done. He was astonished at the thing, and when he thought that he had to pay his proportion towards sustaining a person in the office in that capacity, he felt strongly. He would either have a surveyor or he would have none at all. The Board were now trusting to the resident engineer, whose levels for aught they knew might be one sr two feet wrong. Had they a check upon that? He said they had not. Had they a check upon any of his work? He said they had not, and he asserted that they as ratepayers and representatives of the ratepayers did not do their duty in allowing this work to proceed in the way that it had. That was his feeling, and so strong was it that it was almost beyond expression if he could give vent to his feelings properly in the matter. To think that be must be joined along with them in the matter! He would that he could withdraw himself from them. As regarded the work, he distinctly said that he could not agree with Mr. Carey's remarks in reference to the surveyor. He (Mr. Kershaw) professed to have a know- ledge of the meter quite equal to anybody, and it was his opinion that one surVeyor was sufficient to carry out the whole of the work, with a proper man upon the job to superintend the construction of the works. It was never his intention that Mr. Copeland should carry out the de- tails of the work. Mr. Copeland, as far as he had gone, had had his heart and soul in the work, and he did his duty, until he had met with a few difficulties in the matter. There was no need to engage another man. One man was sufficient for the work now upon the job. They might disagree with him, but there was nothing to supervise. There had been nothing doing. There had not been one week's work done during the last two months, and they wanted another man to superintend that. It was not requisite. The expense of the false bottom would fall upon the contractor, but the Board must look with a broad view upon the matter. If the contractor could not carry out the contract, then it would fall upon the Board, who would have to finish the contract. Therefore the engineer must see that the work was properly constructed and attended to. If the trench was open too long it was the duty of the engineer to give the contractor notice to close it. At the last meeting of the committee the engineer stated that he had asked the surveyor to inspect the work. The Board had had no report from the surveyor. It seemetl to him that there were two sections at this Board, one which opposed the sewer outside and would not take any part,in it, and that was a number ef the new members. It was not very creditable to them to leave the committee as they had done that day. He must say that he did not think it was fair to the chairman to act as they had done in the matter. He only wished to do what was right. If he was wrong, tell him he was in the wrong place. He did not want to occupy the post of chairman, but he wanted their support in these matters when it was necessary. He could not say any- thing else. He would leave the matter to take care of itself.— Mr. SADLER said he thoroughly agreed with Mr. Midwood in his remarks, and that was his reason for taking no part in the discussion or for seconding the minutes. He con- sidered Mr. Kershaw's remarks a most rabid and personal attack on the members, and he for one protested against it. —The CHAIRMAN remarked that Mr. Kershaw appeared a little heated. It the committee were of opinion that Mr. Copeland was a non-efficient resident engineer, he should be called upon to resign. If the majority of the Board were of the same opinion, of coarse he would be obliged to resign. Then if Mr. Higginson was not efficient, he was a servant of the Board, and it was perfectly competent for the Board to call upon him to resign; but as long as they em- ployed two men they ought to trust them. If Mr. Cope- land was so inefficient he ought to have been called upon to resign before now considering the important work he had to do. If the Poard could not trust him to check the work, either appoint a man to check him or appoint another engineer altogether; but to simply get up at the Board, and say this man did not do this and did not do the other, and so on, was not real business; it did not mean anything. I t was simply a weak protest.—Mr. linasnew was understood o say that his words had been misrepresented.—The CHAIRMAN : You said there ought to be a check upon Mr. Copeland. You cannot trust Mr. Copeland.—Mr. KEnsnAw : I did not say so.—The CHAIR- MAN: That is the inference.—Mr. KERSHAW : I say there ought to be a check. If we keep a surveyor he ought to keep a check. I must protest against the construction you have put upon what I have said.—Mr. Menwoon said he should like to correct Mr. Kershaw in one statement. He told them that the extra expenses which were to be incurred now would not be borne by the Board. He (Mr. Midwood) was thoroughly given to understand at the committee that it would be borne by the Board. As a member of the com- mittee, he thought Mr. Kershaw had gone too far, and said sadly too much, for:he had done all in his power to assist him in every way. He must certainly protest against the statements made with regard to the new members.—Mr. HANDLEY said he felt rather surprised at the remarks made about the sewer. He thought the Board ought to take into consideration the weather there had been during the last six weeks. No doubt the contractor had had great difficulties to contend with. Before that meeting there had been noth- ing but praise for the way in which the resident engineer had done his work, and former reports from the committee had been that the work was progressing very satisfactorily. He thought the real explanation why the sewer had not gone on so well as formerly was the very wet weather.—Mr. KERSHAW, in reply to Mr. Midwood, remarked that the expense of providing wood fell upon the Board.—A MEM- BER made a remark to which Mr. Kershaw retorted that the "Committee won't work."—Mr. WRIGHT: The committee will work if the members are used right.—Mr. KERSHAW : Why don't you ask me to go if you won't support me.—Mr. SADLER : You don't want us to vote about a thing of which we know nothing.—Mr.KEUSHAW : I keep nothing from you. —Mr. WRIGHT: Mr. Kershaw says the members of the com- mittee, particularly the new members, won't work. Some ,tune age I went to a meeting of the Sewerage Committee, and gave. my opinion about a matter relating to the sewer. Perhaps my opinion is as good as any, and perhaps not so good as some. (Mr. Kershaw: Hear, hear.) Mr. Kershaw said: Gentlemen, I have not the least sympathy with NI right: lie has come to the Board thoroughly pre- judiced against the whole scheme." I have no sympathy with such language, and I say if he will use us properly we will work on the committee as well as any one. That is my reason for my Present action.—Several attempts were made to pass the minutes, bu Mr. Kerahaw persisted in making a statement. He said Mr. Wright made his language stronger than he used. (Mr. Wright I ought to know.) Unfortunately the last election

turned upon the sewerage, which Mr. Wright opposed. and in the committee en one occasion be said, Mr. Wright, you claim prejudice to this thing.—Mr. WRIGHT: It is all very well to put it in that way.--Mr. Kitassew entered in- to a defence of his conduct on the committee, and the minutes were put to the vote, and carried. Many of the members did not vote, the Chairman remarking that they were not advancing business by doing so.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 13, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 13, 1883.
HEALTH COMMITTEE.

The Medical Officer, in his report to this Committee, stated that during the month of December there had been 88 births and 50 deaths. The deaths included 17 children under ozie year, and 11 between one and five. Zymotic diseases caused seven deaths. The birth rate was 42.2 per 1,000, and the death rate 24 per 1,000. The receipts from the market last month were £l4 10s., being a decrease of £4 4s. 10d. in the corresponding period in 1831. Mr. CARRY moved, and Mr. PANIRITRST seconded, the adoption of the minutes.— Carried.
OENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE : ANN-STREET LEVEL CROSSING.

The railway company's proposal re Ann-street level cross- ing was considered by the committee on the 18th ult., and Messrs. Carey, Kershaw, and Surveyor deputed to see Mr. Worthington with plan, showing suggested alterations in approaches to the proposed bridge, and to call attention to the footpath from Ann-street East to Dock, which the Board will not consent to have stopped .—Lancashire Plateway Co. —The Surveyor and Clerk instructed to see the solicitors to the bill, with the following instructions, aid to report. Upton-lane (Grace's Forth to Crouton): The bridge to be 36 feet wide with gradients of net more than one in 10. Upton-lane (Upton to Birchfield) : The cutting for the rail- way to be so extended as not to raise the road, but if raised, the gradient to be not more than one in 50. Birchfield- road : The bridge to be 42 feet wide, and the level of road unaltered. Coroner's-lane : The bridge to be 30 feet wide and level of road unaltered. Footpaths: The following to have six feet wide wooden bridges: Rock Farm to Cronton ; Farnworth Church to Lunt's Heath, near to entrance to Cranshaw Hall; Farnworth Church to Lunt's Heath Farm; Farnworth Church to Lunt's Heath-lane, near to Coronation Bridge.— Mr. CAREY moved the confirmation of the minutes, and ex- plained the various plans which had been drawn up with regard to Ann-street level crossing. Mr. HANDLEY seconded the motion, which was carrizd.—After consider- able discussion the following resolution was passed : " That plan No. 1, which provides for an arm to Victoria- street, be adopted ; all the roads to Le 30 feet wide. The gradients from Ann-street East and Ann-street Wese to be lin 25, and to Victoria-street to be 1 in 20."—Th Board then rose, after sitting three hours.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

At the fortnightly meeting of this Authority, held, on Tuesday, at Dutton Workhouse, Mr. John Ashton presided, and there were also present—Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. Thomas Massey, Joseph Stokes, Thomai Andrew!, George hitlow, Peter Hall, William Jackson,. Thomas Darbyshire, Robert Ashton, William Pickering, W. Whitlow, John Highfield, Joseph Smith, E. A. Wallington, and John Weir.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICHR'S REPORT.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICHR'S REPORT.

The Medical Officer of Health reported that during the quarter ending December 31st, 1882, the registrar's returns recorded 60 births and 83 deaths in the three districts com- prised in the rural sanitary district of the Runcorn Union. Of the births 81 were males and 79 females; birth rate, 8•3 per 1,000. Of the deaths 43 were males and 40 females; death rate, 4.3 per 1,000; as against 191 births, birth rate, 1.3 per 1,000; and 56 deaths; death rate 2.9 per 1,000 dur- ing the corresponding quarter of 1831. Of the deaths 29 were under five years of age, 15 of these being under one year, and 54 were live years and upwards.

div.head: HAD MILT CASE.
div.p: THE HAD MILT CASE.

Mr. W. H Brook, town clerk of Warrington, attended with Mr. Norman, nuisance inspector for that town, to as- certain the intention of the Authority respecting the prosecu- tion of the person on whose premises diseased meat had been found at Walton Inferior. Mr. Brook said that a month ago Mr. Norman found a portion of a diseased cow in a slaughter- house at Walton Inferior, occupied by Mr. Maddock. It was necessary to prosecute in the interests of the public, and as a deterrent to other butchers. He (Mr. Brook) was instructed to attend the meeting of the Authority to express the opinion that it was desirable Mr. Norman should have power to in- spect the'districts just outside the borough, the two Waltons and Appleton, as they were just outside Warrington, and his Authority were in hopes that the Rural Authority would agree to that. It was not a question of salary; the object was to prevent the trade dealing in bad meat. With respect to the prosecution, he was bound te ask that this be carried on, as the same man had on a previous occasion, when dis- eased meat was found, faithfully promised that a similar case should not occur again.—After discussion, the CHAlR- mert said that at the last mating the matter was deferred for a month, ard he informed Mr. Brook that they were dis- posed to carry out the decision of last meeting, and deal with the matter at the next meeting of the Authority.

div.head: THIS SUTTON WATIlit SUPPLY,
div.p: THIS SUTTON WATIlit SUPPLY,

Mr. WALLINGTON asked the chairman if the proposad water scheme which Mr. Bancroft at the last meeting was instructed to prepare would affect the ratepayers of Sutton in any way.—The CLERK: I think it will, but the Authority have done nothing except ordered a report.—Mr. WAL- LINGTON intimated that he should most decidedly objct to it.

div.head: SOAP WORKS,
div.p: SOAP WORKS,

Messrs. Muir and Massie appeared before the Authority with a written application for the consent of the Authority to establish and carry on the business of soap boilers at their works at Frodsham Bridge. Several questions were put to Mr. Massie by different members of the Authority in refer- ence to the nature of their application and the• general character of the business, and after long consideration the Authority granted consent for the business of soap boilers only.—Mr. Massie thanked the Authority and retired.

div.head: DREADFUL WOUNDING CASE AT WIDNES.
div.p: DREADFUL WOUNDING CASE AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, a farmer named William Percy, whd resides at Gorsey-lane, Moss Bank, Widnes, was brought up in cus- tody charged with unlawfully wounding his wife Margaret on the previous Saturday, with intent to do her grievous bodily harm. Mrs. Percy, who was unconscious; through the illusage she had received, did not appear. From the evi- dence it seemed that the prisoner, who is a man of intemper- ate habits, left home about four o'clock on Saturday after- noon, and returned in a state of intoxication about 11 o'clock the same evening. A warrel took place between the pri- soner and his wife, the former seizing a stick, with which he savagely struck the latter. Margaret Roach, a domestic servant in the prisoner's employ, interfered, when the pri- soner pushed her out of the room and bolted the door. She stood outside for some time, and could hear the quarrel, but at length she left the house and slept in the shippon. About eight o'clock tLe following morning, on entering the kitchen, she found her mistress lying unconscious on the floor. Blood besmeared her face and forehead, and there was every ap- pearance of a struggle having taken place.--In cross-exam- ination by Inspector Barnett, Roach said the prisoner had not abused her mistress before "as she knew of." He had threatened her when drunk; never when sober.—Dr. Cooper said he was called in to see Mrs. Percy. He:found a small cut on the side of the face. The cut was like a puncture, such as might have been caused by the knob of a stick, but it Was not of a serious nature. She was also bruised on the right arm. She was insensible when he was called in, and remained so all Sunday. She I was in a critical state, suffering from concussion of the brain—By the Clerk: It had been brought about by a blow or a fall. He did not think it likely that falling from the bed would give her concussion of the brain.—On the application of Inspector Barnett the prisoner was remanded until Wednesday.—The prisoner said he did not care if they remanded him for seven years; but he denied that he had used a stick to his wife.—The prisoner was again brought before the magistrates on Wednesday, but his wife being still unconscious, he was remanded for a further three days. On inquiry, yesterday, our representative was informed that Mrs. Percy's condition showed no signs of improve- ment. She is still unconscious, and her recovery is, to a great extent, problematical. The prisoner will be again brought before the magistrates to-day, but will be remanded.

PENKETH WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIA- TION.—The members of the above class met on Wednesday erening, under the presidency of Mr. Colin Cooke. An essay on "War," by Mr. Charles Hughes, was read by Mr. C. Parker, in the absence of Mr. Hughes through illness, and it was highly commended. The following members took part in a very animated discussion which followed : Messrs. R. Garnett, A. White, W. Craven, J. Watson, B. Hobson, and C. Parker, and Mrs. R. Garnett, Mrs. Parker; Miss Helen Garnett, &c. The meeting was bigbly appre- ciated.

div.head: A. MAN SUFFOCATED AT WIDNES.
div.p: A. MAN SUFFOCATED AT WIDNES.

Yesterday, Mr. T. W. Barker, the county coroner, held art inquest at the George Inn, Widnes, upon the body of Thomas Carey, 27 years of age, a labourer at Messrs. Hutchinson's Chemical Works, who was found dead there, on Wednesday morning. The deceased, wh9 lived in nu. street, Widnes, bad been employed at the works about 14 months, and he seemed to be a man who possessed good health, never having, his sister Catherine McCue stated, been attended by a doctor in his life. Shortly after three o'clock, on Wednesday morning, the deceased went behind the furnace where he was working to obey a call of nature, although proper provision was made for the workmen in the shape of closets About ten minutes afterwards he was found lying across the manhole of a sewer in a dying state.

The Coroner, in opening the inquiry, said be understood there was a great deal of gas emanated from the manhole of the sewer, and it might be that the deceased had been overcome by it, and suffocated. The doctor had examined the man, but so far as he could judge from external appearances he was unable to say what was the cause of death, :to he (the coroner) thought it would be more satisfactory if a :post mortem examination was made. He had, therefore, directed the doctor to make one, so that the jury might be satisfied as to the cause of death— whether it resulted from natural causes or the poisonous nature of the gas.
Catherine McCue, living at Noithwich, said the deceased was her brother. She last saw him alive on Christmas Day. He was then in good health. _

John Morrissi, labourer at Messrs. Hutchinson's works, said he had never felt any gas coming from the man-hole. The death of the deceased might have been caused by gas, and it might not. He found the deceased lying on his back on the man-hole, with his head near the drainer. There was not then a very strong smell of gas, but it might have been more powerful when the deceased went there. The body of the deceased was removed, and the police and a doctor sent for, but the services of the latter were of no avail. There was no row or fighting in the works. The deceased had never complained of illness. The gas did not smell strong enough to kill anybody. . . . _

Mi: Kyle, the engineer to the firm, produced plans of the place, vthich he explained. A juryman asked if there might be a sudden rush of gas from the manhole ? Mr. Kyle replied that that was impossible. John Marr, labourer, also gave evidence. He said the deceased took drink, and on the night in question he had been out for liquor, but witness did not know how much he had had. He did not bear the deceased call for help. The man who carried him from the place where he died com- plained that the gas was heavy, and did not succeed in their first attempt to bring him away. A juryman remarked that Chat showed that the deceased died through the gas.

Morrissy was re-called, and in reply to the Coroner, he said that any difficulty experienced in removing the de- ceased was owing to the narrowness of the place where he was, and not to the gas. In answer to the Coroner, Mr. Kyle said the men were prohibited from going to the place Under a fine of 55., not on account of the gas, but in the interests of decency. Dr. Cooper deposed that he had made a post mortem ex- amination of the body of the deceased. The probable cause of death was gas poisoning, apparently by sulphuretted hydrogen. He had evidently received a strong dose and died suddenly. The Coroner, in summing up, said if no provision for the purpose mentioned had been made, and the man had gone to the manhole with the- knowledge and sanction of the management the case would have assumed a very different aspect to what it did; but he was glad to find that reason- able provision had been made, and the only verdict which could be returned was one of accidental death.
'hA verdict according to the coroner's suggestion was re- corded.

div.head: PROPOSED ACCIDENT HOSPITAL FOR RUNCORN.
div.p: PROPOSED ACCIDENT HOSPITAL FOR RUNCORN.

"To consider the necessity for the establishment of an Accident Hospital for Runcorn and neighbourhood," a meet- ing was held in the Commissionerarßoard-room, on Wednes- day afternoon. The gathering had been convened by circulars issued by Dr. Steele, who presided, and amongst those present were the Revs. Canon Barclay, M.A., X. Lockwood (vicar of Haltoa), E. Williams (Calvinistic Methodist), Messrs. J. Taylor, J. Meadowcroft, W. Guest,. J. W. Lightburn, and W. Brookes.—The CHAIRMAN said he had long felt that it was not creditable that a town like s Runcorn with 15,000 inhabitants had no place where a man seriously injured in the works or on the railway could be conveyed to receive surgical aid. It was cruel to take him all the distance to Liverpool or Chester, as the case might be. A month since he received a letter from Mr. Clarke Aspinall, city coroner for Liverpool, which gave him (the chairman) a good opportunity of bringing the subject forward, and he had done so. He need hardly say that the Commissioners had no power to levy a rate for the main- tenance of an Accident Hospital. Whatever was dens must be done by donations and subscriptions. He supposed that , Mr. Aspinall wrote to him as the chairman of the Commis-- I sioners under , the impression that the Board could take 'action. The Commissioners were building a hospital, but it Was for infectious diseases, and not for accidents. He thought if the different ministers in the town were tc hold a "Hospital Sunday" once a year a good sum of money might be raised. He saw in that day's paper that they received £lO,OOO in Liverpool on Hospital Sunday, and some years age they raised even a larger sum than that. II they were to rent a house, and engage a nurse, the hospital so started might grow by degrees into something more pretentious. Fortunately there were very few accidents in Runcorn. It would not be advisable to start the hospital as a dispensary where cut fingers and cut heads would be bandaged,. but maintain it ouly for serious accideats, so that men need not be sent to Liverpool.—The Rev. Canon BARCLAY said he had much pleasure in moving that "It is expedient that measures be taken for establishing an Accident Hospital." —The Rev. JNO. LOCKWOOD second:A.—The motion was carried. The CHAIRMAN said he had received a letter from Mr. John Brundrit-expressing his regret at being un- able to be present, and also the following communication: —.‘ Board-room, Ruston Station, London, January 6th, 1883.—Dear Sir,—l have received your letter of yesterday, and will bring it under the consideration of my colleagues- at our next meeting. Like the Runcorn Commissioners, I. am afraid we have no power to apply our funds to the erection of hospitals, and in the past we have always de- clined to do so. We shall be happy, however, to do for Runcorn what we do for other places, and to make an an- nual contribution towards the expenses of any institution which may be started, provided our servants avail themselves of its advantages to any reasonable extent. Thus far we can support the moverntat, but I fear we cannot go further.—l am, yours faithfully, RICHARD MOON.—D. Mr. Steele, Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, Runcorn."— Mr. TAYLOR asked what the feeling in the town was with regard to the stbject, and the CHAIRMAN replied that all those with whom ha had conferred were quite in favour of establishing a hospital. This was not a very encouraging commencement, but sometimes great things were done without much encouragement. He thought they could get a suitable place for £2oa year, and 4150 a year would be ample to meet the expenses.—Mr. LIGHTBURN said there was no. doubt-that an institution of this kind was needed.—ln reply to an inquiry as to what the works would be inclined to do in the matter, the CHAIRMAN said the firm with which he was connected would be very glad to subscribe, and he had not the leastdoubt but that the other works would do the saMe.—Mr. MEADOWCROFT said he should like for his own guidance, some particulars as to the lines upon which the hospital would be founded and the way in which it would work, and so forth. Perhaps, if that information was given, it would lead persons to bestir themselves. He was positively in the dark as to the modes of management and the expense.—The CHAIRMAN said he had not gone into the matter deeply himself, and he suggested that a committee should be formed.—The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD said if that meeting was a fair representation of the feeling of Runcorn it was very apathetic. He men- tioned an accident where a man's life might have been saved had there been a hospital at Runcorn. The Rev. Casols BARCLAY remarked that there was sufficient philanthropy in Runcorn to establish one. The Cl:saunas said the meeting cAled with reference to Tarporley Show was much worse than the present one, but they set to work,and by de- grees raised about £BO. -- Mr. LIGHTBURN was of opinion that a hospital could be maintained for £lOO. a year, and he proposed that a committee, consisting of the Revs. Canon Barclay, J. Lackwood. E. Williams, Dr. Steele, Messrs. Meadowcroft, Taylor' Guest, and himself,- with power to add to their number, be appointed to consider the possibility of forming and sustaining a hospital. Mr. TAYLOR seconded the motion, which ° was carried, and the meeting separated.

WOIMINGMEN'S MISSION MUTUAL IDIPIIOVESIENT SOCIETY.—Last Saturday evening an essay was read by Mr. Williamson on "Which has done most good, the pulpit or the Press." The essay was rather short, but full of in- formation. The essayist upheld the opinion that the pulpit had done the most good. Mr. F. Williams said he could not agree with the essayist in saying that the pulpit had done most good. The Press, he said, far exceeded the pulpit by the distribution of the Word of God, not only i-n our own land, but in foreign countries among the beatban. Mr. J. Monks supported Mr. Williams, and spoke of the great good done by the British and Foreign Bible Society in send- ing bibles and tracts to the inhabitants of Madagascar and the South Sea Islands. Messrs. Long, Tanner, Hill, Dawber, and Ashley also took an active pert in the- debate. The time for closing being up, and no definite conclusion having been come to, it was decide d to finish the subject on the following Saturday. The meeting then terminated.

THIS SALTATION ARMY AT PENKETIa. —The Salvation Army Corps, No. 299. from Widnes, paid a visit to Penketh, on Saturday last. Headed by their large banner, bearing the words "Speed on the Widnes Corps, No. 299," and by their brass band, a large procession of "soldiers" marched through the "%Map to the plot of ground in front of Mr. W. Hankinson's. After about half an hour spent in talking, "firing volleys," and prayer, they fell in and marched to Penketh Tannery, where they exercised themselves in a room provided by Mr. and Mrs. Parker. The corps, which was under the command of Captain Elms and his wife, departed about six o'clock, but before they left refreshments were provided for the "solders" by Mr. and Mrs. Parker, who take great interest Le e Army, All passed off quietly.

He was amongst those who first entered Metz after its fall, and he gave ma- terial assistance in the hospital te the sick and wounded. div.head: VISIT OF MR. BROAINIURST, M.P., TO WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE VISIT OF MR. BROAINIURST, M.P., TO WARRINGTON.

It is announced that Mr. H. Broadhurst, the member for Stoke-upon-Trent, will be present at the meeting in the -Public Hall, on Thursday, January 25th, when J. G. McMinnies, Esq., the member for Warrington, is to address his constituents and the following notice of Mr. Broadhurst, taken from a religions journal, will; we doubt not, be read with interest in view of his approaching visit :—‘4 Mr. Henry Broadhurst, member for Stoke-upon-Trent, was born on April 13th, 1840, at Littlemore, Oxfordshire, being the youngest son of Thomas and Sarah Broadhurst. As is gene- rally known, the surroundings of his early life were humble, his parents being members of the working class, and being 'dependent upon their own exertions for the maintenance of themselves and their children. After a very brief stay at school, Henry at an early age commenced to learn the art of a stonemason, and at 17 he received journeyman's wages. He did his work in an, intelligent, 26aiOUS manner, and immediately earned the esteem of his employers and fellow labourers. At about this time— November, 1857—he became a member of the Masons' Society, and has been an active worker ever since. It has been stated that he held a paid office, but this is incorrect, as-the posts occupied by him were invariably honorary. In the following year Mr. Broadhurst left Oxfordshire for Lon- don, and obtained employment in the firm of Myers and Son. For the next few years he worked in London and in different parts of the country, In 1860 he took to himself a.wife in the city of Norwich, r id five years later finally settled in London. From this period Mr. Broadhurst's career as a public man must be said to have really com- menced. He took an active part in the reform agitation then going on in the metropolis, and has since been. con- gaudy engaged in political and social movements. Not- withstanding the labour involved in this political career, Mr. Broadhurst continued a regular worker at his trade and was engaged on some of the largest buildings in London, including the present Houses of Parliament. in 1872 pres- sure of other duties rendered necessary his retirement from the mechanical work as a mason, and as a mark of esteem he was presented with a valuable watch and chain, Mrs. Broadhurst at the same time receiving a handsome present of plate. For ten years Mr. Broadhurst has represented the Masons' Society at the annual Trades Union Congress, and for the last five years he has, as secretary of the Parliamen- tary Committee, been in almost daily attendance at West- minster Hall. His advice has been sought on matters of importance in relation to the law of master and servant, and as an evidence of the esteem in which he is held it may be mentioned that he was a member of the Eastern Question Association during the Russo-Turkish war, his colleagues including many of the most eminent men,of the present day. Mr. Broadhurst was not the man to go beg- ging for a seat in the House, although many politicians- noted his abilities, and. foresaw what an immense acquisi- tion he would be to the small and feeble labour represen:a- lion in that assembly. It was left to the borough of Stoke- on-Trent to confer on the community the. benefit of Mr. Broadhurst's labours as a • member of Parliament.. The Liberal Council were determined to wrest the seats from the Tory and nondescript members who held them, and Messrs. Melly and Woodall were unanimously selected by that body as the Liberal candidates for the borough. Pressure of business engagements compelled Mr. Melly to retire from the field, and several names were proposed to the Council to fill his place. Among these was that of Mr. Brosdhurst. The nomination was favourably received by the labour section, and after the reading of Mr. Broadhtirst'e letter in reply to the chairman there was a strong feeling in- his favour among the whole of the members. At the meeting at which the proposed candidate expounded his viewathere 'was a crowded attendance, and the exhaustive and manly speech he then made won the heart of every member, and he was, with singular unanimity and cordiality, accepted as a candidate to run with Mr. Woodall. The result of that candidature is well known, and Mr. Broadhurst is now a member of the House of Commons. It was known that on the first opportunity the new member would justify the pro- phecies which had been freely made with regard to his abilities. He not only did so, but he astonished both friend and foe alike when he rose in his place to criticise the Em- ployers' Liability Bill. His maiden speech was most successful, and at its close he received the congratulations of the Premier and many members on both sides of the House. Commenting on:the event a Manchester contempo- rary said :—' The most distinct success attained by any new member this session is certainly of Mr. Broadhurst, member for Stoke, and secretary to the Parliamentary Committee of the Trade Union Congress. Mr. Broadhurst, on the second reading of the Employers' Liability Bill, spoke as a working man's representative, and spoke like a working man, but with rare force and energy, and with full and well- marshalled information. The arrangement of a speech and the judgment displayed as to the value and, the sequence of the strongest points of an address are thought to be among the severest tests of Parliamentary ability, and in this respect Mr. Broadhurst's success was genuine. Mr. Broad- hurst might, it is said by his friends, have made a personal point, which he did not. He alluded to the fact that he had been a working stonemason, but be might have told the House that he helped to lay some of the stones of that build- ing wherein the Parliament, of which_ be is now a member who will certainly be heard with attention, assembles.' It is interesting to note that prior to delivering the speech referred to, Mr. Broadhurst paid a visit to his mother, who 1 is in her eightieth year, and on his return from Oxfordshire ' he bad to receive several deputations on the question of the bill. On Friday Mr. Broadhurst rose shortly after mid-. 'night during the discussion on the proposed monument to , the Prince Imperial. Several members of the House at the same moment attempted to catch the Speaker's eye,' but were greeted with loud shouts of 'Broadhurst,' and they accordingly gave way. Mr. Broadhurst then made a short but telling speech against the erection, and receivad the hearty congratulations and thanks of the Premier and many members of both sides of the House. There is about Mr. Broadhurst's manner a ring of sincerity that gannet be questio.led. His utterance is deliberate and distinct, con- veying the impression that every word is weighed, and it is impassible fo2 his bitterest opponent to treat his remarks with contempt.- His political views are in general those of the Liberal party, and he persistently advocates an equit- able distribution of land, and a more just levying of the land tax. Mr. Broadhurst attends the Wesleyan chapel on Brixton Rise, and advocates complete religious liberty. The statement that ho is an atheist, or that he is in any way a supporter of Mr. Bradlaugh is utterly untrue." We notice that Mr. Broadhurst, along vrith Mr. H. B. Sheridan, M.P., and Mr. G. W. Hastings, M.P., have just been invited to investigate the subject of female labour in the Black Country. The question was discussed at the last meeting of the South Staffordshire and East Worcestershire Trades Council, and it was made abundantly clear that it is- high time something was done. One of the speakers stated that he had seen women carrying i hundredweight of iron on their shoulders, and in one instance a NWIRan wilecAing from two to three hvnclredwelght of ctain:

div.head: LANCASHIRE PLA.TEWAY SCHEME. THE BILL WITHDRAWN.
div.p: THE LANCASHIRE PLA.TEWAY SCHEME. THE BILL WITHDRAWN.

The Manchester Examiner and Times announces that the promoters of the Lancashire Plateway Scheme have decided to withdraw their Bill for the coming session. The secretaries to the company, Messrs. Thornley and Cameron, solicitors, Liverpool, have issued a circular to subscribers to the guarantee fund, in which they say: " We beg to inform you that the promoters, feeling that the interests of the scheme would be better 9erved by withdrawing the Bill for this session, have decided to do so, in order that they may bring it forward next year more perfected."

div.head: BAD MEAT AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: BAD MEAT AT WARRINGTON.

At Warrington Borough Court, on, Monday, before the Mayor, Major Cartwright, and Mr. X. Fakelough, John Mynekvme was summoned'fOr having, on the Ist January, deposited on his premises for the purpose of preparation for sale for the food of man 51 pigs plucks', the same being unfit for food.—Mr. W. H. Brook- (Town, Clerk) appeared to prosecute, and Mr. Cottingham (barrister) defended.— Mr. Brook said the defendant was a butcher, carrying on business in Priestley-street, and occupied a slaughter-house off Froghall-lane. On Monday,. the let inst., Inspector Norman visited the slaughter-house at halfepast 10 in the morning, and found there were 51 pigs' plucks which were in a condition totally unfit, as he considered, for human food. He removed them to the Town Hall, where they were inspected by Mr. Litton and by fa ordered to be destroyed. He (the Town Clerk) had reason to believe that the defence which would be set up was-that they wore not intended for human food. The charge was that they were deposited in this place for the purpose of preparation for sale, and were intended for the food of man. He thought there weuld be no dispute as to- the meat being bad, and the whole question would turn on whether or not they were intended for the food of man. The Bench would hear that these plucks came on the premises on Thursday night or Friday morning, and they continued there until they, were seized on Monday. It was not for him to prove that the meat was intended for the food of man; the defendant mast prove ; that was not the case; and he could only leave the Bench ' to draw their own conclusions from the fact that on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday this meat was allowed to be on the place, which was no less an offence against the law. If the defendant did not intend them for food it was an extraor- dinary thing that he placed himself in the clutches of the law. If the defendant did not intend to use them, be, of course, could not ask for that penalty which he should ask for if the Bench thought they were intended for food. It was absolutely necessary this sort of thing should he put a stop to. This was not the first time defendant had been be- fore the court, and if the Bench thought defendant was guilty he must ask them to inflict that penalty;. but, on the other hand, if he was not guilty, he was entitled to be ac- quitted —lnspector Norman deposed to visiting defendant's premises on New Year's day, and finding in the slaughter-house 51 pigs' plucks hanging up in the usual way. He examined them, and found soma wero highly deeomposed, and others decomposed to a considerable ex- tent. He considered they were all unfit for human food. He enquired for defendant, but he was not at homer He seized the plucks and took them to the Town Hall, where they were examined by the medical officer of health, who oertified that they were unfit for human food, and they were inspected by Captain Litton, J.P., who gave an order for them to be de- stroyed. Next morning defendant came to his office and said "You seized these plucks, then? He (witness) re- plied "Yes, and very properly so." Defendant pulled a letter out of his pocket, and said he received, the plucks on Saturday or Friday—he could not tell which—but he in- tended to send them back. He told defendant he had nothing to do with the letten—Cross-examined : Defendant did not tell him that he was keeping the plucks for him to see. He saw a skip ontside which contained the plucks—Mr. Cutting- ham said he did not dispute the propriety of the seizure at all. The plucks were not fit for food, and they were not in the state he expected them to be. lie admitted they were an improper consignment so far as the condition of the plucke were concerned, but defendant had no, intention to sell them. In reply to Mr. Fairclough. Inspector Norman said the plucks had gone bed.—This was the case for the prosecution.--Mr. Coifing- ham, in addressing the Bench, said the question was a very serious one in regard to the defendant, who is a butcher very well known in the town. The Bench would, tof course, understand that in all trades there was considerable rivalry, but that rivaley was considerably increased through the defendant beinga native of another couotry, and pushing a successful trade In Warrington for a considerable time. In this instance the meat was seized properly enough, and was unquestionable, in a condition unfit to bs offered for sale. Defendant sold the plucks on commission for some dealers in Ireland, and a person named Riley consigned to him these particular plucks, oral upon his receiving them he found they were not in a proper condition. He therefore determined to send them back or to have them destroyed, but preparatory to doing that he thought it necessary to detain them and keep them on his premises until such tim3 as the inspector came to see them, so as. to have the inspee- tor's certificate as against the consignor for his consignment, Thereupon he told 1::s man to take possession of the plucks and on no account to dispose of thorn. This occurred, during Chrietrnas week. Defendant had to go away from home, and he left his. premises in the care Of this man. While he was absent the inspector visited the premises and found the plucks, •ezich had not improved in condition from the time they arrived. He contended the pluseks were not intended for food,, and that defendant was going to return than—Annie Walker, housekeeper for de- fendant, said she received the hamper of plucks. Defen- dant left home eaely, and was, away each day up,to Twee- day. He slept at home every night, but she never men- tioned the plucks to him.—Mtchael Hynes, carter, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany, deposed to deliverireeetbe plucks on the fleth Decem- 'bee about 3-3 C p.m.—Christlan Smith, foreman butcher for defendant, said his employer saw the plucks on Friday night, and gave him orders net to remove them or destroy them until someone had seen them. They were never touched afterwards. Nothing was done in the way of pre- paring them for sale. None of the plucks had been sold or 1 offered for-sale. If they bad been fit for sale they would have beca sold on Sottertlay.—Cross-examined We only received onei hamper that week. They sold the plucks wholesale, and they wore sent out direct from the slaughter-house. -- Richard Wood goods agent for the London and North-Western Railway, stated, that at the beginning of December defendant refused a coosigninenb of plucks because they were in a bad state. Defendant had a consignment once a waek.—The:defend- dant then gave evidence. He said when he saw the plucks they werain a state unfit for human feed, and he at once told his man what the latter had told the Bench. If he had been at home he would have examined the goods before he signed for them, and pal Bs. 44. carriage. If he had received them and found them bad he would have at once got a certificate and destroyed them. If they had been in- tended for sale they would have been sold on Friday night or Saturday morning at the latest, as there was a very good demand for them.---In reply to the Mayor, delendant stated that the consign.ors paid the carriage. Ho did not make " savoury duds " from pigs plucks. They were made from liver.—P.S. Bowen was then called and he said he had been a butcher all his life prior to joining the police force. ISavoury ducks were made from cow's liver. It would not pay to makv them out of pigs ptv.ks.—.The 13ench retired,

rers are fairly employed, and in Botanies demand is good • At Huddersfield low mitings are in brisk demand, other branches quiet. At Nottingham the hosiery trade has slightly improved, and manufacturers are generally well employed on spring orders.
